nodes.characterTrait_source: Enki and Ninhursag (ETCSL 1.1.1)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Mother-goddess; matronly. Her omega-shaped emblem appears on kudurrus.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard Mesopotamian iconography; kudurru emblem

nodes.name: Nanna
nodes.domain: the moon, time-reckoning, dreams, divination via lunar omens, kingship of Ur, the lunar cycle
nodes.domain_source: Enlil and Ninlil (ETCSL 1.2.1) — birth and theogony; Nanna's Journey to Nippur (ETCSL 1.5.1); Sumerian Nanna hymns (ETCSL 4.13); the Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur
nodes.object: crescent boat, lapis-lazuli beard, herder's staff
nodes.object_source: Standard iconography; Sumerian Nanna hymns; Ur III period royal art
nodes.animals_source: Standard iconography (Nanna as "frisky calf of Enlil"); Sumerian Nanna hymns
nodes.significantEvent: Firstborn son of Enlil and Ninlil (in the netherworld, per ETCSL 1.2.1). Husband of Ningal. Father of Inanna and Utu. Patron god of Ur. In Nanna's Journey to Nippur (ETCSL 1.5.1), travels by reed-boat from Ur to Nippur to receive blessings from his father Enlil.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Enlil and Ninlil (ETCSL 1.2.1); Nanna's Journey to Nippur (ETCSL 1.5.1); Sumerian Nanna hymns (ETCSL 4.13); Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur
nodes.characterTrait_source: Sumerian Nanna hymns (ETCSL 4.13); Nanna's Journey to Nippur (ETCSL 1.5.1); Enlil and Ninlil (ETCSL 1.2.1)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Bearded god with the lapis-lazuli beard, crescent moon above or as horns; sails the celestial reed-boat. Patron of Ur, his great ziggurat at Ur.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Sumerian Nanna hymns; Ur III royal art (Stele of Ur-Nammu); standard iconography
nodes.birthCircumstances: Firstborn son of Enlil and Ninlil, born in the netherworld (Enlil and Ninlil, ETCSL 1.2.1).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Enlil and Ninlil (ETCSL 1.2.1) lines 64-150
nodes.eventTypes_source: Enlil and Ninlil (ETCSL 1.2.1); Nanna's Journey to Nippur (ETCSL 1.5.1); Sumerian Nanna hymns
nodes.birthTypes_source: Enlil and Ninlil (ETCSL 1.2.1)

nodes.name: Ningal
nodes.domain: reed marshes, the moon (as consort), motherhood; the Akkadian Nikkal
nodes.domain_source: Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur (Ningal as the lamenting goddess of Ur); Asher-Greve & Westenholz 2013 Goddesses in Context p. 57
nodes.significantEvent: Wife of Nanna. Mother of Inanna and Utu. In the Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur, weeps for her ruined city. Daughter of Ningikuga and Enki (per Asher-Greve & Westenholz reconstruction).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur (ETCSL 2.2.2); Asher-Greve & Westenholz 2013
nodes.object_source: Sumerian Ningal hymns; the Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur
nodes.characterTrait_source: Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur (ETCSL 2.2.2); Sumerian Nanna-Ningal cycle
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Goddess of the reed marshes and consort of Nanna; standard Sumerian goddess iconography.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Sumerian iconography; Lamentation over Ur
nodes.eventTypes_source: Sumerian Nanna-Ningal cycle; Lamentation over Ur
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Ningikuga and Enki (per Asher-Greve & Westenholz 2013).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Asher-Greve & Westenholz 2013, Goddesses in Context p. 57
nodes.birthTypes_source: Asher-Greve & Westenholz 2013

nodes.name: Utu
nodes.domain: the sun, justice, oath, illumination of hidden truths, the rising-up over Mount Mashu, judge of the netherworld in his nightly transit, defender of travellers
nodes.domain_source: Codex Hammurabi prologue (Shamash as guardian of justice); Hymn to Shamash (BWL Lambert pp. 121-138); Gilgamesh III (Utu as patron of Gilgamesh's expedition); Sumerian Utu hymns; Inanna's Descent (ETCSL 1.4.1) — Utu raises Dumuzi up as a snake to escape
nodes.object: saw-toothed weapon (the šaššāru), solar disc, beard of lapis lazuli
nodes.object_source: Standard Utu/Shamash iconography; the saw-toothed weapon at his rising appears on Akkadian-period seals and reliefs
nodes.significantEvent: Son of Nanna and Ningal. Brother of Inanna. God of justice and the sun. Patron of kings (especially Gilgamesh in the Cedar Forest expedition, *Gilgamesh* III). In Inanna's Descent answers her cry by raising Dumuzi up (transformed into a snake) so he can flee the demons. In the Hymn to Shamash, judges all and illuminates evil in the heart.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Codex Hammurabi prologue; Hymn to Shamash (BWL pp. 121-138); Gilgamesh III; Inanna's Descent (ETCSL 1.4.1); Sumerian Utu hymns
nodes.characterTrait: just, illuminating, oath-keeper, traveller-protector, patron of kings
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hymn to Shamash (BWL Lambert pp. 121-138); Codex Hammurabi prologue and epilogue; Sumerian Utu hymns
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Bearded god rising over the eastern mountains at dawn; saw-toothed weapon (the šaššāru) at his shoulder; lapis-lazuli beard; solar disc and rays. Standard Akkadian-period seal type: god rising between the twin peaks of Mount Mashu.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Akkadian-period cylinder seals (the sun-rising type); Hymn to Shamash; Standard iconography on kudurrus
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Nanna and Ningal; brother of Inanna.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Standard Sumerian theology; ORACC AMGG entry on Nanna
nodes.eventTypes_source: Codex Hammurabi; Hymn to Shamash; Gilgamesh III; Inanna's Descent
nodes.birthTypes_source: Standard Sumerian theology; ORACC AMGG entry on Nanna

nodes.name: Ereshkigal
nodes.domain: the netherworld (Kur, Kigallu), death, the binding of the dead, sovereignty over the great below
nodes.domain_source: Inanna's Descent (ETCSL 1.4.1); Ishtar's Descent (Akkadian); Nergal and Ereshkigal (the Sultantepe and Amarna versions, in Foster Before the Muses pp. 506-524)
nodes.object: the lapis-lazuli measuring rod and line; the seven Anunna who sit in judgement before her
nodes.object_source: Inanna's Descent (ETCSL 1.4.1) lines 167-180
nodes.significantEvent: Queen of the Kur, the netherworld. In Inanna's Descent, kills Inanna and hangs her on a hook; is later mollified by Enki's emissaries. In Nergal and Ereshkigal, gives birth to Nungal alone (in some recensions); after Nergal's descent and her threat to raise the dead unless he becomes her husband, marries him.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Inanna's Descent (ETCSL 1.4.1) ~167-260; Ishtar's Descent; Nergal and Ereshkigal (Foster Before the Muses pp. 506-524)
nodes.characterTrait: terrifying, sovereign, deeply mournful, wrathful, ultimately maritally bound to Nergal
nodes.characterTrait_source: Inanna's Descent (ETCSL 1.4.1); Ishtar's Descent (Akkadian); Nergal and Ereshkigal (Foster Before the Muses pp. 506-524)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: In Ishtar's Descent depicted as breasted, scratching herself, in mourning posture; queenly. The Burney Relief (BM 2003,0718.1) is sometimes identified with her, though the identification is contested.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Ishtar's Descent (Akkadian); Foster Before the Muses pp. 498-505; Burney Relief British Museum entry (with note on contested identification)
nodes.birthCircumstances: Parentage ambiguous in the corpus. In some traditions, daughter of Anu (and thus sister to Ishtar in the Akkadian recension); in others, daughter of Nanna and Ningal (paralleling Inanna in the Sumerian recension), making her the literal 'elder sister' addressed in Inanna's Descent.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Inanna's Descent (ETCSL 1.4.1) — 'elder sister' address; standard Akkadian theology — daughter of Anu
nodes.eventTypes_source: Inanna's Descent; Ishtar's Descent; Nergal and Ereshkigal
nodes.birthTypes_source: Inanna's Descent (ETCSL 1.4.1); standard Akkadian theology

nodes.name: Nergal
nodes.domain: war, plague, fire, the destructive aspect of the sun, kingship of the netherworld (after his marriage to Ereshkigal); also called Erra in his rampage-aspect
nodes.domain_source: Nergal and Ereshkigal (Foster Before the Muses pp. 506-524); Erra Epic (Cagni 1977); ETCSL 1.2.1 (sibling of Nanna, son of Enlil and Ninlil)
nodes.object_source: Standard Nergal/Erra iconography from Akkadian-period seals onward
nodes.animals_source: Standard Nergal-Erra iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Son of Enlil and Ninlil (per ETCSL 1.2.1, where he is born as Nergal-Meslamtaea, brother of Nanna). Descends to the netherworld in Nergal and Ereshkigal; after a complex episode of disrespect and threat, marries Ereshkigal and becomes king of the netherworld with her. In the Erra Epic, his rampage devastates the land; he is calmed by his vizier Ishum.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Nergal and Ereshkigal (Sultantepe and Amarna versions, Foster pp. 506-524); Erra Epic; ETCSL 1.2.1
nodes.characterTrait: violent, war-loving, plague-bringing, raging; eventually maritally and royally bound to Ereshkigal
nodes.characterTrait_source: Erra Epic (Cagni 1977); Nergal and Ereshkigal (Foster Before the Muses pp. 506-524)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Warrior god with mace or scimitar; lion-headed staff; standing on the lion. In his Erra-aspect, distinguished by violence-iconography (severed heads, raging fire).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard Nergal-Erra iconography from Akkadian-period seals onward; Erra Epic
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Enlil and Ninlil; brother of Nanna (per Enlil and Ninlil, ETCSL 1.2.1, where he is born as Nergal-Meslamtaea).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Enlil and Ninlil (ETCSL 1.2.1)
nodes.eventTypes_source: Nergal and Ereshkigal; Erra Epic; ETCSL 1.2.1
nodes.birthTypes_source: Enlil and Ninlil (ETCSL 1.2.1)

nodes.name: Ninurta
nodes.domain: warrior god, agriculture, the plough, mountain-peaks, the storm-bird Anzu pursuit, royal warriorship
nodes.domain_source: Lugal-e (= Ninurta's Exploits, ETCSL 1.6.2); Anzu (Standard Babylonian, SAACT 3 — Vogelzang); Sumerian Ninurta hymns
nodes.object: mace Sharur (the talking weapon), bow, throw-stick
nodes.object_source: Lugal-e (ETCSL 1.6.2) — Sharur converses with Ninurta
nodes.significantEvent: Son of Enlil (in some traditions by Ninlil, in others by Ninhursag). Defeats the Anzu bird who has stolen the Tablet of Destinies, recovers it for his father. In Lugal-e, defeats the demon Asag and organizes the irrigation of Sumer.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Anzu (SAACT 3); Lugal-e (ETCSL 1.6.2)
nodes.characterTrait: warrior, agricultural-organizer, dutiful son, defeater of monsters
nodes.characterTrait_source: Lugal-e (ETCSL 1.6.2); Anzu (SAACT 3); Sumerian Ninurta hymns
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Young warrior god with mace Sharur; bow; throw-stick; the lion-griffin (sometimes shown as his attribute). Cult center at Nippur.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Lugal-e (ETCSL 1.6.2) — Sharur converses with Ninurta; standard Sumerian-Akkadian warrior-god iconography
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Enlil; mother varies (Ninlil in some traditions, Ninhursag in others, particularly in the Lugal-e tradition where Ninurta returns to his mother in the mountains).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Lugal-e (ETCSL 1.6.2); standard genealogies
nodes.birthTypes_source: Lugal-e (ETCSL 1.6.2); standard genealogies

nodes.name: Adad
nodes.domain: storm, thunder, rain, lightning, divination (haruspicy), the destructive flood
nodes.domain_source: Codex Hammurabi prologue; Atrahasis (Adad's rains in the flood); Adad-Hadad-Ishkur cult corpus; standard Mesopotamian storm-god material
nodes.object: thunderbolt, lightning-bundle, his standard bull-mount (storm-god-on-bull standard iconography across NW Semitic)
nodes.object_source: Standard Adad-Hadad iconography (the lightning-bundle); the bull-mount appears on Old Babylonian, Middle Assyrian, and Neo-Assyrian seals
nodes.significantEvent: Storm god. In Atrahasis, his rains (with the contributions of other gods) constitute the flood. Cognate of West-Semitic Hadad and Ugaritic Baal-Hadad. Sumerian counterpart: Ishkur.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Atrahasis II-III; Codex Hammurabi prologue; Adad hymns
nodes.characterTrait_source: Atrahasis II-III; Codex Hammurabi prologue; Adad hymns
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Bearded warrior god holding lightning-bundle and axe; horned crown; standing on or beside his bull. Standard NW Semitic / Mesopotamian storm-god type.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard Adad-Hadad iconography (Old Babylonian onward); the lightning-bundle is his constant attribute
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Anu in some traditions; son of Enlil in others. Consort of Shala.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Standard Mesopotamian theology; cf. ORACC AMGG entry on Adad
nodes.birthTypes_source: Standard Mesopotamian theology

nodes.name: Sarpanitu
nodes.domain: consort of Marduk, queen of Babylon
nodes.domain_source: Standard Babylonian theology; Enuma Elish VII passim (where Marduk's consort is invoked among the fifty names); Babylon temple-tradition
nodes.significantEvent: Consort of Marduk; mother of Nabu. Patroness of Babylon alongside her husband. In some interpretations, the source of the obscure Hebrew name "Succoth-benoth" (2 Kings 17:30) via folk-etymology.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Standard Babylonian theology; Esagila tradition
nodes.characterTrait_source: Esagila cult tradition; Babylonian theology
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Consort of Marduk; standard queenly goddess iconography. Patroness alongside her husband at Babylon's Esagila temple.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Babylonian iconography; standard theology

nodes.name: Nabu
nodes.domain: writing, scribes, wisdom, the destinies, the heir of Marduk, patronage of Borsippa
nodes.domain_source: Erra Epic; standard Borsippa cult-corpus; the Nabu hymn corpus; Codex Hammurabi epilogue
nodes.object: stylus, the wedge-shaped writing reed, the Tablet of Destinies (in some traditions)
nodes.object_source: Standard Nabu iconography; Borsippa Ezida cult
nodes.significantEvent: Son of Marduk and Sarpanitu. Patron of scribes, the alphabet, writing. Holder of the Tablet of Destinies in some Neo-Babylonian traditions. Consort of Tashmetu.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Borsippa cult corpus; Erra Epic; Nabu hymns
nodes.characterTrait_source: Nabu hymns; Borsippa cult corpus; Erra Epic
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Bearded god in standard divine garb, holding the cuneiform stylus and clay tablet (his standard attribute). Cult center at Borsippa's Ezida temple, near Babylon.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Neo-Babylonian iconography; Borsippa Ezida cult; standard Nabu emblem (the writing-stylus on a tablet) on kudurrus
nodes.eventTypes_source: Borsippa cult corpus; Erra Epic; Nabu hymns
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Marduk and Sarpanitu.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Babylonian Borsippa cult tradition
nodes.birthTypes_source: Babylonian Borsippa cult tradition

nodes.name: Asalluhi
nodes.domain: incantation, magic, healing-via-spell, intercessor between Enki and the suffering; later identified with Marduk
nodes.domain_source: Maqlû incantation series; Šurpu incantation series; the Marduk-Asalluhi identification documented in Lambert 2013
nodes.significantEvent: Son of Enki/Ea. The pattern incantation-formula in many ritual texts has Asalluhi go to his father Ea reporting a sufferer's plight; Ea instructs him in the remedy. In Babylonian theology, eventually identified with Marduk (one of his fifty names).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Maqlû I-IX; Šurpu II-III; Enuma Elish VII (Marduk's name Asalluhi)
nodes.object: incantation-formulae; the magical pure-water and tamarisk used in exorcism rites
nodes.object_source: Maqlû I-IX; Šurpu II-III; Bīt mēseri
nodes.characterTrait_source: Maqlû I-IX; Šurpu II-III
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Young god in standard divine garb; iconographically merges with Marduk in later periods (one of Marduk's fifty names is Asalluhi).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Enuma Elish VII (Marduk's name Asalluhi); standard Mesopotamian iconography
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Enki/Ea.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Maqlû I-IX (the standard incantation-formula 'Asalluhi went to his father Ea')
nodes.birthTypes_source: Maqlû I-IX (the standard incantation-formula 'Asalluhi went to his father Ea')

nodes.name: Dumuzi
nodes.domain: shepherding, fertility, the dying-and-returning consort of Inanna, the spring-summer vegetation cycle, mourning rites
nodes.domain_source: Inanna's Descent (ETCSL 1.4.1); Dumuzid and Geshtin-ana (ETCSL 1.4.1.1); Dumuzid's Dream (ETCSL 1.4.3); the Inanna-Dumuzi courtship cycle (ETCSL 4.08.01-33); In the Desert by the Early Grass
nodes.object: shepherd's pipe, crook, staff, his flock of sheep (his pastoral domain). Standard Sumerian Dumuzi-Inanna courtship cycle imagery.
nodes.object_source: Sumerian Dumuzi-Inanna courtship cycle (ETCSL 4.08); In the Desert by the Early Grass; Dumuzid's Dream (ETCSL 1.4.3)
nodes.significantEvent: Husband of Inanna. When Inanna returns from the netherworld and finds him enthroned in fine garments instead of mourning her, she designates him as her substitute; demons drag him to the netherworld. His sister Geshtinanna shares the substitution: each spends six months below, six months above (ETCSL 1.4.1.1). His annual cult-mourning is the festival of Tammuz (the Akkadian form). Cognate of Tammuz.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Inanna's Descent (ETCSL 1.4.1) ~340-415; Dumuzid and Geshtin-ana (ETCSL 1.4.1.1); Dumuzid's Dream (ETCSL 1.4.3)
nodes.deathCircumstances: Seized by the galla-demons of the netherworld as Inanna's substitute; later shares the substitution alternately with his sister Geshtinanna.
nodes.characterTrait: pastoral, beloved, beautiful, ultimately doomed; dying-and-returning
nodes.characterTrait_source: Sumerian Dumuzi-Inanna courtship cycle (ETCSL 4.08); Inanna's Descent (ETCSL 1.4.1); Dumuzid's Dream (ETCSL 1.4.3)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Young shepherd-god in pastoral garb. In Inanna's Descent, when seized by demons, he is dressed in royal garments — for which Inanna designates him as her substitute (he failed to mourn her).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Inanna's Descent (ETCSL 1.4.1) ~340-380; Sumerian Dumuzi-Inanna courtship cycle
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Sirtur (Duttur), the divine ewe-mother. His mother is mentioned in ETCSL 1.4.1.1 (Dumuzid and Geshtin-ana).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: ETCSL 1.4.1.1; Sumerian Dumuzi corpus
nodes.birthTypes_source: ETCSL 1.4.1.1 (Dumuzid and Geshtin-ana — his mother Sirtur)
nodes.eventTypes_source: Inanna's Descent (ETCSL 1.4.1) ~340-415; Dumuzid's Dream (ETCSL 1.4.3); Dumuzid and Geshtin-ana (ETCSL 1.4.1.1); Dumuzi-Inanna courtship cycle (ETCSL 4.08)

nodes.name: Geshtinanna
nodes.domain: the vine, dream-interpretation, scribal arts of the netherworld, sisterly devotion, alternating netherworld-substitute
nodes.domain_source: Dumuzid and Geshtin-ana (ETCSL 1.4.1.1); Dumuzid's Dream (ETCSL 1.4.3) — interprets her brother's dream foretelling his death
nodes.significantEvent: Sister of Dumuzi. In Dumuzid's Dream interprets his prophetic dream of his impending death. In Dumuzid and Geshtin-ana, refuses to betray his hiding-place under torture. Volunteers (or is appointed) to share his netherworld substitution: alternating six months below and six months above.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Dumuzid and Geshtin-ana (ETCSL 1.4.1.1); Dumuzid's Dream (ETCSL 1.4.3)
nodes.object_source: Sumerian Geshtinanna name-etymology (geštin = wine/vine)
nodes.characterTrait: loyal sister, dream-interpreter, scribal of the netherworld, devoted
nodes.characterTrait_source: Dumuzid and Geshtin-ana (ETCSL 1.4.1.1); Dumuzid's Dream (ETCSL 1.4.3)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Goddess of the vine; standard Sumerian goddess iconography. In the netherworld becomes the divine scribe (sometimes identified with Belit-ṣeri).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Sumerian Dumuzi-Geshtinanna cycle; standard iconography
nodes.birthCircumstances: Sister of Dumuzi; daughter of Sirtur in some traditions.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: ETCSL 1.4.1.1; Sumerian Dumuzi corpus
nodes.birthTypes_source: ETCSL 1.4.1.1; Sumerian Dumuzi corpus

nodes.name: Gula
nodes.domain: healing, medicine, the sick-bed, dogs, the city of Isin (her cult center), boundary-stone protection
nodes.domain_source: Bullutsa-rabi's Gula Hymn (Lambert 1967, Or 36); ORACC AMGG entry on Gula; Codex Hammurabi epilogue (Gula invoked among the avenging deities)
nodes.object_source: Bullutsa-rabi's Gula Hymn; standard kudurru-iconography (the dog symbol is hers)
nodes.animals_source: Standard Gula iconography; her dog-companion appears on kudurrus
nodes.significantEvent: Pre-eminent healing goddess of the Mesopotamian pantheon. Patroness of physicians (asû). In Bullutsa-rabi's hymn enumerates her powers as life-giver and life-taker. Identified or partially overlapping with Bau, Nintinugga, Ninisinna. Replaces the misplaced "Kudurru of Gula" entry, which conflated her cult-symbol with the artifact bearing it.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Bullutsa-rabi's Gula Hymn (Lambert 1967 Or 36 pp. 105-132); ORACC AMGG; Codex Hammurabi epilogue
nodes.characterTrait: healer and harmer, life-giver and life-taker, oath-enforcer (Codex Hammurabi epilogue invokes her wrath against violators)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Bullutsa-rabi's Gula Hymn (Lambert 1967, Or 36); Codex Hammurabi epilogue
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Goddess in standard royal-divine garb seated on a throne; her dog beside her; sometimes shown holding a scalpel or healing-implement. Cult center at Isin.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Bullutsa-rabi's Gula Hymn; standard iconography on kudurrus and seals; the Isin temple-dog burials
nodes.eventTypes_source: Bullutsa-rabi's Gula Hymn; Codex Hammurabi epilogue
familyRoles: consort of Ninurta in some traditions
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Anu in some traditions; consort of Ninurta or Pabilsag in different recensions.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: ORACC AMGG entry on Gula
nodes.birthTypes_source: ORACC AMGG entry on Gula

nodes.name: Lamashtu
nodes.domain: attack on pregnant women and infants, miscarriage, infant death, malevolent disease, demoness daughter of Anu
nodes.domain_source: The Lamashtu incantation series (Farber 2014, Lamaštu: An Edition); SA.GIG; Pazuzu and Lamashtu apotropaic amulet corpus
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: long-haired hag with a lion's head, donkey's teeth, naked breasts often suckling a piglet and a dog, talons, snakes in her hands
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Pazuzu-Lamashtu amulet iconography (Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian)
nodes.significantEvent: Demoness; daughter of Anu in the Lamashtu series. Attacks pregnant women, infants, and herds. Held in check by apotropaic amulets, especially those of Pazuzu (her appropriate counter-demon).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Lamashtu series (Farber 2014); Pazuzu-Lamashtu amulet corpus
nodes.object: snake (held in her hand), comb (in some incantations), kindling (her demonic implements)
nodes.object_source: Pazuzu-Lamashtu amulet iconography (Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Lamashtu incantation series (Farber 2014); SA.GIG; Pazuzu-Lamashtu amulet inscriptions
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Anu, expelled from heaven for her malevolence (per Lamashtu series).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Lamashtu incantation series (Farber 2014)
nodes.eventTypes_source: Lamashtu incantation series (Farber 2014); Pazuzu-Lamashtu amulet corpus
nodes.birthTypes_source: Lamashtu incantation series (Farber 2014) — Lamashtu as daughter of Anu, expelled from heaven

nodes.name: Pazuzu
nodes.domain: king of the wind-demons; apotropaic against Lamashtu; the southwest wind; counter-demonic protection
nodes.domain_source: Pazuzu apotropaic amulets and figurines (1st millennium BCE); the Pazuzu inscription corpus
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: humanoid head with bared teeth, four wings, lion paws, eagle talons, scorpion tail, erect phallus
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Pazuzu amulet iconography (e.g. the bronze Pazuzu head Louvre MNB 467)
nodes.significantEvent: King of the wind-demons. Counter-demonic figure: Pazuzu amulets are placed on or near pregnant women and newborns to repel Lamashtu. Not a benevolent god — an apotropaic deployment of the demonic against the demonic.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Pazuzu amulet inscriptions; Pazuzu-Lamashtu amulet corpus; Heeßel 2002
nodes.object: amulets, his bronze figurine-form, the chains he might bind Lamashtu with (in apotropaic art)
nodes.object_source: Pazuzu amulet inscriptions; Heeßel 2002
nodes.characterTrait_source: Pazuzu amulet inscriptions; Pazuzu-Lamashtu amulet corpus
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Hanbi (a minor demonic deity), per the Pazuzu inscription corpus.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Pazuzu amulet inscriptions (Heeßel 2002)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Pazuzu amulet inscriptions (Heeßel 2002) — son of Hanbi

nodes.name: Gilgamesh
nodes.domain: kingship of Uruk, heroic exploit, the quest for immortality, builder of the walls of Uruk; later, judge of the netherworld
nodes.domain_source: Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh tablets I-XII (George 2003); Sumerian Gilgamesh poems (ETCSL 1.8.1.1-5: Gilgamesh and Aga, Gilgamesh and the Bull of Heaven, Death of Gilgamesh, Gilgamesh-Enkidu-Netherworld, Gilgamesh and Huwawa A and B); the Sumerian King List (Gilgamesh as fifth king of post-Flood Uruk dynasty)
nodes.object: great walls of Uruk, copper-banded box (in the Standard Babylonian preface), bow, axe
nodes.object_source: Gilgamesh I 1-26 (the walls); George 2003
nodes.significantEvent: Two-thirds divine, one-third human (Gilgamesh I 47-48). Son of Lugalbanda and the goddess Ninsun. King of Uruk; in his early oppressive period his subjects pray for relief, leading to Aruru's creation of Enkidu. Quests with Enkidu against Humbaba in the Cedar Forest. Refuses Ishtar's offer of marriage; she sends the Bull of Heaven, which they slay; in retaliation the gods kill Enkidu. Devastated, Gilgamesh quests for immortality, finds Utnapishtim, learns the flood story, fails to claim immortality (loses the plant of rejuvenation to a snake). Returns to Uruk, accepting mortality; his fame survives in his city walls.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh I-XI (George 2003); Sumerian Gilgamesh poems (ETCSL 1.8.1.1-5)
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Lugalbanda (mortal king of Uruk) and the goddess Ninsun.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Gilgamesh I 35-37; Sumerian King List
nodes.deathCircumstances: Dies a mortal death after returning to Uruk. In the Sumerian Death of Gilgamesh (ETCSL 1.8.1.3) is given a place as judge of the netherworld.
nodes.deathCircumstances_source: Death of Gilgamesh (ETCSL 1.8.1.3); Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Nether World (ETCSL 1.8.1.4)
nodes.characterTrait: oppressive in his early kingship, then quested-driven, devoted in friendship, shattered by Enkidu's death, ultimately accepting of mortality
nodes.characterTrait_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh tablets I-XI (George 2003); Sumerian Gilgamesh poems (ETCSL 1.8.1.1-5)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Two-thirds divine, one-third human (Gilgamesh I 47-48). Of immense stature; bearded; royal garb. The famous lapis-lazuli tablet describes his appearance.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Gilgamesh I 47-48; the Sumerian Gilgamesh poems
nodes.eventTypes_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh I-XI; Sumerian Gilgamesh poems (ETCSL 1.8.1.1-5)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Gilgamesh I 47-48; Sumerian King List
nodes.deathTypes_source: Death of Gilgamesh (ETCSL 1.8.1.3); Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Nether World (ETCSL 1.8.1.4)

nodes.name: Enkidu
nodes.domain: wild-man companion of Gilgamesh, civilizational transformation via Shamhat, hunter, foil to royal power
nodes.domain_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh I-VIII; Sumerian Gilgamesh-Enkidu-Netherworld (ETCSL 1.8.1.4)
nodes.significantEvent: Created by Aruru from clay (Gilgamesh I 101-112) at Anu's command, as a foil to Gilgamesh. Lives in the wild with the animals; civilized by Shamhat; befriends Gilgamesh. Quests with him against Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven. After the gods condemn him for the Bull-killing, dies a slow death (Gilgamesh VII), leaving Gilgamesh stricken.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh I-VIII; ETCSL 1.8.1.4
nodes.birthCircumstances: Created by the goddess Aruru from clay, on Anu's command, as a counterpart to Gilgamesh.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Gilgamesh I 101-112
nodes.deathCircumstances: After he and Gilgamesh slay the Bull of Heaven and Humbaba, the gods (Anu, Enlil, and Shamash) decree that one of them must die. The lot falls on Enkidu, who sickens and dies after a long-detailed death-bed account.
nodes.object: the bow he forges with Gilgamesh; the cedar-axe of the Cedar Forest expedition; the door of Humbaba's lair (later Enkidu speaks to it on his deathbed, Gilgamesh VII)
nodes.object_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh II-VII
nodes.characterTrait: initially wild, then civilized, fiercely devoted to Gilgamesh, doomed
nodes.characterTrait_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh I-VIII
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Initially: hairy, naked, wild; eats grass with the gazelles, drinks at waterholes with the animals (Gilgamesh I 195-228). After Shamhat's seduction and the bread-and-beer civilizing meal: human in form, equal to Gilgamesh in stature.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh I 195-296
nodes.birthTypes_source: Gilgamesh I 101-112

nodes.name: Utnapishtim
nodes.domain: flood-survival, immortality granted, the far-distant land of Dilmun-equivalent, witness of the antediluvian world
nodes.domain_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh tablet XI (the flood story); Atrahasis (Akkadian, the older form, where his name is Atrahasis "Exceedingly Wise"); Sumerian Flood Story (ETCSL 1.7.4 — where his name is Ziusudra, "Long-lived life")
nodes.significantEvent: Warned by Enki/Ea (in defiance of Enlil's decree) of the coming flood; builds a great cube-shaped boat; survives the seven-day flood with his family and animals; lands on Mount Nimush. Releases dove, swallow, raven. Sacrifices to the gods. Granted immortality by Enlil and settled at the mouth of the rivers. In Gilgamesh XI, recounts the flood to Gilgamesh and gives him the (lost) plant of rejuvenation.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh XI; Atrahasis II-III; Sumerian Flood Story (ETCSL 1.7.4)
nodes.object: the great cube-shaped boat (six decks, seven stories); pitch and bitumen for caulking; the dove, swallow, and raven released from the boat; the plant of rejuvenation given to Gilgamesh; the horns and skirts of his sacrificial offerings
nodes.object_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh XI 24-206
nodes.characterTrait: wise, obedient to Ea's warning, sacrificial, eventually immortal-counselor
nodes.characterTrait_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh XI; Atrahasis II-III
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: In Gilgamesh XI 1-7, Gilgamesh first sees Utnapishtim and finds him no different in appearance from a mortal man; only the gods' decree distinguishes him. Settled at the mouth of the rivers (the 'far away' of the Mesopotamian cosmography).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh XI 1-7, 196-206
nodes.birthCircumstances: A mortal king of Shuruppak (per Sumerian King List and the Sumerian Flood Story, where his name is Ziusudra son of Ubara-Tutu).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Sumerian King List; Sumerian Flood Story (ETCSL 1.7.4); Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh XI 11
nodes.eventTypes_source: Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh XI; Atrahasis II-III; Sumerian Flood Story (ETCSL 1.7.4)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Sumerian King List; Gilgamesh XI 11

nodes.name: Yarikh
nodes.domain: the moon, the lunar cycle, illumination, light-giving — Ugaritic *yrḫ*
nodes.domain_source: KTU 1.24 (the Marriage of Nikkal and Yarikh); KTU 1.114 (the marzeah text where Yarikh acts strangely as a dog at El's banquet); pantheon list KTU 1.47 / 1.118 (line 17, Yarikh among major deities)
nodes.object: crescent emblem; bridal payment of silver, gold, and lapis-lazuli (the bride-price he gives for Nikkal in KTU 1.24)
nodes.object_source: KTU 1.24 lines 17-50 (the bride-price); standard Levantine moon-god iconography
nodes.characterTrait: shining, ardent suitor, paying-the-bride-price, in KTU 1.114 oddly canine and beggar-like at El's drunken feast
nodes.characterTrait_source: KTU 1.24 (his suit for Nikkal); KTU 1.114 (his strange behavior at El's marzeah)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Moon-god; crescent emblem on his head in some Levantine iconography. Cognate with Sumero-Akkadian Sin/Nanna.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard Late Bronze Age Levantine moon-god iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Marries Nikkal (= Mesopotamian Ningal), with Ḫiriḫibi (Khirkhib, "summer-king") as marriage-broker and the Kotharat (the seven goddesses of conception/childbirth) blessing the union (KTU 1.24). In KTU 1.114, attends El's drunken banquet where he behaves like a dog under the table.

nodes.name: Nikkal
nodes.domain: the moon (as consort of Yarikh), childbirth (via association with the Kotharat), fruit-bearing — Ugaritic *nkl*, cognate of Sumero-Akkadian Ningal
nodes.domain_source: KTU 1.24 (the Marriage of Nikkal and Yarikh); the Hurrian-Ugaritic Hymn to Nikkal (RS 15.30+15.49 = Hurro-Ugaritic Song 6, the famous earliest extant musical notation); pantheon list KTU 1.47 / 1.118
nodes.object: fruits and produce of marriage (her domain emblem); bride-veil
nodes.object_source: KTU 1.24 (the marriage scene)
nodes.characterTrait: bride, fruitful, blessed by the Kotharat
nodes.characterTrait_source: KTU 1.24
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Goddess in bridal aspect; standard Late Bronze Age goddess iconography. Her name *nkl* derives from *kallatu* "bride" (Akkadian).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: KTU 1.24; etymological note (Wyatt 2002 *Religious Texts from Ugarit*)
nodes.significantEvent: The bride of Yarikh in KTU 1.24, the Marriage of Nikkal and Yarikh. The Kotharat (the seven goddesses of conception/childbirth) bless their union. Her name and cult continue into the Hurrian Hymn to Nikkal (RS 15.30+, c. 14th c. BCE), which preserves the earliest known musical notation.
nodes.significantEvent_source: KTU 1.24; Hurro-Ugaritic Hymn to Nikkal
nodes.birthTypes_source: KTU 1.24 (her father Ḫiriḫibi negotiates the marriage)
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Ḫiriḫibi ("summer-king") in KTU 1.24, who acts as marriage-broker and bride's father in the negotiations.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: KTU 1.24

nodes.name: Shahar
nodes.domain: dawn, the morning twilight (Ugaritic *šḥr*) — paired twin with Shalim
nodes.domain_source: KTU 1.23 line 52 ff. (the Goodly Gods liturgy — El's mating produces Shahar and Shalim); Isaiah 14:12 (Hebrew *helel ben šaḥar* "Day-Star, son of Dawn", later misread as "Lucifer")
nodes.characterTrait: twin, primordial, dawning, voracious (in KTU 1.23 the Goodly Gods are voracious eaters whose appetite spans the cosmos)
nodes.characterTrait_source: KTU 1.23
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Personification of dawn; not described in detail beyond his role in KTU 1.23 as one of the "Goodly Gods" with his twin.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: KTU 1.23
nodes.significantEvent: Born of El and one of the two human women in the Goodly Gods liturgy (KTU 1.23 line 52 ff.). Twin of Shalim (Dusk). The two are described as voracious cosmic-spanning eaters. Later memorialized in Hebrew Bible polemic (Isaiah 14:12) as the father of *helel*, the falling Day-Star.
nodes.significantEvent_source: KTU 1.23; Isaiah 14:12
nodes.birthTypes_source: KTU 1.23
nodes.birthCircumstances: Born of El and one of the two human women he mates with in the Goodly Gods liturgy (KTU 1.23 line 52 ff.); twin of Shalim.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: KTU 1.23

nodes.name: Shalim
nodes.domain: dusk, the evening twilight (Ugaritic *šlm*) — paired twin with Shahar; the toponymic root of Jerusalem (*Yerushalayim*) and a divine name in early Canaanite-Hebrew religion
nodes.domain_source: KTU 1.23 line 52 ff. (the Goodly Gods liturgy); the Egyptian Execration Texts (early 2nd millennium BCE) list a ruler of Jerusalem with the theophoric name Yaqar-Ammu, and later Amarna Letter EA 287 from Abdi-Ḫeba of Urusalim — preserving the toponym preserving Shalim
nodes.characterTrait_source: KTU 1.23
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Personification of dusk; twin of Shahar in KTU 1.23.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: KTU 1.23
nodes.significantEvent: Born of El and one of the two human women in the Goodly Gods liturgy (KTU 1.23). Twin of Shahar. His name is preserved in the toponym Jerusalem (*Yerushalayim*, originally "foundation of Shalim") and in personal names from the Iron Age.
nodes.significantEvent_source: KTU 1.23; Egyptian Execration Texts; Amarna Letter EA 287; Iron Age onomastic evidence (Yerushalayim etymology)
nodes.birthTypes_source: KTU 1.23
nodes.birthCircumstances: Born of El and one of the two human women in the Goodly Gods liturgy (KTU 1.23); twin of Shahar.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: KTU 1.23

nodes.name: Pidray
nodes.domain: mist, light, dew, atmospheric brilliance — Ugaritic *pdry bt ʾar* "Pidray daughter of Light"
nodes.domain_source: KTU 1.3 III 6-8; 1.4 I 16-18; KTU 1.24 line 26 (in Yarikh's alternate-bride list — Yarikh's preferred match before Nikkal); pantheon list KTU 1.47 / 1.118
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Goddess of light/mist; not described iconographically in detail.
nodes.significantEvent: Daughter of Baal. In KTU 1.24, she is listed as the alternative bride that Yarikh's family proposes, but Yarikh chooses Nikkal instead. Frequently invoked alongside her sisters Tallay and Arsay in Baal Cycle passages.
nodes.birthTypes_source: KTU 1.3, 1.4 — daughter of Baal
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Baal.

nodes.name: Tallay
nodes.domain: rain, showers (Ugaritic *ṭl* "dew/rain") — *ṭly bt rb* "Tallay daughter of Showers"
nodes.domain_source: KTU 1.3 III 6-8; 1.4 I 16-18; pantheon list KTU 1.47 / 1.118
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Goddess of rain-showers; not described iconographically in detail.
nodes.significantEvent: Daughter of Baal. Invoked alongside her sisters Pidray and Arsay in Baal Cycle passages enumerating Baal's family.
nodes.birthTypes_source: KTU 1.3, 1.4 — daughter of Baal
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Baal.

nodes.name: Arsay
nodes.domain: earth, the underworld (Ugaritic *ʾrṣ* "earth/underworld") — *ʾarṣy bt yʿbdr* "Arsay daughter of Yaʿbidir/the Wide One"
nodes.domain_source: KTU 1.3 III 6-8; 1.4 I 16-18; pantheon list KTU 1.47 / 1.118
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Earth/underworld goddess; not described iconographically in detail.
nodes.significantEvent: Daughter of Baal. The third of his three daughters, sister to Pidray and Tallay. Her domain is more chthonic than her sisters' — possibly cognate with Mesopotamian Ereshkigal in some readings.
nodes.birthTypes_source: KTU 1.3, 1.4 — daughter of Baal
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Baal.

nodes.name: Lotan
nodes.domain: the seven-headed cosmic serpent of the primordial sea — Ugaritic *ltn* (literally "the writhing one"); cognate with biblical Leviathan (*lwytn*)
nodes.domain_source: KTU 1.5 I 1-3 (Mot's taunt to Baal: "When you struck Litan the wriggling serpent, finished off the writhing serpent, the seven-headed one..."); KTU 1.3 III 38-44 (Anat's boast: "Did I not crush El's beloved Yam? Did I not destroy the great river-god? Did I not muzzle Tunannu and bind him? I crushed the wriggling serpent, the seven-headed potentate"); cognate with biblical Leviathan in Isaiah 27:1, Psalm 74:14, Psalm 104:26, Job 41
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Seven-headed serpent of the cosmic sea, with multiple coils; cognate with biblical Leviathan and the Mesopotamian sea-monsters of the Tiamat tradition.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: KTU 1.5 I 1-3; KTU 1.3 III 38-44; biblical Leviathan parallels (Psalm 74:14 — "the heads of Leviathan", Job 41)
nodes.significantEvent: Defeated by Anat (per her boast in KTU 1.3 III 38-44) and by Baal (per Mot's taunt in KTU 1.5 I 1-3, which credits Baal with the defeat). The cognate biblical Leviathan is defeated by YHWH (Psalm 74:14, Isaiah 27:1).
nodes.birthTypes_source: KTU 1.5 I 1-3 (primordial sea-creature)
nodes.birthCircumstances: Primordial sea-monster; emerged from the cosmic sea.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: KTU 1.5 I 1-3
nodes.deathTypes_source: KTU 1.5 I 1-3 (Mot credits Baal); KTU 1.3 III 38-44 (Anat credits herself) — both traditions preserved
nodes.deathCircumstances: Defeated and crushed in primordial combat. Two parallel attributions: Mot says Baal struck him down (KTU 1.5 I 1-3); Anat boasts of her own slaying (KTU 1.3 III 38-44). Likely two recensions of the same myth.

nodes.name: Eshmun
nodes.domain: healing, Sidonian patron-deity, vegetation-life-force, identified by Greeks with Asclepius
nodes.domain_source: Eshmunazar II sarcophagus inscription (KAI 14, Sidon, 5th c. BCE); Tabnit sarcophagus inscription (KAI 13); Bodashtart inscriptions; Damascius, Vita Isidori (preserved by Photius) — the Eshmun-Asklepios identification and the famous Phoenician myth of Eshmun's self-castration to escape Astronoë
nodes.object: staff with a serpent (his iconic emblem, the source of the medical caduceus-cognate); bowl
nodes.object_source: Hellenistic-period Eshmun iconography from the Eshmun temple at Bostan esh-Sheikh (Sidon); the standard Asclepius-Eshmun iconography
nodes.animals_source: The serpent is closely identified with Eshmun as his symbolic-emblematic creature — the parallel of Greek Asclepius. Cognate with the Mesopotamian Ningishzida tradition of healing-snake imagery. Symbolic embodiment, not mere companion.
nodes.characterTrait: healing, life-restoring, ardent, in some traditions self-castrated (the Astronoë myth)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Damascius via Photius; Eshmunazar II sarcophagus
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Healer-god in Hellenistic-period iconography appearing similar to Asclepius (bearded, robed, with serpent-staff). The Eshmun temple at Sidon (Bostan esh-Sheikh) preserves architectural fragments and a sacred pool.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Eshmun temple architecture at Bostan esh-Sheikh; Hellenistic-period iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Patron-god of Sidon (alongside Astarte). In the Astronoë myth (preserved by Damascius via Photius, c. 6th c. CE), the goddess Astronoë pursues Eshmun in love; he flees and self-castrates with an axe to escape her, dies, and is restored to life by her — the Phoenician dying-and-rising god parallel to Tammuz and Adonis. Identified by the Greeks with Asclepius from at least the 5th c. BCE onward.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Damascius, Vita Isidori (in Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 242); the Eshmun temple at Sidon
nodes.birthTypes_source: Damascius via Photius — son of Sadyk (one of the seven Cabeiri) per Damascius
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Sadyk per Damascius (Sadyk being one of the seven Cabeiri / Phoenician cosmogonic ancestors). Consort of Astarte in some Sidonian traditions.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Damascius, Vita Isidori; Sidonian inscriptional context
nodes.deathCircumstances: In the Astronoë myth: pursued by Astronoë in love, flees, self-castrates with an axe to escape her, dies, is restored by her. The dying-and-rising pattern parallels Tammuz/Adonis.

nodes.name: Melqart
nodes.domain: kingship of Tyre, royal patronage, the sea, navigation, colonization, dying-and-rising — the name *mlk-qrt* means "King of the City" (Tyre)
nodes.domain_source: Tyrian and Carthaginian inscriptions; the Bredsch Cippi (8th c. BCE); the bilingual Maltese Cippus of Melqart (KAI 47, 2nd c. BCE — the Phoenician-Greek bilingual that aided Phoenician decipherment); Herodotus 2.44 (his visit to the Tyrian temple of Heracles-Melqart); Josephus, Antiquities 8.5.3 (the egersis, Melqart's annual resurrection festival)
nodes.object: lion-skin and club (in his Heracles-Melqart Hellenistic syncretism); the ceremonial pyre at his egersis
nodes.object_source: Hellenistic-period Heracles-Melqart iconography; Josephus, Ant. 8.5.3 (the egersis, the annual resurrection festival in the month of Peritios); the Bredsch and Cyprus stelae
nodes.characterTrait: royal, sea-faring, colonizing, dying-and-rising, Heraclean (in Greek interpretation)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Herodotus 2.44; Josephus; Phoenician colonial inscriptions
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: In Phoenician iconography (e.g., the Aleppo stele BM 125008, "Bar-Rakib and Melqart"), Melqart appears as a bearded warrior-king holding the *ankh*-like sign of life and a battle-axe. In Hellenistic-period syncretism with Heracles, he is depicted with the lion-skin and club.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Aleppo / Bredsch stele BM 125008 (9th c. BCE); Hellenistic Heracles-Melqart coinage of Tyre
nodes.significantEvent: Patron-god of Tyre and of the Tyrian colonies (Carthage, Cadiz/Gadir, etc.). His annual *egersis* — the "awakening" or resurrection festival in the month of Peritios — was central to Tyrian religion (Josephus, Ant. 8.5.3). The Bible references him as the "Baal" of Jezebel's patronage in 1 Kings 16:31, 18:19. Identified by Greeks with Heracles from at least the archaic period; this identification powered the spread of his cult through the western Mediterranean.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Herodotus 2.44; Josephus, Ant. 8.5.3; 1 Kings 16:31, 18:19; the Phoenician colonial-inscriptional record
nodes.deathCircumstances: In the annual egersis ("awakening") cult-cycle, Melqart was understood to die and be resurrected each year; the burning of his image and its restoration were central rites at Tyre and her colonies.

nodes.name: Tanit
nodes.domain: mother-goddess of Carthage, fertility, the moon, war, the heavens — her epithet *pnh bʿl* "Face of Baal" (i.e., countenance of Baal-Hammon)
nodes.domain_source: Carthaginian votive inscriptions (KAI 78-100 and many others); the Tanit symbol (the trapezoid-crescent-disc figure) on Carthaginian stelae throughout the Punic west; the Cypriot Eshmunazar II sarcophagus (KAI 14, references "Tanit-pnh-Baal"); Herodian inscriptions of the Punic west
nodes.object: the Tanit-symbol (trapezoid body, raised arms, crescent on top); pomegranate; dove; lion-emblem in some contexts
nodes.object_source: Standard Carthaginian votive iconography; the "Sign of Tanit" (or "Tinnit-symbol") on thousands of Punic-period stelae
nodes.characterTrait: maternal, royal, sometimes warlike, aniconic-stylized (her trapezoidal symbol is more characteristic than figurative iconography)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Punic votive corpus
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: In figurative iconography (rare relative to her stylized symbol), depicted as a frontal-facing matronly goddess. The "Sign of Tanit" — a trapezoidal body topped by a horizontal bar (arms outstretched) and a crescent disc above — is her iconographic signature, found on thousands of Punic stelae.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Punic votive iconography; Carthage Tophet excavations
nodes.significantEvent: Chief goddess of Carthage and of the Punic colonies. Paired with Baal-Hammon as the divine couple of the Carthaginian state cult. Recipient of the *molk*-sacrifices at the Carthage Tophet. After Carthage's destruction in 146 BCE, her cult continued under the Roman name Caelestis ("Heavenly One") — the Punic mother-goddess Romanized.
nodes.significantEvent_source: KAI corpus; Carthage Tophet stelae; Stager & Wolff 1984 *The Carthage Tophet*; Roman-period Caelestis inscriptions

nodes.name: Baal-Hammon
nodes.domain: chief god of Carthage and the Punic west, kingship, the sun (in some readings), the divine consort of Tanit; identified by Greeks and Romans with Cronos/Saturn
nodes.domain_source: Carthaginian votive corpus (thousands of inscriptions, especially the Tophet stelae); KAI 65-77; the bilingual Pyrgi tablets (5th c. BCE — Phoenician-Etruscan); Diodorus Siculus 20.14 (the Carthaginian image of Cronos, properly Baal-Hammon); Roman-period Saturn-cult inscriptions of North Africa
nodes.object: throne flanked by sphinxes; ram-horned crown; staff; the bronze image at Carthage with downward-tipping hands (per Diodorus Siculus 20.14)
nodes.object_source: Carthaginian iconography on stelae; Diodorus Siculus 20.14
nodes.animals_source: Standard Punic Baal-Hammon iconography includes the ram-horned crown — symbolic embodiment-emblem (cognate with the bull-horned high-god type elsewhere in the Levant)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Punic votive corpus; Diodorus Siculus 20.14
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: On Carthaginian stelae, depicted as a bearded enthroned god with ram-horned crown, flanked by sphinxes. Diodorus Siculus 20.14 describes a colossal bronze image at Carthage with arms outstretched and palms tipped downward, into which sacrificial victims were placed.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Punic votive iconography; Diodorus Siculus 20.14
nodes.significantEvent: Chief god of Carthage. With Tanit, recipient of the *molk*-sacrifices at the Tophet. Identified by Greeks with Cronos, by Romans with Saturn (after 146 BCE the cult of Saturn in North Africa is recognizably the continuation of Baal-Hammon's cult). The famous Carthaginian child-sacrifice tradition is principally directed to him.
nodes.significantEvent_source: KAI corpus; Carthage Tophet stelae; Stager & Wolff 1984; Diodorus Siculus 20.14; Cleitarchus fr. 9; Roman-period Saturnus inscriptions of North Africa

nodes.name: Chemosh
nodes.domain: national god of Moab; war, divine sanction of conquest, royal patronage
nodes.domain_source: Mesha Stele (KAI 181, Moabite, c. 840 BCE — the principal primary source); Numbers 21:29 ("the people of Chemosh"); 1 Kings 11:7, 33; 2 Kings 23:13; Jeremiah 48:7, 13, 46
nodes.characterTrait_source: Mesha Stele
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: No iconographic depiction confirmed; the Mesha Stele preserves only the name and not a portrait.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Mesha Stele (KAI 181)
nodes.significantEvent: On the Mesha Stele (c. 840 BCE), King Mesha of Moab attributes his earlier oppression by Israel to Chemosh's anger and his subsequent victory over the Israelites to Chemosh's favor. He records sacrificing the people of Nebo to Chemosh and dragging the sacred vessels of YHWH before him (KAI 181 lines 12-18). The Hebrew Bible polemicizes against Chemosh as the "abomination of Moab" (1 Kings 11:7).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Mesha Stele lines 5-18; Numbers 21:29; 1 Kings 11:7

nodes.name: Milcom
nodes.domain: national god of Ammon; royal patronage
nodes.domain_source: 1 Kings 11:5, 33; 2 Kings 23:13; Jeremiah 49:1, 3 (variantly Malcam); Zephaniah 1:5; Amman citadel inscription (the Ammonite "Citadel Inscription", c. 9th c. BCE — possibly invokes Milcom). Note: name is etymologically related to *mlk* "king", and may be a title meaning "their king" applied to a local national god rather than a proper name distinct from El or Baal-style high gods
nodes.characterTrait_source: 1 Kings 11; the Ammonite Citadel Inscription
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: No iconographic depiction confirmed from primary sources.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Ammonite primary corpus is sparse
nodes.significantEvent: National god of Ammon; the Hebrew Bible records Solomon building him a high place outside Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7) and Josiah destroying it (2 Kings 23:13). The biblical references frequently confuse Milcom with Moloch — the Hebrew text variously preserves the consonants *mlk(m)* such that the same passage is sometimes read as "Milcom" (Ammonite god) and sometimes as "Moloch" (child-sacrifice deity).
nodes.significantEvent_source: 1 Kings 11:5-7; 2 Kings 23:13; Jeremiah 49:1-3

nodes.name: Kirta
nodes.domain: heroic king (semi-divine), royal patronage of El, divinely-promised dynasty
nodes.domain_source: KTU 1.14-1.16 (the Kirta Epic, in three tablets — the only surviving copy of this composition)
nodes.object: his royal weapons; the dream-vision he receives from El; his bow
nodes.object_source: KTU 1.14 I-III (the dream-vision); 1.14 II 9-25
nodes.characterTrait: grieving, faithful, fertile-with-divine-help, eventually neglectful of his vow, ill, near-death, restored
nodes.characterTrait_source: KTU 1.14 I-VI (his grief over lost family, his obedience to El, his neglect of vow); 1.16 I-VI (his illness)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Mortal heroic king; described as having lost wife and seven children to plague at the start of the epic; later restored, marrying Hurriya and fathering a new dynasty.
nodes.significantEvent: Kirta has lost his wife and seven children to plague (Resheph kills a fifth, Yam takes others, etc.; KTU 1.14 I 18-21). El appears to him in a dream and instructs him to march on Udum to claim Hurriya as his bride. Kirta does so, with divine help, and gets Hurriya as wife. He vows a sacrifice to Athirat for the gift of children but neglects to fulfill the vow; he and his family fall ill. His son Ilu-haʾu (the future Yassib) attempts to usurp the throne; Kirta curses him with Horon and Athtart. Kirta is restored by El's intervention.
nodes.birthTypes_source: KTU 1.14 — Kirta as son of El (in poetic apposition; the relation is more "favored-by" than literal)
nodes.birthCircumstances: A mortal king; in the epic he is repeatedly addressed as "son of El" (in the sense of divine favorite), but his literal genealogy is that of a Levantine king of Hubur.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: KTU 1.14 I-VI

nodes.name: Danel
nodes.domain: heroic king of Hrnmy (Hurnamiya); pious patriarch; mourning-father
nodes.domain_source: KTU 1.17-1.19 (the Aqhat Epic). NOTE: this Ugaritic Danel is likely the "righteous Daniel" referenced alongside Noah and Job in Ezekiel 14:14, 20 and Ezekiel 28:3 — distinct from the later biblical Daniel of the eponymous book.
nodes.object: incense-burner (with which he ritually petitions for a son); the threshing-floor where he holds court; Aqhat's great bow forged by Kothar-wa-Khasis
nodes.object_source: KTU 1.17 I 1-25 (the seven-day vigil); 1.17 V (the bow gift)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Mortal patriarch and king; described as performing a seven-day petition-ritual for a son, sleeping by night and offering incense by day until Baal intervenes with El.
nodes.significantEvent: Childless, Danel performs a seven-day petition-ritual for a son. Baal intercedes with El, who grants him Aqhat. When Aqhat is grown, Kothar-wa-Khasis gives him a magnificent bow; Anat covets it, offers Aqhat gold and immortality in exchange; he refuses; she contrives his death through Yatpan. Danel curses the land; his daughter Pughat seeks vengeance.
nodes.birthTypes_source: KTU 1.17 — Danel as a mortal Levantine king
nodes.birthCircumstances: A mortal Levantine king of Hrnmy / Hurnamiya.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: KTU 1.17 I-II

nodes.name: Aqhat
nodes.domain: heroic son, hunter, possessor of the divine bow, Anat's victim
nodes.domain_source: KTU 1.17-1.19 (the Aqhat Epic)
nodes.object: the magnificent bow forged for him by Kothar-wa-Khasis (the central plot-device of the epic)
nodes.object_source: KTU 1.17 V 1-39 (the bow-gift)
nodes.characterTrait: proud, principled (refuses Anat's offer of immortality), young, hunter
nodes.characterTrait_source: KTU 1.17 VI 16-50 (his refusal of Anat's offer)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Young heroic son of Danel; described as receiving the bow from Kothar-wa-Khasis at his coming-of-age.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: KTU 1.17 V
nodes.significantEvent: Granted to Danel by El's intercession after the seven-day petition. Receives a magnificent bow from Kothar-wa-Khasis. Anat covets the bow and offers him gold, silver, and immortality in exchange; he refuses, telling her that mortal women cannot bear arrows and that all mortals must die. In retaliation Anat petitions El for permission; she sends her henchman Yatpan to kill Aqhat at a hunt, transforming Yatpan into a vulture or vulture-rider. Aqhat's killing causes a drought across the land; his sister Pughat sets out to avenge him.
nodes.birthTypes_source: KTU 1.17 I-II — Aqhat granted to Danel by El after the seven-day petition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Granted to Danel and his wife by El's intercession after Danel's seven-day petition-ritual. Baal personally intercedes with El on Danel's behalf.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: KTU 1.17 I-II
nodes.deathCircumstances: After refusing Anat's offer of immortality in exchange for his bow, Anat petitions El for permission to harm him; she sends her henchman Yatpan in vulture-form (or as a vulture-rider) who attacks Aqhat at a hunt and kills him. The bow falls into the sea; the land suffers drought.

nodes.name: Pughat
nodes.domain: heroic vengeance, sisterly devotion, divinely-aided pursuit
nodes.domain_source: KTU 1.19 (the Aqhat Epic, third tablet — the surviving portion focuses on Pughat's avenging quest)
nodes.object: sword (concealed beneath her garment when she goes to Yatpan); cup of wine (with which she gets him drunk)
nodes.object_source: KTU 1.19 IV
nodes.characterTrait_source: KTU 1.19
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Young woman; in KTU 1.19 IV she disguises herself in warrior-garb beneath women's clothing to approach Yatpan.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: KTU 1.19 IV
nodes.significantEvent: Daughter of Danel and sister of Aqhat. After Aqhat's death by Yatpan (Anat's henchman), Pughat sets out to avenge him. She disguises herself in warrior's armor beneath women's clothing, presents herself to Yatpan as a hostess, gets him drunk on wine, and (in the surviving fragment) prepares to kill him; the tablet breaks off at this climactic moment.
nodes.significantEvent_source: KTU 1.19 IV (the surviving narrative; the tablet ends before the killing is completed)
nodes.birthTypes_source: KTU 1.17-1.19 — daughter of Danel and his wife
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Danel and sister of Aqhat.

nodes.name: YHWH
nodes.domain: covenant deity of Israel, creator of heaven and earth, holy (qādōš), jealous (qannāʾ), just, merciful, the Tetragrammaton (the four-letter Name יהוה, ineffable in later Jewish practice and read as Adonai or Hashem)
nodes.domain_source: The Tanakh (Hebrew Bible) passim. The principal self-disclosure passages: Exodus 3:14 (ʾehyeh ʾăšer ʾehyeh, "I am that I am" / "I will be what I will be"); Exodus 6:2-3 (revelation of the Name to Moses); Exodus 20:1-17 (the Decalogue); Exodus 34:6-7 (the thirteen attributes of mercy); Deuteronomy 6:4-5 (the Shema, "YHWH is one")
nodes.object: throne (Isaiah 6:1, Ezekiel 1:26, Daniel 7:9); the Ark of the Covenant (Exodus 25:10-22, in which the cherubim flank the divine presence); the Tabernacle and the Jerusalem Temple (his cultic dwelling-places); the divine glory / kavod (Exodus 33:18-23, Ezekiel 1:28); the pillar of cloud and fire (Exodus 13:21-22); the bow in the clouds (Genesis 9:13)
nodes.object_source: Exodus 25:10-22; Exodus 33:18-23; Isaiah 6:1; Ezekiel 1; Genesis 9:13
nodes.characterTrait: holy, just, merciful, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love (ḥesed), jealous, faithful, ineffable, sovereign, creator, redeemer, covenant-keeper
nodes.characterTrait_source: Exodus 34:6-7 (the thirteen attributes); Deuteronomy 7:9; Psalm 86:15, 103:8, 145:8; the prophets passim
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Aniconic — explicitly forbidden (Exodus 20:4, Deuteronomy 5:8) to make any image of him. In theophanies, manifests as the kavod (glory): Moses sees only his "back" (Exodus 33:23) but never his face ("no man shall see me and live", Exodus 33:20); Isaiah sees him enthroned, high and lifted up, his train filling the temple (Isaiah 6:1); Ezekiel sees the chariot-throne and the four-faced cherubim (Ezekiel 1); Daniel sees the Ancient of Days, white-haired, on the throne of fire (Daniel 7:9-10).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Exodus 33:18-23, 20:4; Isaiah 6:1-4; Ezekiel 1:4-28; Daniel 7:9-10
nodes.significantEvent: Creates heaven and earth (Genesis 1-2). Covenants with Noah (Genesis 9), Abraham (Genesis 15, 17), Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19-24), David (2 Samuel 7). Calls Abram from Ur. Delivers Israel from Egypt (Exodus 1-15). Gives the law at Sinai. Conducts Israel through the wilderness, into Canaan. Speaks through prophets (Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, etc.). Permits the Babylonian exile and the destruction of the First Temple (586 BCE) as judgment, then returns the people via Cyrus. Promises the messianic restoration.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Genesis 1-50; Exodus through Deuteronomy; the historical books; the prophets
familyRoles: father (creator-father of all, covenant-father of Israel)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Theological — uncreated, eternal (Psalm 90:2 'from everlasting to everlasting you are God')

nodes.name: Allah
nodes.domain: the One God of Islam (al-Wāḥid al-Aḥad), creator (al-Khāliq), most merciful (al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm), the source of revelation, the only deity (lā ilāha illā Allāh, "there is no god but Allah" — the first part of the shahāda); identified with the God of the Hebrew Bible and Christianity per Islamic theology
nodes.domain_source: The Quran in toto, especially Surah al-Fātiḥah (1, the opening chapter, recited in every prayer); Surah al-Ikhlāṣ (112, the chapter of pure monotheism); Ayat al-Kursī (the Throne Verse, 2:255); the 99 Beautiful Names (al-asmāʾ al-ḥusnā); Hadith literature; classical kalām (Islamic systematic theology) — Ashʿarī, Māturīdī, Muʿtazilī schools
nodes.object: the Quran (his very speech, kalām Allāh, uncreated per the Ashʿarī majority); the Pen (al-qalam, with which the divine decree was written, Surah 68:1, 96:4); the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ, Surah 85:22); the Throne (al-ʿArsh, Surah 20:5, 7:54); the Footstool/Seat (al-Kursī, Surah 2:255)
nodes.characterTrait: al-Raḥmān (the Merciful — most-frequent divine name in Quran), al-Raḥīm (the Compassionate), al-Mālik (the King), al-Quddūs (the Holy), al-Salām (the Peace), al-Ḥakīm (the Wise), al-Khāliq (the Creator), al-ʿAdl (the Just), al-Ḥaqq (the Truth), and ~90 other Beautiful Names
nodes.characterTrait_source: Quran passim; the Beautiful Names tradition (al-asmāʾ al-ḥusnā), enumerated in Tirmidhi and other ḥadīth collections
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Aniconic per Islamic theology — no image of Allah is permissible, and depictions are strictly forbidden. Allah is laysa kamithlihi shayʾ ("there is nothing like Him", Surah 42:11). The Quran uses anthropomorphic-but-incomparable language: established on his Throne (istawā ʿalā l-ʿarsh, Surah 20:5); has hands (Surah 5:64, "Allah's hand is over their hands"; Surah 38:75, "what I created with my own two hands"); face (Surah 28:88, "Everything will perish except his face"); eyes (Surah 11:37, "build the ship under our eyes"). Classical kalām: the Atharī school reads literally with bilā kayf ("without asking how"); the Ashʿarī and Māturīdī schools allow metaphorical/figurative interpretation; the Muʿtazilī read all anthropomorphic language metaphorically.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Quran 42:11, 20:5, 5:64, 38:75, 28:88, 11:37; classical Islamic theology
nodes.significantEvent: Creates the heavens and earth in six days (Surah 7:54, 10:3, 32:4); creates Adam from clay (Surah 15:26-29); commands the angels and Iblīs to bow to Adam; covenants with the prophets — Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, Solomon, Jesus, Muhammad and others (Surah 33:7, the Covenant of the Prophets); reveals the Tawrāt (Torah) to Moses, the Zabūr (Psalms) to David, the Injīl (Gospel) to Jesus, and finally the Quran to Muhammad piecemeal over 23 years via Gabriel; will judge all souls on the Last Day.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Quran passim; especially 7:11-25 (Adam-Iblīs narrative), 33:7 (Covenant of Prophets), 96:1-5 (first revelation), 99 (the Last Day)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Surah 112:3 — "He begets not, nor is He begotten" (lam yalid wa lam yūlad)

nodes.name: God-the-Father
nodes.domain: first person of the Christian Trinity, identified with YHWH of the Hebrew Bible, Father of Jesus Christ "in a unique sense" (only-begotten, John 3:16) and Father of all believers by adoption (Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6)
nodes.domain_source: New Testament passim; principally the Synoptic Gospels and John on Jesus's relation to the Father; the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:9-13 / Luke 11:2-4); the Gethsemane prayer (Matthew 26:39-42); the Trinitarian formulae (Matthew 28:19, 2 Corinthians 13:14, Ephesians 4:4-6); the Apostles' Creed; the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (325/381 CE); the Athanasian Creed; classical Trinitarian theology (Cappadocian Fathers, Augustine, Aquinas)
nodes.object: throne (Revelation 4-5); the seven seals (Revelation 5); the Lamb beside the throne (=Christ); the Holy Spirit proceeding from him (Western Christian filioque) or from him through the Son (Eastern Orthodox)
nodes.object_source: Revelation 4-5; the Nicene Creed and the filioque controversy
nodes.characterTrait: Father, all-loving (1 John 4:8 "God is love"), just, merciful, omniscient, omnipotent, omnipresent, source (archē, fons divinitatis) within the Trinity — the principle from which the Son is eternally begotten and the Spirit eternally proceeds
nodes.characterTrait_source: NT passim; classical Trinitarian theology
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Aniconic in early Christian theology (continuous with Jewish aniconism). Explicit depictions of the Father in Christian art emerge late (medieval period), are theologically contested (Eastern Orthodox iconography traditionally restricted depictions of the Father; the Council of the Hundred Chapters, Moscow 1551, debated this), and follow the Daniel 7:9 "Ancient of Days" type — bearded white-haired old man enthroned. Scripturally described as Spirit (John 4:24).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: John 4:24; Daniel 7:9 (the Ancient of Days type adopted into Christian Father-iconography); Stoglavy Synod 1551
nodes.significantEvent: In Christian theology: creates the world (with the Son and through the Spirit, per the Trinitarian doctrine of inseparable divine operations); covenants with Israel; sends the Son to incarnate (John 3:16); raises Jesus from the dead (Acts 2:24, Romans 4:24); pours out the Holy Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2); will be all-in-all at the consummation (1 Corinthians 15:28).
nodes.significantEvent_source: NT passim; the Christian creedal tradition
nodes.birthTypes_source: Christian theology — uncreated, eternal

nodes.name: Holy Spirit
nodes.domain: third person of the Christian Trinity (Pneuma Hagion in Greek, Spiritus Sanctus in Latin); the breath/wind of God (Hebrew rūaḥ, also feminine grammatically); presence of God; sanctifier; gift-giver; comforter (paraclete, John 14:26); the indwelling presence in believers
nodes.domain_source: Genesis 1:2 (the rūaḥ ʾĕlōhīm hovering over the waters); Numbers 11:25; Judges 14-15 (the Spirit empowers Samson); 1 Samuel 16:13 (the Spirit comes upon David); Isaiah 11:2, 61:1; Joel 2:28-29 (the eschatological outpouring); the four Gospels (descent at Jesus's baptism — Mark 1:10, etc.); Acts 2 (Pentecost); 1 Corinthians 12 (the gifts); Romans 8 (the indwelling Spirit); the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed
nodes.object: wind/breath (rūaḥ, pneuma — the etymological objects); fire (the tongues of fire at Pentecost, Acts 2:3-4); oil (the chrism of anointing, anciently associated with the Spirit); water (the baptismal sign, John 3:5)
nodes.object_source: Acts 2:2-4; biblical use of the Spirit-symbols of wind, fire, oil, water
nodes.animals_source: Mark 1:10 par. Matthew 3:16, Luke 3:22, John 1:32 — at Jesus's baptism, the Holy Spirit descends "as a dove" upon him. This is the canonical symbolic embodiment-form of the Spirit.
nodes.characterTrait: comforter (paraclete), advocate, sanctifier, gift-giver, breath, indwelling presence, "the Spirit of truth" (John 14:17, 16:13), interceding with "groanings too deep for words" (Romans 8:26)
nodes.characterTrait_source: John 14-16 (the farewell discourse); Romans 8
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Aniconic; manifests as breath/wind, as the dove descending at Jesus's baptism (Mark 1:10), as tongues of fire at Pentecost (Acts 2:3-4). The Hebrew rūaḥ is grammatically feminine; the Greek pneuma is grammatically neuter; the Latin spiritus is grammatically masculine — leading to varying gendering of the Spirit across Christian languages and traditions (Syriac Christianity preserved a feminine-Spirit emphasis especially in the early period).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Mark 1:10; Acts 2:1-4; etymology of rūaḥ / pneuma / spiritus
nodes.significantEvent: Hovers over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2). Empowers prophets, judges, and kings (Numbers 11:25, Judges 14, 1 Samuel 10). The Messianic Spirit (Isaiah 11:2). Conceives Jesus in Mary (Luke 1:35). Descends as dove at Jesus's baptism (Mark 1:10). Drives Jesus into the wilderness (Mark 1:12). Leads Jesus throughout his ministry. Promised by Jesus as the Paraclete (John 14:16, 26). Descends at Pentecost in tongues of fire (Acts 2). Indwells believers (Romans 8); distributes gifts (1 Corinthians 12); produces fruit in believers (Galatians 5:22-23).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Genesis 1:2; Mark 1:10; Acts 2; Pauline corpus
nodes.birthTypes_source: Christian theology — eternally proceeds from the Father (and from the Son, per Western filioque clause)

nodes.name: Iblis
nodes.domain: Islamic primary devil-figure; refuser of obeisance to Adam; ancestor of the shayāṭīn (devils/satans); whisperer (al-waswās); accursed (al-rajīm)
nodes.domain_source: Quran: 2:34, 7:11-25, 15:28-43, 17:61-65, 18:50, 20:115-123, 38:71-85; ḥadīth tradition; classical Islamic exegesis (Tabari, Ibn Kathir)
nodes.object: whisperings (waswasa) — his characteristic mode of action upon humans; the throne / seat upon which he attempts to be exalted
nodes.object_source: Quran 50:16, 114:1-6 (the surah of refuge, against the whisperings of the slinking whisperer)
nodes.characterTrait: arrogant (the cardinal sin in his refusal), prideful, refusing, deceiving, granted respite, despairing-of-mercy
nodes.characterTrait_source: Quran 7:12 (his refusal: "I am better than him; you created me from fire and him from clay"); 38:74-75 (his pride); 17:62 (his boast)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: In Quranic theology, Iblīs is a jinn — created from smokeless fire (Quran 15:27, 55:15) — not an angel. The Quran says explicitly "he was of the jinn and disobeyed his Lord's command" (Surah 18:50), which addresses the apparent puzzle: when Allah commanded the angels to bow to Adam, Iblīs refused; how could he refuse if angels by definition obey? The classical answer is that he was among the angels but not of their nature — a jinn raised among them.
nodes.significantEvent: When Allah creates Adam from clay and commands the angels to bow to him, Iblīs refuses, citing his fiery superiority over Adam's clay (Quran 7:12, 15:33, 38:76). For this refusal he is cursed and expelled from heaven (Surah 7:13-18). He requests respite until the Day of Resurrection to tempt humanity, which is granted: "I will lie in wait for them on your straight path; I will come at them from before and behind, from their right and their left, and you will not find most of them grateful" (Surah 7:16-17). He whispers to Adam and Eve in the garden, leading to their fall (Surah 7:20-22, 20:120). At the Last Day, he will disavow his followers (Surah 14:22).
nodes.birthCircumstances: Created from smokeless fire as a jinn; raised among the angels.
nodes.deathTypes_source: Quran 7:14-15 — granted respite until the Day of Resurrection
nodes.deathCircumstances: Granted respite by Allah until the Day of Resurrection (Quran 7:14-15); his ultimate fate is final separation in the Fire (the Day of Disavowal, Surah 14:22).

nodes.name: Asmodeus
nodes.domain: demon of lust and marriage-disrupting; in Tobit kills Sarah's seven husbands; in rabbinic tradition the king of demons (under or alongside Solomon); etymologically from Persian/Avestan Aēšma-daēva (the demon of Wrath)
nodes.domain_source: Tobit 3:7-17, 6:14-18, 8:1-3 (Catholic/Orthodox deuterocanon); b. Pesachim 110a; b. Gittin 68a-b (Asmodeus and Solomon — he tricks Solomon and rules in his place); Testament of Solomon (Christian-era pseudepigraphon, c. 1st-3rd c. CE); the etymological link to Avestan Aēšma-daēva is established in scholarship (cf. Yasht 11.6)
nodes.object: in Tobit, the heart and liver of the great fish (which Tobias burns to drive him out); in Testament of Solomon, the bonds with which Solomon binds him
nodes.object_source: Tobit 6:7, 8:2-3; Testament of Solomon 5
nodes.characterTrait: lustful, jealous, rage-formed (per the Persian etymology), cunning, kingly-among-demons
nodes.characterTrait_source: Tobit 3:8 (kills the seven husbands "out of jealousy"); Testament of Solomon 5; b. Gittin 68
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: In the Testament of Solomon, three-headed (with the heads of an ox, a human, and a ram), or sometimes with cock-feet and the legs of a serpent; in Tobit, no physical description.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Testament of Solomon 5
nodes.significantEvent: In Tobit, kills Sarah's seven successive bridegrooms on their wedding nights, before consummation, out of jealous love for her. Tobias arrives, Raphael instructs him to burn the heart and liver of the great fish on coals; the smoke drives Asmodeus to the deserts of Upper Egypt where Raphael binds him (Tobit 8:2-3). In the Babylonian Talmud (b. Gittin 68), Solomon needs the shamir worm to cut stones for the Temple without iron; only Asmodeus knows where it is. Solomon's servant Benaiah captures Asmodeus by inebriating him; Asmodeus eventually escapes, throws Solomon to the ends of the earth, and rules in Solomon's likeness for a time. In the Testament of Solomon, Asmodeus's undoing is the angel Raphael and the smoke of fish liver — explicitly drawing on Tobit.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Tobit 3-8; b. Gittin 68a-b; Testament of Solomon 5
nodes.eventTypes_source: Tobit; b. Gittin; Testament of Solomon
nodes.birthTypes_source: Demonological tradition — created/begotten of the demonic order
nodes.birthCircumstances: Demonic; etymologically derived from the Avestan Aēšma-daēva ("Wrath-demon"), one of the dēvas opposed to Ahura Mazda in Zoroastrianism. The figure is imported into Second-Temple Judaism (Tobit, c. 3rd-2nd c. BCE) and naturalized into rabbinic and Christian demonology.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Avestan Yasht 11.6; the Tobit-Talmud-Solomonic literature

nodes.name: Beelzebub
nodes.domain: prince of demons in the New Testament; Hebrew Bible: the Philistine god of Ekron (Baal-Zebub, "Lord of the Flies" — a polemical Hebrew distortion of Canaanite Baal-Zebul "Prince Baal"); in later Christian demonology, one of the chief princes of hell
nodes.domain_source: 2 Kings 1:2-16 (Ahaziah inquires of "Baal-Zebub the god of Ekron"); Mark 3:22, Matthew 12:24, Luke 11:15 (Beelzebul as "the prince of demons"); Matthew 10:25; Testament of Solomon 6 (Beelzebul as fallen prince of angels); medieval Christian demonology (the four crown princes of hell)
nodes.object: in Testament of Solomon, the seal-ring with which Solomon binds him
nodes.object_source: Testament of Solomon 6
nodes.animals_source: Per the Hebrew name baʿal zebûb "lord of the flies" (2 Kings 1:2). The fly is the symbolic-emblematic animal of the polemical Hebrew name. The original Canaanite-Philistine name was baʿal zəbūl ("Prince Baal"), distorted to "Lord of the Flies" by Hebrew biblical polemic.
nodes.characterTrait: deceitful, prince-of-demons, accuser, in NT the alleged source of Jesus's exorcistic power per Pharisaic accusation
nodes.characterTrait_source: Mark 3:22-30 par. (the Beelzebul controversy); Testament of Solomon 6
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: In the Testament of Solomon, formerly the highest-ranking angel, now leader of the demons. Medieval demonology (e.g., Le Grand Grimoire) gives various horrific descriptions; these are post-biblical accretions.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Testament of Solomon 6; medieval Christian demonology
nodes.significantEvent: In 2 Kings 1, the Israelite king Ahaziah, after falling through a lattice, sends to inquire of Baal-Zebub the god of Ekron whether he will recover; the prophet Elijah intercepts the messengers and announces Ahaziah's death for inquiring of a foreign god. In the Synoptic Gospels, the Pharisees accuse Jesus of casting out demons by Beelzebul; Jesus responds with the "kingdom divided against itself" parable (Mark 3:22-27). In the Testament of Solomon, Solomon binds Beelzebul and forces him to confess his identity as a former chief angel.
nodes.significantEvent_source: 2 Kings 1:2-16; Mark 3:22-30 par.; Testament of Solomon 6
nodes.eventTypes_source: 2 Kings; Synoptic Gospels; Testament of Solomon
nodes.birthTypes_source: Demonological tradition; in Testament of Solomon, originally a chief angel who fell
nodes.birthCircumstances: In origin a Canaanite/Philistine deity (Baal-Zebul, "Prince Baal"), demonized by Hebrew biblical polemic into Baal-Zebub ("Lord of the Flies"); naturalized into Second-Temple Jewish and NT demonology as a prince of demons.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: 2 Kings 1; Synoptic Gospels; the Hebrew zebul/zebub etymology

nodes.name: Azazel
nodes.domain: in Leviticus 16, the wilderness-recipient of the Yom Kippur scapegoat; in 1 Enoch, chief of the Watchers — the fallen angels who taught humanity forbidden arts; the prototype of the corrupting fallen angel
nodes.domain_source: Leviticus 16:8, 16:10, 16:26 (the scapegoat sent "to Azazel"); 1 Enoch 6-13 (the Book of the Watchers — Azazel as chief of the Watchers); 1 Enoch 8:1-3 (Azazel teaches sword-making, armor, women's adornments); 1 Enoch 9:6, 10:4-8 (Azazel's judgment); 4 Q En (Qumran Enoch fragments); Apocalypse of Abraham 13-14 (Azazel as the fallen serpent)
nodes.object: in 1 Enoch, the metallurgical and military arts he teaches humans (swords, knives, shields, breastplates, ornaments and dyes, antimony for the eyes); in his judgment, the jagged rocks of Dudael under which he is bound
nodes.object_source: 1 Enoch 8:1-3 (the forbidden arts); 1 Enoch 10:4-6 (binding in Dudael)
nodes.characterTrait: corrupting, knowledge-revealing, transgressive, prideful, ultimately bound and condemned
nodes.characterTrait_source: 1 Enoch 6-10; Apocalypse of Abraham 14
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: In 1 Enoch, an angelic Watcher (one of the bnê hāʾĕlōhīm of Genesis 6:1-4); in Apocalypse of Abraham 23, takes the form of a great serpent or peacock-winged dragon when leading the daughters of men astray.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: 1 Enoch 6-10; Apocalypse of Abraham 23
nodes.significantEvent: In Leviticus 16, the high priest casts lots over two goats on Yom Kippur — one "for YHWH", one "for Azazel". The Azazel-goat receives the symbolic transfer of Israel's sins and is sent into the wilderness, "to Azazel". Whether "Azazel" here is a place-name, a desert-demon, or a personified abstraction is debated. In 1 Enoch 6-13, two hundred Watchers descend on Mount Hermon and lust after human women, taking them as wives and producing the Nephilim giants. Azazel is named as their chief; he teaches humanity metalworking (especially weapons), women's makeup, sorcery, and astrology. The four archangels (Michael, Sariel, Raphael, Gabriel) plead with God; Raphael is sent to bind Azazel hand and foot, cast him into Dudael in the wilderness, cover him with jagged rocks, and leave him in darkness until the Day of Judgment, when he will be cast into the fire.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Leviticus 16; 1 Enoch 6-10
