nodes.birthTypes_source: 1 Enoch — among the Watchers (bnê ʾĕlōhīm)
nodes.birthCircumstances: Originally an angelic Watcher; among the two hundred who descend on Mount Hermon and fall through lust for human women (Genesis 6:1-4 / 1 Enoch 6).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: 1 Enoch 6:1-7
nodes.deathCircumstances: Bound by Raphael at God's command; cast into Dudael in the wilderness; covered with jagged rocks; left in darkness until the Day of Judgment when he will be cast into the fire forever (1 Enoch 10:4-8).

nodes.name: Samael
nodes.domain: rabbinic angel of death and venom (Hebrew sam = "poison/drug"); the angel-rider of the serpent of Eden; in Kabbalah, the consort of Lilith and the demonic counterpart of YHWH; in some traditions identified with Satan
nodes.domain_source: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan to Genesis 3 (Samael riding the serpent); Pirkei de Rabbi Eliezer 13, 21 (Samael, Eve, and the serpent); 3 Enoch 14:2, 26:12 (Samael in the heavenly court); Treatise on the Left Emanation (Isaac ha-Cohen, 13th c. — Samael and Lilith as the demonic dyad); Zohar passim; Bahir
nodes.object: serpent (which he rides); the cup of poison (sam = poison, hence his name "venom of God")
nodes.object_source: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan to Genesis 3:6; Pirkei de Rabbi Eliezer 13
nodes.characterTrait: poisonous, deceiving, accusing, prideful, in Kabbalah the head of the sitra aḥra ("the other side")
nodes.characterTrait_source: Pirkei de Rabbi Eliezer 13; 3 Enoch; Treatise on the Left Emanation
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Angelic in form; in Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, he is the angel who rides the serpent (the serpent being his mount, not himself); in the Treatise on the Left Emanation and the Zohar, the head of a counter-divine pleroma whose ten emanations parallel the ten Sefirot. Sometimes described as one-eyed.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan to Genesis 3:6; Treatise on the Left Emanation; Zohar
nodes.significantEvent: In Pirkei de Rabbi Eliezer 13, Samael is the chief of the heavenly hosts who envies Adam's status and descends to earth, riding the serpent, to seduce Eve. In Kabbalistic tradition (especially Isaac ha-Cohen's Treatise on the Left Emanation, c. 1240s), Samael is the demonic counterpart of YHWH, paired with Lilith as the demonic counterpart of the Shekhinah. In rabbinic tradition (b. Bava Batra 16a), Samael, Satan, and the angel of death are one and the same — the seducer who descends, the accuser who ascends, and the executioner.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Pirkei de Rabbi Eliezer 13, 21; b. Bava Batra 16a; Treatise on the Left Emanation; Zohar
nodes.eventTypes_source: Pirkei de Rabbi Eliezer; Talmud; Kabbalistic literature
nodes.birthTypes_source: Rabbinic angelology
nodes.birthCircumstances: Angelic; in Pirkei de Rabbi Eliezer, the chief of the heavenly hosts before his fall.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Pirkei de Rabbi Eliezer 13

nodes.name: Mastema
nodes.domain: prince of evil spirits in the Book of Jubilees; accuser, tester; given charge of one-tenth of the evil spirits to do God's work of testing humanity; sometimes identified with Satan (the name mastēmâ means "hostility/animosity")
nodes.domain_source: Jubilees 10:7-12, 11:5, 11:11, 17:15-18, 18:9-12, 48:2-3, 48:9-19 (the principal source); Damascus Document (CD-A); 4 Q387 fr. 2 (Qumran); 1 QM (the War Scroll) uses the term mastēmâ for the spirits of Belial's lot
nodes.object: one-tenth of the evil spirits (granted to him by God after the flood for the work of testing humanity)
nodes.object_source: Jubilees 10:8-9
nodes.characterTrait_source: Jubilees 10-18; Qumran texts
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Angelic prince; not visually described in detail in the sources.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Jubilees
nodes.significantEvent: In Jubilees 10:8-12, after the flood, Noah prays for protection from the evil spirits troubling his grandchildren; God commands the angels to bind all the evil spirits, but Mastema asks for one-tenth to be left to him for the work of testing humanity. God grants this. In Jubilees 17:15-18, Mastema is the prosecuting accuser who proposes the testing of Abraham (the Akedah) — equivalent to Satan in Job. In Jubilees 48:2-3, Mastema is the angel who attacks Moses on the way to Egypt (= Exodus 4:24-26, where YHWH himself attacks Moses; Jubilees rewrites this as Mastema). In Jubilees 48:9-19, Mastema and his spirits aid the Egyptian magicians against Moses.
nodes.birthTypes_source: Jubilees — angelic origin
nodes.birthCircumstances: Angelic prince; possibly originally one of the Watchers, or possibly a separate divine official.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Jubilees

nodes.name: Shekhinah
nodes.domain: divine presence (literally "dwelling", from the root šākan "to dwell"); the indwelling presence of God in the Tabernacle, the Temple, with Israel in exile, with the studious; in Kabbalah, the tenth Sefirah (Malkhut), the divine femininity, the "bride" of Tiferet seeking reunion
nodes.domain_source: Targum Onkelos passim (substituting "the Shekhinah of YHWH" where the Hebrew has YHWH himself in anthropomorphic contexts); m. Avot 3:2 (where two study Torah, the Shekhinah is between them); b. Sanhedrin 39a; b. Berakhot 6a; Sifre Numbers 161 (the Shekhinah's exile with Israel); Zohar; Sefer Yetzirah; Bahir; Lurianic Kabbalah
nodes.object: cloud of presence (Exodus 40:34-35, the cloud that fills the Tabernacle); the kavod (glory) of YHWH; in Kabbalah, the Sefirah of Malkhut; the moon (in lunar-Shekhinah symbolism)
nodes.object_source: Exodus 40:34-35; 1 Kings 8:10-11 (the cloud filling Solomon's Temple); Targum Onkelos; Zohar
nodes.characterTrait: indwelling, intimate, mournful (in exile), wandering with Israel, the divine feminine
nodes.characterTrait_source: Targum Onkelos; rabbinic literature; Kabbalah
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Aniconic in classical rabbinic theology; in Kabbalah, the lowest Sefirah (Malkhut/Kingdom), the divine femininity who receives from the upper Sefirot; in Lurianic Kabbalah, in exile (galut ha-shekhinah) since the destruction of the Temple, awaiting reunion with Tiferet at the messianic restoration.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Targum Onkelos; Kabbalistic tradition
nodes.significantEvent: Dwells in the Tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-35: "the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of YHWH filled the tabernacle"). Fills Solomon's Temple at its dedication (1 Kings 8:10-11). Departs from the First Temple before its destruction (Ezekiel 10-11 — the kavod departs from the threshold, then over the city, then to the eastern mountain). Goes into exile with Israel (Sifre Numbers 161, b. Megillah 29a — "wherever Israel was exiled, the Shekhinah was exiled with them"). In Kabbalah, awaits reunion with the upper Sefirot at the messianic age; her exile is the cosmic problem that prayer and mitzvot work to repair (tikkun).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Exodus 40:34-35; 1 Kings 8:10-11; Ezekiel 10-11; b. Megillah 29a; Lurianic Kabbalah
familyRoles: mother of the people of Israel
nodes.birthTypes_source: In rabbinic theology, an aspect of YHWH's presence (not a separate being); in Kabbalah, the tenth Sefirah, eternally emanating from the divine root

nodes.name: Sandalphon
nodes.domain: archangel of song and prayer; weaver of crowns from the prayers of Israel; in some traditions identified with the prophet Elijah ascended; companion or twin of Metatron; one of the great angelic princes of the divine throne
nodes.domain_source: b. Hagigah 13b (the principal source); Hekhalot Rabbati; Sefer Hekhalot (3 Enoch); Pirkei de Rabbi Eliezer 4; medieval angelology; Maaseh Merkavah
nodes.object: crowns (which he weaves from the prayers of Israel and crowns God with); the throne-chariot (he stands behind it)
nodes.object_source: b. Hagigah 13b; Hekhalot Rabbati
nodes.characterTrait: musical, prayer-weaving, immense in stature, towering
nodes.characterTrait_source: b. Hagigah 13b
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: In b. Hagigah 13b: "Sandalphon stands behind the chariot and weaves crowns for his Master out of the prayers [of Israel]... his height is a journey of 500 years", a hyperbolic expression of his cosmic stature. His name is of disputed Greek origin — possibly synadelphos ("brother together with") in reference to Metatron, or related to sandalion ("sandal/threshold").
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: b. Hagigah 13b
nodes.significantEvent: Stands behind the divine throne-chariot (merkavah); receives the prayers of Israel as they ascend through the heavens; weaves them into crowns; speaks the divine name and the crowns mount up of themselves to crown God (b. Hagigah 13b). In some Hekhalot and medieval traditions, the ascended prophet Elijah (2 Kings 2:11), now serving as the angel of fire and song. Sometimes paired or contrasted with Metatron — both are exalted angelic figures, both are in some traditions transformed mortals (Metatron from Enoch, Sandalphon from Elijah).
nodes.significantEvent_source: b. Hagigah 13b; Hekhalot Rabbati; medieval angelology
nodes.birthTypes_source: In Elijah-identification: 2 Kings 2:11 (Elijah's ascension)
nodes.birthCircumstances: Created angelic being; in some traditions, identified with the ascended prophet Elijah (taken up to heaven by a fiery chariot, 2 Kings 2:11), now serving as the angel of fire and song.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: 2 Kings 2:11; medieval angelology

nodes.name: Leviathan
nodes.domain: cosmic sea-monster; primordial chaos-serpent; eschatological beast; Hebrew livyātān, cognate of the Ugaritic Lotan/Litan
nodes.domain_source: Job 41 (the principal description); Job 3:8 ("those who curse the day, who are skilled to rouse up Leviathan"); Psalm 74:14 ("you crushed the heads of Leviathan"); Psalm 104:26 (Leviathan plays in the sea); Isaiah 27:1 ("YHWH with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan, the fleeing serpent, the twisting serpent, and slay the dragon that is in the sea"); 1 Enoch 60:7-9; 4 Ezra 6:49-52; 2 Baruch 29:4; b. Bava Batra 74b-75a (rabbinic eschatological feast)
nodes.animals_source: Symbolic embodiment as the cosmic-sea adversary. Job 41:1 (livyātān = the great fish/sea-creature); Isaiah 27:1 (nāḥāš bārîaḥ "fleeing serpent" and nāḥāš ʿăqallātôn "twisting serpent" — close verbal parallels to the Ugaritic descriptors of Lotan).
nodes.characterTrait: monstrous, untamable by humans, primordial-sea-formed, defeated/fed-to-the-righteous in eschatology
nodes.characterTrait_source: Job 41; rabbinic eschatology
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Job 41 description: rows of shields are his back, sealed close as with a tight seal; his sneezings flash forth light, his eyes are like the eyelids of dawn; out of his mouth go flaming torches, sparks of fire leap forth; from his nostrils come forth smoke as from a boiling pot; his breath kindles coals, a flame comes forth from his mouth; his sinews are knit together, his flesh is firm, no weapon avails against him.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Job 41:7-29 (the entire description)
nodes.significantEvent: Crushed by YHWH in primordial combat (Psalm 74:14, "you crushed the heads of Leviathan in pieces, you gave him as food to the creatures of the wilderness"). Plays in the sea (Psalm 104:26, the more domesticated reading). Will be slain by YHWH at the end of days (Isaiah 27:1). In rabbinic tradition (b. Bava Batra 74b-75a), Leviathan and Behemoth were originally created male and female; God killed the female to prevent their reproduction (which would have destroyed the world); both will be slain at the messianic age and fed to the righteous at the eschatological banquet, with the sukkot of the righteous made of Leviathan's skin.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Psalm 74:14; Psalm 104:26; Isaiah 27:1; b. Bava Batra 74b-75a
birthTypes: primordial monster — created on the fifth day (rabbinic)
nodes.birthTypes_source: b. Bava Batra 74b (created on the fifth day, originally male and female)
nodes.birthCircumstances: Primordial sea-monster; in rabbinic tradition (b. Bava Batra 74b), created on the fifth day of creation, originally as a male-female pair; God killed the female to prevent their offspring from destroying the world.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: b. Bava Batra 74b; Isaiah 27:1
nodes.deathCircumstances: Crushed by YHWH at creation (Psalm 74:14); will be slain by YHWH at the end of days (Isaiah 27:1); in rabbinic eschatology, slain and fed to the righteous at the messianic banquet.

nodes.name: Behemoth
nodes.domain: cosmic land-monster; primordial chaos-beast; Hebrew bĕhēmôt (intensive plural of bĕhēmâ "beast"); paired with Leviathan as the great primordial creatures of land and sea
nodes.domain_source: Job 40:15-24 (the principal description); 1 Enoch 60:7-10 (paired with Leviathan); 4 Ezra 6:49-52; 2 Baruch 29:4; b. Bava Batra 74b-75a
nodes.animals_source: Symbolic embodiment as the primordial land-beast. Job 40:15 ("Behemoth, which I made as I made you, eats grass like an ox"). Modern interpretation often identifies the Job description with the hippopotamus (or possibly an elephant or aurochs), though in apocalyptic and rabbinic tradition Behemoth is a primordial cosmic beast vastly greater than any natural creature.
nodes.characterTrait: monstrous, immovable, primordial-land-formed, peaceful-grazing in Job's description but cosmically vast
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Job 40 description: eats grass like an ox; his strength is in his loins; his power in the muscles of his belly; he makes his tail stiff like a cedar; the sinews of his thighs are knit together; his bones are tubes of bronze, his limbs like bars of iron; he is the first of the great acts of God; he lies under the lotus plants in the covert of the reeds and in the marsh; though the river is turbulent he is not frightened; he is confident even when Jordan rushes against his mouth.
nodes.significantEvent: God's second exhibit to Job after the bird-and-beast catalogue (Job 40:15-24); paired with Leviathan in Job 40-41 as the cosmic creatures God displays to demonstrate his power. In 1 Enoch 60:7-9, separated from Leviathan at creation: "the female monster is named Leviathan, to dwell in the abysses of the ocean over the fountains of the waters, but the male is named Behemoth, who occupies with his breast a waste wilderness named Dendain". In rabbinic eschatology (b. Bava Batra 75a), both will be slain at the messianic age and fed to the righteous at the eschatological banquet.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Job 40:15-24; 1 Enoch 60:7-10; b. Bava Batra 75a
birthTypes: primordial — first of God's great works
nodes.birthTypes_source: Job 40:19 ("he is the first of the works of God"); 1 Enoch 60:7-9
nodes.birthCircumstances: Primordial; "the first of the works of God" (Job 40:19); separated from Leviathan at creation (1 Enoch 60:7-9, where Behemoth dwells on the dry land of Dendain and Leviathan in the deeps).
nodes.deathCircumstances: In rabbinic eschatology, slain at the messianic age and fed to the righteous at the eschatological banquet alongside Leviathan.

nodes.name: Asherah (Israelite)
nodes.tradition: Abrahamic (Iron-Age Israelite, continuation of Canaanite Athirat)
nodes.domain: Iron-Age Israelite goddess; continuation in Israelite religion of the Canaanite Athirat tradition; per the Kuntillet ʿAjrud and Khirbet el-Qom inscriptions, consort of YHWH in popular Iron-Age religion (contested); the asherah-pole is her cultic emblem condemned by the Deuteronomistic Historians; possibly identical with the "Queen of Heaven" of Jeremiah
nodes.domain_source: Kuntillet ʿAjrud inscriptions (8th c. BCE Hebrew, on storage jars and plaster — "YHWH of Samaria and his Asherah", "YHWH of Teman and his Asherah"); Khirbet el-Qom Inscription III (8th c. BCE — "Uriyahu the rich wrote it: blessed be Uriyahu by YHWH and by his Asherah"); Deuteronomy 7:5, 12:3, 16:21; Judges 3:7, 6:25-30; 1 Kings 14:15, 14:23, 15:13, 16:33, 18:19; 2 Kings 13:6, 17:10, 17:16, 18:4, 21:3, 21:7, 23:4, 23:6-7, 23:14-15; Jeremiah 7:18, 44:17-25 ("the Queen of Heaven", malkat ha-šāmayim — debated identification); Judean pillar figurines (8th-7th c. BCE; Kletter 1996)
nodes.object: the asherah / asherah-pole — her wooden cultic emblem (sacred tree or pillar) frequently planted beside altars and high places, condemned in Deuteronomistic polemic; the Judean pillar figurines (popular Iron-Age clay matron-figurines, often attributed to her cult); cakes and incense and libations offered to the "Queen of Heaven" by the women of Judah (Jeremiah 44:19)
nodes.object_source: Deuteronomy 16:21; 2 Kings 21:7 (Manasseh's asherah image in the Temple); 2 Kings 23:6 (Josiah destroys it); Jeremiah 44:19; Kletter 1996 *The Judean Pillar-Figurines*
nodes.characterTrait: maternal, fertility-associated, popular among Iron-Age Israelites and Judeans (especially women per Jeremiah 44), consort of YHWH in popular religion (contested), suppressed by the Deuteronomistic reforms
nodes.characterTrait_source: Kuntillet ʿAjrud / Khirbet el-Qom inscriptions; Jeremiah 44:15-25; Hebrew Bible polemic against the asherah-cult
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: No formal cult-statue with confirmed Asherah-identification has survived; the cultic emblem is the wooden asherah-pole or sacred tree (per the Hebrew Bible polemic against "groves" and "trees"). The Judean pillar figurines (8th-7th c. BCE, ~1000 known examples) — small clay matron-figurines with prominent breasts and pillar-bodies — are popularly attributed to her cult, though the identification is contested.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Hebrew Bible polemic; Kletter 1996
nodes.significantEvent: Continuation of Late Bronze Age Canaanite Athirat (the Ugaritic mother of the seventy gods, consort of El) in Iron-Age Israelite popular religion. The Kuntillet ʿAjrud and Khirbet el-Qom inscriptions (8th c. BCE) attest "YHWH and his Asherah" in popular blessing-formulae — the major epigraphic challenge to a uniformly aniconic, monotheistic early Israelite religion. The Deuteronomistic Historians polemicize against the asherah-pole and suppress her cult: 2 Kings 18:4 (Hezekiah cuts down the asherah), 2 Kings 21:7 (Manasseh installs an asherah in the Jerusalem Temple itself), 2 Kings 23:6-7 (Josiah destroys it). Jeremiah 7:18 and 44:17-25 polemicize against the worship of the "Queen of Heaven" (malkat ha-šāmayim) by women baking cakes for her — possibly Asherah, though the identification is debated (also could be Astarte/Ishtar).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Kuntillet ʿAjrud and Khirbet el-Qom inscriptions; 2 Kings 18:4, 21:7, 23:6-7; Jeremiah 7:18, 44:17-25
nodes.birthTypes_source: Continuation from Late Bronze Age Canaanite Athirat

nodes.name: Frigg
nodes.domain: queen of the Aesir, marriage, motherhood, foreknowledge (sees fate without speaking), the household, the divine matron — wife of Odin and mother of Baldr
nodes.domain_source: Snorri, Gylfaginning 9, 20, 35, 49; Vǫluspá 33; Vafþrúðnismál 1-4; Lokasenna 25-29; Grímnismál prose introduction; Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum 1.7 (the Frigg-Othinus narrative)
nodes.object: her hall Fensalir ('marsh-halls'); her spindle/distaff (in late tradition the constellation Orion's belt is called Frigg's distaff); the falcon-feather cloak (sometimes — though more commonly attributed to Freyja)
nodes.object_source: Vǫluspá 33 (Fensalir); Gylfaginning 20, 35; late folk-tradition for the distaff-constellation
nodes.characterTrait: foreknowing, silent, sorrowful (over Baldr), maternal, queenly, sometimes secretive (in Vafþrúðnismál she advises Odin against the contest)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Vafþrúðnismál 1-4; Gylfaginning 20, 35, 49; Lokasenna 25-29
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Queenly goddess; not described in detail beyond her dignity. Sits in Hliðskjálf with Odin (Grímnismál prose intro). Her tears in mourning Baldr are emphasized in Gylfaginning 49.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Grímnismál prose intro; Gylfaginning 20, 49
nodes.significantEvent: Wife of Odin, mother of Baldr. Foresees fate but does not speak it (a major Eddic motif — she alone knows what Odin himself cannot fully grasp). In Gylfaginning 49, when Baldr begins to have nightmares of his death, Frigg extracts oaths from all things in creation — fire, water, iron, all metals, stones, earth, trees, sicknesses, beasts, birds, poisons, serpents — not to harm her son. She overlooks only the mistletoe, deeming it too young. Loki, disguised as a woman, learns this secret from her; uses the mistletoe to kill Baldr. After Baldr's death, Frigg asks who will ride to Hel to ransom him; Hermóðr volunteers. Her tears in mourning are formidable. In Saxo's parallel narrative (Gesta Danorum 1.7), Frigga (Frigg) commits adultery and is the subject of an unusual narrative about Odin's exile.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Gylfaginning 49; Vafþrúðnismál 1-4; Saxo 1.7
nodes.birthTypes_source: Snorri's genealogies — daughter of Fjǫrgynn (a poorly-attested figure)
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Fjǫrgynn per Snorri; her exact origins are sparsely documented.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Snorri's Edda

nodes.name: Sif
nodes.domain: grain and harvest (her golden hair is the wheat-field), wife of Thor, matron of the Aesir, prophetess (in Hárbarðsljóð 48 she is called 'Thor's wife who knows the wise things')
nodes.domain_source: Snorri, Gylfaginning 31; Skáldskaparmál 4, 14, 35; Hárbarðsljóð 48; Lokasenna 53-54; Þrymskviða 24
nodes.object: her golden hair (made by the dwarves Sons of Ivaldi after Loki cut off her original hair); spindle/textile work
nodes.object_source: Skáldskaparmál 35 (the dwarven gifts narrative — Loki cuts off Sif's hair in malice; Thor compels him to have the dwarves make a magical hair of gold that grows like real hair)
nodes.characterTrait: graceful, golden-haired (the central iconographic trait), prophetess (Hárbarðsljóð 48), sometimes accused (Lokasenna 53-54 — Loki claims to have been her lover)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hárbarðsljóð 48; Lokasenna 53-54; Skáldskaparmál 14
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Golden-haired matron; her hair (after the dwarven re-creation) is golden, grows naturally, and is identified with the wheat-field in skaldic kennings (Sif's hair = wheat).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Skáldskaparmál 35; standard skaldic kennings
nodes.significantEvent: Wife of Thor; mother of Þrúðr (with Thor) and Ullr (by an unknown previous union). In the central dwarven-gifts narrative (Skáldskaparmál 35), Loki maliciously cuts off Sif's hair while she sleeps; Thor compels Loki to have it replaced — Loki goes to the dwarven sons of Ivaldi who forge for him golden hair (which becomes Sif's), Skíðblaðnir (Freyr's ship), and Gungnir (Odin's spear); the contest leads to the creation of Mjǫllnir, Gullinbursti, and Draupnir.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Skáldskaparmál 35
nodes.birthTypes_source: Snorri's tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Aesir goddess; specific genealogy sparsely attested.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Snorri

nodes.name: Idun
nodes.domain: youth, vitality, the apples of immortality, springtime renewal — keeper of the apples that the gods eat to remain young
nodes.domain_source: Snorri, Gylfaginning 26; Skáldskaparmál 1-3 (the Þjazi-Idun narrative); Haustlǫng (Þjóðólfr ór Hvini); Lokasenna 16-18; Hrafnagaldur Óðins (later)
nodes.object: the eski-box (the small ash-wood casket) in which she keeps her apples; the apples of immortality (the central object of the cult of youth)
nodes.object_source: Skáldskaparmál 1-3; Gylfaginning 26
nodes.characterTrait: young, gentle, devoted, naïve (allows herself to be deceived by Loki in the Þjazi narrative)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Skáldskaparmál 1-3
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Young goddess of perpetual youth; wife of Bragi. Her form is small enough to be carried in nut-form by Loki (Skáldskaparmál 3).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Skáldskaparmál 3
nodes.significantEvent: In the Þjazi narrative (Skáldskaparmál 1-3), the giant Þjazi forces Loki to lure Idun out of Asgard with her apples; Þjazi seizes her in eagle-form and carries her to his hall Þrymheimr. Without the apples, the gods grow old. Loki, threatened with death, is forced to recover her: transforms into a falcon (using Freyja's cloak), turns Idun into a nut, and flies back. Þjazi pursues in eagle-form; the gods kindle fires on Asgard's walls; Þjazi catches fire and falls; the gods kill him. Skaði (Þjazi's daughter) comes seeking vengeance; receives marriage to a god (Njǫrðr).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Skáldskaparmál 1-3; Haustlǫng (the skaldic shield-poem narrating this)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Snorri's tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Ívaldi (one of the dwarven smiths) in some traditions — but this is contested.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hrafnagaldur Óðins (a late composition); Snorri

nodes.name: Skadi
nodes.domain: winter, hunting, skiing, the snow-covered mountains, vengeance (for her father Þjazi) — Jötunn-goddess (giant-bride accepted into the Aesir)
nodes.domain_source: Snorri, Gylfaginning 23; Skáldskaparmál 1, 3, 22; Ynglinga saga 8; Lokasenna 49-52
nodes.object: bow and skis; the venomous serpent she binds over Loki's face during his binding (Gylfaginning 50)
nodes.object_source: Gylfaginning 23 (her skiing), 50 (the serpent over Loki); Skáldskaparmál (her bow)
nodes.characterTrait: fierce, vengeful, hunting, dwells in the mountains, mismatched marriage (the famous failed-marriage with Njǫrðr — she cannot bear his sea, he cannot bear her mountains)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Gylfaginning 23; Skáldskaparmál 1; Lokasenna 49-52
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Tall giantess; armed with bow; skis. After her marriage-by-feet-choice (she chose by feet, hoping to get Baldr; got Njǫrðr), they parted unable to share residence — she returns to her father's mountains at Þrymheimr.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Gylfaginning 23
nodes.significantEvent: Daughter of the giant Þjazi (whom the Aesir killed for the Idun-abduction). Comes to Asgard demanding vengeance and a husband; the gods agree she may choose a husband by his feet alone (the famous bizarre clause — she expects Baldr's perfect feet; gets Njǫrðr's, the sea-god). They marry but cannot agree on residence: Njǫrðr cannot bear the wolves and barren mountains of Þrymheimr; Skaði cannot bear the gulls and sea-noise of Nóatún. They part. In Gylfaginning 50, after Loki's binding, Skaði sets a venomous serpent over his face so its venom drips on him — Sigyn holds the bowl to catch the venom. In Ynglinga saga 8, Skaði leaves Njǫrðr and lives with Odin, bearing many sons by him.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Gylfaginning 23, 50; Skáldskaparmál 1; Ynglinga saga 8
nodes.birthTypes_source: Gylfaginning 23 (daughter of Þjazi)
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of the giant Þjazi.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Gylfaginning 23

nodes.name: Sigyn
nodes.domain: wifely devotion, suffering, the bowl-bearer over Loki's bound face
nodes.domain_source: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50; Vǫluspá 35; Skáldskaparmál 19
nodes.object: the bowl with which she catches the venom dripping over Loki's face
nodes.object_source: Gylfaginning 50; Vǫluspá 35
nodes.characterTrait: devoted, patient, suffering, faithful to her husband even bound
nodes.characterTrait_source: Gylfaginning 50; Vǫluspá 35
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Aesir-goddess; not described in detail beyond her bowl-bearing posture beside the bound Loki.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Gylfaginning 50
nodes.significantEvent: Wife of Loki and mother of his sons Narfi (also called Nari) and Váli (the wolf-transformed son who slays his brother — not the same as Odin's son Váli). After Loki is bound for his role in Baldr's death, Skadi sets a venomous serpent over his face; Sigyn stands beside him holding a bowl to catch the venom. When the bowl fills, she must empty it; while she does, the venom drips onto Loki's face — his writhing causes the earthquakes of the human world.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Gylfaginning 50; Vǫluspá 35
familyRoles: mother of Narfi and the wolf-Váli
nodes.birthTypes_source: Snorri's tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Aesir goddess; specific genealogy not detailed.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Snorri

nodes.name: Eir
nodes.domain: healing, medicine — the chief physician among the Aesir
nodes.domain_source: Snorri, Gylfaginning 35 (listed among the Aesir goddesses); Skáldskaparmál 75 (Þulur — list of valkyries — where Eir also appears as a valkyrie name); Fjǫlsvinnsmál 38 (Eir on the mountain Lyfjaberg as one of Menglǫð's handmaidens)
nodes.object_source: Fjǫlsvinnsmál 38; Gylfaginning 35
nodes.characterTrait_source: Gylfaginning 35
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Goddess in the Aesir court; not described in detail.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Gylfaginning 35
nodes.significantEvent: Listed among the Aesir goddesses (Gylfaginning 35) as 'the best physician'. In Fjǫlsvinnsmál 38, appears as one of nine maidens on Menglǫð's mountain Lyfjaberg (the 'mountain of healing'); whoever climbs that hill receives healing from her. Sometimes also listed among valkyries (Skáldskaparmál Þulur).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Gylfaginning 35; Fjǫlsvinnsmál 38

nodes.name: Fenrir
nodes.domain: the great wolf, eschatological devourer of Odin, son of Loki, bound monster of Lyngvi on Lake Ámsvartnir
nodes.domain_source: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34, 51; Vǫluspá 39, 53; Vafþrúðnismál 46-47; Lokasenna 41; Bragi gamli (skaldic)
nodes.object: the chain Gleipnir (made by the dwarves from six impossible ingredients: the noise of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish, and the spittle of a bird); the sword propped in his jaws to keep them open while bound
nodes.object_source: Gylfaginning 34 (the famous binding narrative)
nodes.animals_source: Fenrir IS the wolf — embodiment as the cosmic-monster wolf
nodes.characterTrait: ravenous, strong, growing-too-fast (the gods became afraid of him as he matured), bound by deception, awaiting Ragnarök
nodes.characterTrait_source: Gylfaginning 34; Vǫluspá 39, 53
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Vast wolf; grows so quickly that the gods can no longer ignore the threat. Bound on the desolate island Lyngvi on Lake Ámsvartnir; his mouth held open by a sword propped between palate and jaw; the river Vǫn flows from his mouth as his slaver. At Ragnarök, breaks free.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Gylfaginning 34, 51
nodes.significantEvent: Son of Loki and the giantess Angrboða; sibling of Jörmungandr and Hel. Raised among the Aesir at first, but grew so monstrous that they decided to bind him. They tried three fetters: Lœðingr (he broke it easily), Drómi (also broke), then the dwarven-forged Gleipnir. Suspicious that Gleipnir was magical, Fenrir agreed to be bound only if one of the gods would place a hand in his mouth as security. Týr volunteered. When the binding held, Fenrir bit off Týr's hand at what became the 'wolf-joint' (wrist). At Ragnarök, Fenrir breaks free, swallows Odin, and is then killed by Vídar, who steps on the wolf's lower jaw with his great shoe and tears the mouth apart (Vǫluspá 53-55; Gylfaginning 51).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Gylfaginning 34, 51; Vǫluspá 53-55
familyRoles: father of the wolves Sköll and Hati (in some genealogies)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Gylfaginning 34
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Loki and the giantess Angrboða.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Gylfaginning 34
deathTypes: killed by Vídar at Ragnarök (jaws torn apart)
nodes.deathCircumstances: Killed by Vídar at Ragnarök: Vídar steps on Fenrir's lower jaw with his great shoe (made over generations from leather-trimmings) and rips the wolf's mouth apart.

nodes.name: Ymir
nodes.domain: primordial giant, the first being from the chaos-gap, the cosmos-body — from whose dismembered form the world is made
nodes.domain_source: Snorri, Gylfaginning 5-8; Vǫluspá 3; Vafþrúðnismál 21, 28; Grímnismál 40-41
nodes.object: his own body (which becomes the cosmos: flesh = earth, blood = sea, bones = mountains, teeth = rocks, skull = heaven, brain = clouds, hair = trees, eyelashes = Midgard)
nodes.object_source: Gylfaginning 8; Grímnismál 40-41
nodes.characterTrait: primordial, asexual-generative (sons born from his sweat; daughter from his armpit; six-headed son from his feet), monstrous
nodes.characterTrait_source: Gylfaginning 5; Vafþrúðnismál 33
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Vast primordial giant; born of the meeting of fire (Muspell) and ice (Niflheim) in the void Ginnungagap. From his sweat are born the proto-giants: from his left armpit a male and female, from his feet a six-headed son. Fed by the milk of the primordial cow Audhumla, who licks the salt-ice to free the first divine ancestor Búri.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Gylfaginning 5; Vafþrúðnismál 21
nodes.significantEvent: Born of the meeting of fire and ice in Ginnungagap (Gylfaginning 5; Vafþrúðnismál 21). From his body the proto-giants emerge. Slain by Odin and his brothers Vili and Vé (Gylfaginning 7): from his flesh they shape earth, from his blood seas, from his bones mountains, from his skull heaven, from his brain clouds, from his eyelashes Midgard. The drowning-flood of his blood kills all giants except Bergelmir and his wife, who escape in a hollowed-out tree (Vafþrúðnismál 35; Gylfaginning 7).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Gylfaginning 5-8; Vafþrúðnismál 21, 28, 35; Vǫluspá 3
birthTypes: primordial — emerged from the meeting of fire and ice in Ginnungagap
nodes.birthTypes_source: Gylfaginning 5; Vafþrúðnismál 21
nodes.birthCircumstances: Emerged from the meeting of fire (sparks from Muspell) and the rime-ice (from Niflheim) in the void Ginnungagap.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Gylfaginning 5; Vafþrúðnismál 21
deathTypes: slain by Odin, Vili, and Vé
nodes.deathCircumstances: Slain by Odin, Vili, and Vé. From his body they form the cosmos: flesh becomes earth, blood becomes the sea (and a great flood that drowns the giants except Bergelmir's family), bones become mountains, teeth and shattered bones become rocks, skull becomes the sky (held up by four dwarves at the corners), brain becomes clouds, hair becomes trees, eyelashes become Midgard.

nodes.name: Audhumla
nodes.domain: primordial cow whose milk feeds Ymir and whose ice-licking frees Búri (the first divine ancestor)
nodes.domain_source: Snorri, Gylfaginning 6; this Snorri-only narrative is not in the Poetic Edda but is consistent with Vafþrúðnismál's primordial-emergence theme
nodes.object: milk (which feeds Ymir) and the salt-ice she licks (which contains the buried Búri)
nodes.object_source: Gylfaginning 6
nodes.animals_source: Audhumla IS the cow — embodiment as the primordial bovine
nodes.characterTrait_source: Gylfaginning 6
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Primordial cow; emerged from the melting rime-ice of Niflheim. Four streams of milk flow from her udders, which nourish Ymir.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Gylfaginning 6
nodes.significantEvent: Emerges from the melting rime-ice with Ymir at the dawn of the cosmos. Nourishes Ymir with her milk. Licks the salt-ice for three days, gradually freeing the first divine ancestor Búri: on the first day a hair-strand emerges, on the second a head, on the third a whole man.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Gylfaginning 6
birthTypes: primordial — emerged from the melting rime-ice
nodes.birthTypes_source: Gylfaginning 6
nodes.birthCircumstances: Emerged simultaneously with Ymir from the melting rime-ice of Niflheim.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Gylfaginning 6

nodes.name: Búri
nodes.domain: first divine ancestor, freed from the salt-ice by Audhumla, father of Borr, grandfather of Odin
nodes.domain_source: Snorri, Gylfaginning 6
nodes.characterTrait_source: Gylfaginning 6
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Tall, fair, strong man revealed from the ice over three days.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Gylfaginning 6
nodes.significantEvent: Revealed from the salt-ice as Audhumla licked it: hair on the first day, head on the second, the whole man on the third. Father of Borr, who fathered Odin, Vili, and Vé. Founder of the Aesir lineage.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Gylfaginning 6
nodes.birthTypes_source: Gylfaginning 6
nodes.birthCircumstances: Emerged from the salt-ice over three days as Audhumla licked it.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Gylfaginning 6

nodes.name: Surt
nodes.domain: fire-giant of Muspelheim, eschatological burner of the world, wielder of the flaming sword at Ragnarök
nodes.domain_source: Vǫluspá 52; Vafþrúðnismál 17-18; Snorri, Gylfaginning 4, 51
nodes.object: the flaming sword (brighter than the sun); the fires of Muspelheim
nodes.object_source: Vǫluspá 52; Gylfaginning 51
nodes.characterTrait_source: Vǫluspá 52; Gylfaginning 4
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Fire-giant; rides at the head of Muspelheim's sons at Ragnarök, the flaming sword in hand. So bright that the heavens split (Vǫluspá 52).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Vǫluspá 52
nodes.significantEvent: Guards the southern realm of Muspelheim from the beginning of the cosmos (Gylfaginning 4). At Ragnarök, leads the sons of Muspell across Bifrǫst (which breaks under their weight, Gylfaginning 51); engages Freyr in combat and kills him (Freyr is weaponless because he gave his sword to Skírnir to win Gerðr — Vǫluspá 53). Surt's flaming sword sets the world ablaze, consuming everything in the final cosmic conflagration.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Vǫluspá 52-57; Vafþrúðnismál 17-18; Gylfaginning 51
nodes.birthTypes_source: Gylfaginning 4
nodes.birthCircumstances: Primordial fire-giant; guards Muspelheim from the beginning.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Gylfaginning 4
nodes.deathCircumstances: His fate after Ragnarök is not explicitly narrated, though the world he burns is succeeded by a new earth (Vǫluspá 59-65).

nodes.name: Sól
nodes.domain: the sun, daily celestial transit, light — driver of the sun-chariot pursued by the wolf Sköll
nodes.domain_source: Vafþrúðnismál 23; Snorri, Gylfaginning 11-12; Vǫluspá 5, 40; Grímnismál 37-39
nodes.object: her sun-chariot (drawn by the horses Árvakr and Alsviðr, with cooling-bellows blowing under their shoulders to keep them from burning, per Grímnismál 37-38); the shield Svalinn that protects her from the sun's heat
nodes.object_source: Grímnismál 37-39
nodes.characterTrait_source: Vafþrúðnismál 23; Grímnismál 37-39
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Sun-driving maiden; daughter of the mortal Mundilfari. Drives the sun-chariot pulled by Árvakr and Alsviðr.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Gylfaginning 11; Grímnismál 37-39
nodes.significantEvent: Daughter of Mundilfari, who named her Sól (Sun) for her beauty; the gods placed her in the heavens to drive the sun-chariot. Wife of Glenr per Gylfaginning 11. Pursued daily by the wolf Sköll, who at Ragnarök will catch and devour her (Vǫluspá 40; Vafþrúðnismál 46-47). Before her death, she bears a daughter who will take her place in the new world (Vafþrúðnismál 47).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Gylfaginning 11-12; Vafþrúðnismál 23, 46-47; Vǫluspá 40
nodes.birthTypes_source: Gylfaginning 11 (originally mortal daughter of Mundilfari)
nodes.birthCircumstances: Mortal daughter of Mundilfari; her father's pride at her beauty (he named her Sun, her brother Moon) caused the gods to place her in the heavens to drive the sun.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Gylfaginning 11
deathTypes: devoured by wolf Sköll at Ragnarök
nodes.deathCircumstances: Devoured by the wolf Sköll at Ragnarök; before her death, she bears a daughter who will take her place in the new sun.

nodes.name: Nanna (Norse)
nodes.domain: wife of Baldr; dies of grief at his funeral pyre
nodes.domain_source: Snorri, Gylfaginning 49; Vǫluspá 33 (implicit in Baldr-funeral context); Skáldskaparmál 5; Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum 3 (the very different Saxo version)
nodes.object: her ring (which she sends back from Hel with Hermóðr); her tapestry/textile
nodes.object_source: Gylfaginning 49
nodes.characterTrait: loving, devoted, grief-stricken, faithful in death
nodes.characterTrait_source: Gylfaginning 49
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Goddess of the Aesir; not described in detail.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Gylfaginning 49
nodes.significantEvent: Wife of Baldr; mother of Forseti. After Baldr's death at the hands of Hǫðr (Loki's instigation), Nanna dies of grief at his funeral pyre — they are burned together. When Hermóðr rides to Hel to ransom Baldr, Nanna sends back a ring (Fullr's ring) to Frigg, a robe to Frigg, and the ring Draupnir back to Odin.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Gylfaginning 49
nodes.birthTypes_source: Skáldskaparmál 5
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Nepr per Snorri (Skáldskaparmál 5).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Skáldskaparmál 5
nodes.deathCircumstances: Dies of grief at Baldr's funeral; her body is placed on the pyre with his, and they are burned together. Her spirit accompanies him to Hel.

nodes.name: Ran
nodes.domain: the sea (especially as drowner of sailors), the great net with which she catches the drowned, wife of Ægir, mother of the nine wave-maidens
nodes.domain_source: Snorri, Skáldskaparmál 25, 33; Reginsmál prose; Sonatorrek (Egill Skallagrímsson, 10th c.); Eyrbyggja saga; Friðþjófs saga
nodes.object: the great net (with which she catches drowning sailors); the gold she keeps at the sea-bottom (Reginsmál — Loki must borrow it to pay Otr's wergild)
nodes.object_source: Reginsmál prose; Skáldskaparmál 25
nodes.characterTrait_source: Sonatorrek (Egill's elegy for his drowned son); standard skaldic tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Sea-giantess; mother of the nine wave-daughters (with Ægir); keeps drowned sailors in her hall beneath the sea.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Skáldskaparmál 25
nodes.significantEvent: Wife of Ægir; mother of the nine wave-maidens (the daughters of Ægir and Rán). Catches drowning sailors in her great net; takes them to her sea-hall. In Reginsmál, Loki must borrow Rán's net to capture Andvari (the dwarf) and seize the cursed gold to pay Otr's wergild. In Egill's Sonatorrek, the bereaved father grieves his son drowned by Rán.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Reginsmál prose; Skáldskaparmál 25, 33; Sonatorrek; Eyrbyggja saga
nodes.birthTypes_source: Snorri
nodes.birthCircumstances: Sea-giantess of primordial age.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Snorri

nodes.name: Gefjun
nodes.domain: agricultural plowing, virgin maidenhood (in some traditions), the receipt-of-the-unmarried-dead, the goddess who plowed Zealand free from Sweden
nodes.domain_source: Snorri, Gylfaginning 1, 35; Ynglinga saga 5; Bragi gamli (skaldic, cited in Skáldskaparmál); Lokasenna 19-21
nodes.object: the plow (with which she plows Zealand free); her four sons-as-oxen (transformed from her giant-fathered children)
nodes.object_source: Gylfaginning 1; Ynglinga saga 5
nodes.characterTrait: wise, fertile, virgin (per Snorri — Gylfaginning 35 lists her among the unmarried goddesses), creative, sometimes accused (Lokasenna 19-21 — Loki claims she was bought for a necklace)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Gylfaginning 35; Lokasenna 19-21
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Aesir-goddess; not described in detail.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Gylfaginning 35
nodes.significantEvent: King Gylfi of Sweden gives her as much land as four oxen can plow in a day and a night. She begets four giant-children by an unnamed giant, transforms them into oxen, and plows a vast area free from Sweden — that land becomes Zealand in Denmark, and the lake left where it was becomes Lake Mälaren. In Gylfaginning 35, listed among the Aesir goddesses; receives 'those who die unmarried'. In Lokasenna 19-21, Loki accuses her of taking a necklace in exchange for sexual favors from a youth.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Gylfaginning 1; Ynglinga saga 5; Bragi gamli (the famous Bragi poem cited in Skáldskaparmál)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Snorri
nodes.birthCircumstances: Aesir-goddess; specific genealogy not detailed.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Snorri

nodes.name: Andvari
nodes.domain: dwarf-treasure-keeper, source of the cursed Volsung-gold, riverdweller in pike-form
nodes.domain_source: Reginsmál prose and verses 1-5; Skáldskaparmál 39; Vǫlsunga saga 14
nodes.object: his treasure-hoard (the gold beneath the waterfall); the ring Andvaranautr ('Andvari's gift'); the curse he places on the gold
nodes.object_source: Reginsmál prose; Skáldskaparmál 39; Vǫlsunga saga 14
nodes.animals_source: Andvari transforms into a pike (fish) when caught — embodiment via shapeshifting
nodes.characterTrait_source: Reginsmál; Vǫlsunga saga 14
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Dwarf; takes the form of a pike to dwell in the waterfall (later called Andvarafall). Caught by Loki with Rán's net.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Reginsmál prose
nodes.significantEvent: When the Aesir kill Otr (Hreiðmarr's son, in otter-form), Hreiðmarr demands gold wergild enough to cover Otr's body. Loki goes to seize Andvari's treasure: borrows Rán's net, catches Andvari in pike-form. Andvari unwillingly surrenders all his gold but tries to keep the ring Andvaranautr; Loki seizes it too. Andvari curses the ring and all the gold to be the death of whoever owns it. The curse plays out through Hreiðmarr's death (slain by his sons), Fáfnir's transformation into dragon, Sigurðr's quest, Brynhildr's death, the destruction of the Gjúkungs and Burgundians — the entire Volsung-Nibelung cycle.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Reginsmál; Skáldskaparmál 39; Vǫlsunga saga 14
nodes.birthTypes_source: Vǫlsunga saga 14
nodes.birthCircumstances: Dwarf; specific genealogy not detailed.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Vǫlsunga saga 14

nodes.name: Saga
nodes.domain: drinking-companion of Odin in the hall Sǫkkvabekkr ('the sinking hall'); some scholars identify her with Frigg as an alternate aspect; possibly history/saga-telling personified
nodes.domain_source: Grímnismál 7 (the only major Eddic mention); Snorri, Gylfaginning 35 (listed among the Aesir goddesses)
nodes.object: the cup with which she shares drink with Odin
nodes.object_source: Grímnismál 7
nodes.characterTrait: drinking-companion of Odin, dwelling in the sinking-hall
nodes.characterTrait_source: Grímnismál 7
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Aesir-goddess; not described in detail.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Gylfaginning 35
nodes.significantEvent: In Grímnismál 7, Saga dwells in Sǫkkvabekkr ('the sinking hall'), where 'cool waves resound around it; Odin and Saga drink there gladly, every day, from golden cups'. Some scholars identify her with Frigg as an alternate aspect (since Frigg too is paired with Odin in drinking); others see her as a separate figure of history/saga-telling.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Grímnismál 7
nodes.birthTypes_source: Snorri
nodes.birthCircumstances: Aesir-goddess; specific genealogy not detailed.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Snorri

nodes.name: Vishnu
nodes.domain: preserver of the cosmos (sthiti); supreme being in Vaiṣṇavism; avatar-incarnator descending in each age to restore dharma; dweller in Vaikuṇṭha on cosmic serpent Śeṣa; four-armed bearer of conch-discus-mace-lotus
nodes.domain_source: Rig Veda 1.154-155 (three strides); Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; Bhagavad Gītā; Bhāgavata Purāṇa; Viṣṇu Purāṇa; Pañcarātra and Vaikhānasa Āgamas; Divyaprabandham (Tamil)
nodes.object: conch (Pāñcajanya), discus (Sudarśana), mace (Kaumodakī), lotus (padma); cosmic serpent Śeṣa as couch; Vaikuṇṭha (abode); bow Śārṅga; yellow garments (pītāmbara)
nodes.object_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.9, 8.7; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1; Mahābhārata, Śānti Parvan
nodes.characterTrait: preserver, sustainer, compassionate (kṛpālu), boon-giving, avatar-descending, lawful, accessible to bhakti, serene
nodes.characterTrait_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa passim; Bhagavad Gītā 12; Viṣṇu Sahasranāma
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Four-armed, dark blue or cloud-colored (śyāmala/nīla-meghaśyāma); bears conch-discus-mace-lotus; śrīvatsa mark on chest; kaustubha-jewel; yellow silken garments; reclines on Śeṣa floating on the cosmic ocean during pralaya; from his navel sprouts the lotus from which Brahmā emerges.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.9; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1; Vaiṣṇava iconography
nodes.significantEvent: In Vedic stratum, god of the three world-spanning strides (Trivikrama, RV 1.154). In Purāṇic theology, supreme being who incarnates as the daśāvatāra (Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha [in some lists], Kalki). Bhagavad Gītā 4.7-8: 'whenever there is decline of dharma and rise of adharma, I manifest myself'.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Rig Veda 1.154-155; Bhāgavata Purāṇa (daśāvatāra accounts); Bhagavad Gītā 4.7-8; Viṣṇu Purāṇa
nodes.eventTypes_source: Rig Veda; Bhāgavata Purāṇa; Bhagavad Gītā
nodes.birthTypes_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.1.1
nodes.birthCircumstances: Eternal, beginningless. In avatar-form, born in many ages from various mothers (Devakī for Kṛṣṇa, Kausalyā for Rāma).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Vaiṣṇava theology

nodes.name: Brahma
nodes.domain: creator of the cosmos (sṛṣṭi); demiurge; source of the Vedas; four-faced; born from Viṣṇu's navel-lotus; his day is a kalpa (4.32 billion years); cursed to receive almost no temples
nodes.domain_source: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; Manu Smṛti 1; Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2-3; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1; Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa
nodes.object: four Vedas (one per face); rosary (akṣamālā); water-pot (kamaṇḍalu); swan (haṃsa) as vāhana; lotus seat
nodes.object_source: Purāṇic iconography
nodes.characterTrait: creative, knowledge-bearing, distracted, self-engendered, often cursed
nodes.characterTrait_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3-4; Śiva Purāṇa (Brahmā-Bhairava); Matsya Purāṇa
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Four-faced (catur-mukha), four-armed; originally five-headed but Śiva-as-Bhairava cut off the fifth for pride/untruthfulness; long white beard; red-skinned; rides the haṃsa.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Purāṇic iconography; Śiva Purāṇa (five-to-four head transition)
nodes.significantEvent: Emerges from a lotus growing from Viṣṇu's navel at the start of each cosmic cycle (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.8). Recites the four Vedas from his four faces. The Liṅgodbhava: Brahmā and Viṣṇu argue who is supreme; infinite liṅga of fire appears; Brahmā as swan flies up to find its top, Viṣṇu as boar digs down for its bottom; both fail; Śiva manifests from the liṅga; Brahmā lies that he reached the top and is cursed never to have widespread worship.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.8; Śiva Purāṇa; Liṅga Purāṇa 17
nodes.birthTypes_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.8
nodes.birthCircumstances: Born from the lotus growing from Viṣṇu's navel at the beginning of each kalpa.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.8
nodes.deathCircumstances: Lives a hundred Brahmā-years (one Brahmā-day = 4.32 billion human years); at his life's end the cosmos dissolves into Viṣṇu (mahāpralaya); the next Brahmā emerges in the next cycle.

nodes.name: Lakshmi
nodes.domain: wealth, prosperity, fortune, beauty, royal authority (śrī); divine consort of Viṣṇu; lotus-goddess; mother of Kāma; giver of mokṣa
nodes.domain_source: Śrī-sūkta (late RV appendix); Mahābhārata, Sabhā Parvan; Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.8; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1; Padma Purāṇa; Lakṣmī Tantra
nodes.object: lotus (in two of four hands, also her seat); golden pots overflowing with gold; the cosmic elephants Aṣṭadiggaja bathing her
nodes.object_source: Śrī-sūkta; Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.8; Vaiṣṇava iconography
nodes.characterTrait: auspicious, fickle (cala-lakṣmī — famously restless), wealth-bestowing, royal, lotus-loving, devoted to Viṣṇu
nodes.characterTrait_source: Mahābhārata, Sabhā Parvan; Purāṇic tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Four-armed (supreme form) or two-armed; golden-complexioned (heṃa-varṇa); seated/standing on lotus; lotuses in two hands; gold coins from third hand; flanked by white elephants (the famous Gaja-Lakṣmī iconography from Sāñcī, c. 1st c. BCE).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Śrī-sūkta; Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.8; Sāñcī iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Emerges from the cosmic ocean during the churning (samudra-manthana) when gods and demons churned for amṛta; arises seated on a lotus, chooses Viṣṇu as husband by garlanding him (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.8). In each Viṣṇu avatar she descends as consort — Sītā for Rāma, Rukmiṇī or Rādhā for Kṛṣṇa.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.8; Padma Purāṇa; Rāmāyaṇa
birthTypes: emerged from the churning of the cosmic ocean
nodes.birthTypes_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.8
nodes.birthCircumstances: Emerged from the cosmic ocean during the churning by gods and demons.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.8

nodes.name: Saraswati
nodes.domain: wisdom, learning, music, the arts, eloquence, speech (vāc), the Vedas; the (now-lost) river Sarasvatī; consort of Brahmā
nodes.domain_source: Rig Veda 6.61, 7.95-96 (Sarasvatī as river-goddess); Devī Māhātmya; Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa; Padma Purāṇa; Sarasvatī-stotra
nodes.object: vīṇā (Indian lute); palm-leaf book (Vedas); rosary (akṣamālā); water-pot; white lotus or haṃsa (swan) as vāhana; white garments
nodes.object_source: Purāṇic-iconographic tradition
nodes.characterTrait: wise, eloquent, musical, scholarly, gracious, pure-white, peaceful (śānta)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Rig Veda 6.61; Devī Māhātmya; Purāṇic tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Four-armed (supreme form) or two-armed; pure white in complexion (śveta-varṇa); seated on white lotus or riding the haṃsa; holding vīṇā, book, and rosary; clothed in white; calm-faced.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Purāṇic-iconographic tradition
nodes.significantEvent: Originally a Vedic river-goddess (RV 6.61.13: 'best of mothers, best of rivers, best of goddesses'). By late-Vedic period identified with Vāc (Speech). In Purāṇas, consort of Brahmā and goddess of all learning. The narrative of Brahmā's incestuous attraction (and his fifth head being cut off by Śiva-Bhairava) involves Sarasvatī. Invoked daily by students before study.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Rig Veda 6.61, 7.95-96; Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa; Skanda Purāṇa
birthTypes: emerged from Brahmā in self-engendered creation
nodes.birthTypes_source: Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa; Matsya Purāṇa
nodes.birthCircumstances: Emerges from Brahmā (variously his face, his thought, or his half) in some accounts.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa

nodes.name: Parvati
nodes.domain: consort of Śiva; daughter of the mountain (Himavān); the gentle aspect of the Mahādevī (fierce aspects are Durgā and Kālī); mother of Gaṇeśa and Skanda; cosmic feminine principle as Śiva's eternal companion
nodes.domain_source: Kālidāsa, Kumārasambhava (the central poetic source); Skanda Purāṇa; Śiva Purāṇa, Pārvatī-khaṇḍa; Liṅga Purāṇa
nodes.object: lotus, mirror (in Pārvatī-side of Ardhanārīśvara); trident and sword in warrior-aspect; sweets for Gaṇeśa
nodes.object_source: Śaiva iconography
nodes.characterTrait: gracious (saumyā), gentle, devoted-wife, ascetic (in tapas-period before winning Śiva), motherly, capable of fierce manifestations
nodes.characterTrait_source: Kumārasambhava; Śiva Purāṇa
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Two- or four-armed; golden- or fair-complexioned (contrasting with dark Kālī); long black hair; sari and ornaments; often seated next to Śiva or on lion-mount; sometimes nursing Gaṇeśa or Skanda.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Śaiva iconographic tradition
nodes.significantEvent: Born as daughter of Himavān (king of Himalayas) and Menā after Satī's self-immolation at Dakṣa's sacrifice. Recognized from childhood as Śiva's destined consort. Performs intense tapas to win him, accepting privation; Śiva incinerates Kāma with his third eye when Kāma tries to make him fall in love. Eventually wins Śiva and marries him. Becomes mother of Gaṇeśa (created from her own bodily-substance, beheaded by Śiva, revived with elephant's head) and Skanda. In fierce manifestations, she is Durgā and Kālī.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Kumārasambhava; Śiva Purāṇa; Skanda Purāṇa, Maheśvara-khaṇḍa
nodes.birthTypes_source: Śiva Purāṇa; Kumārasambhava
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Himavān and Menā; reincarnation of Satī (who self-immolated at Dakṣa's sacrifice).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Kumārasambhava; Śiva Purāṇa

nodes.name: Ganesha
nodes.domain: remover of obstacles (Vighneśvara); patron of beginnings; lord of the Gaṇas; wisdom, learning, success; elephant-headed son of Śiva and Pārvatī; first-worshipped at every Hindu rite
nodes.domain_source: Śiva Purāṇa, Rudra-saṃhitā, Kumārakhaṇḍa 13-20; Mudgala Purāṇa; Gaṇeśa Purāṇa; Mahābhārata frame-narrative
nodes.object: modaka (sweet rice-ball); goad (aṅkuśa); noose (pāśa); broken tusk (used to write the Mahābhārata for Vyāsa); lotus; axe; vāhana: mūṣika (mouse/rat)
nodes.object_source: Gāṇapatya iconography; Mahābhārata frame-narrative
nodes.characterTrait: wise, obstacle-removing, sweet-toothed, pot-bellied, scribe (wrote the Mahābhārata on a broken tusk), patient, first-honored at every ritual
nodes.characterTrait_source: Mahābhārata frame-narrative; Gāṇapatya tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Elephant-headed (with one broken tusk); pot-bellied (lambodara); four-armed; reddish-skinned; rides the mūṣika. The elephant-head was given after Śiva beheaded him; Śiva revived him with the head of the first creature his attendants found.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Śiva Purāṇa, Kumārakhaṇḍa 13-20
nodes.significantEvent: Created by Pārvatī from saffron-paste of her own body to guard her bath. Śiva returned, was blocked by the unknown boy at the door, beheaded him in rage. Pārvatī demanded restoration. Śiva's attendants brought the head of the first creature facing north — an elephant. Gaṇeśa thereafter is chief of Śiva's gaṇas and first-worshipped at all Hindu rites. Also broke off his right tusk as a pen when writing the Mahābhārata as dictated by Vyāsa. In a cosmic race with Skanda for a divine mango, won by circumambulating his parents instead of the universe ('my parents are my universe').
nodes.significantEvent_source: Śiva Purāṇa, Rudra-saṃhitā, Kumārakhaṇḍa 13-20; Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan
nodes.birthTypes_source: Śiva Purāṇa
nodes.birthCircumstances: Created by Pārvatī from saffron-paste of her body (without Śiva); beheaded by Śiva; revived with elephant's head.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Śiva Purāṇa, Kumārakhaṇḍa 13-20

nodes.name: Kartikeya
nodes.domain: war, divine general (Devasenāpati), youth, slayer of demon Tāraka, son of Śiva, six-faced (Ṣaṇmukha), the Tamil god Murugan, Skanda, peacock-rider, spear-wielder
nodes.domain_source: Kālidāsa, Kumārasambhava; Mahābhārata, Vana Parvan 224-230 (Skanda-jananī); Skanda Purāṇa (the largest Purāṇa, focused on him); Tamil bhakti (Tirumurugāṟṟuppaṭai)
nodes.object: spear (vēl/śakti — iconic weapon, given by Pārvatī); bow; rooster banner (kukkuṭa-dhvaja); vāhana: peacock (Paravāṇi)
nodes.object_source: Kumārasambhava; Skanda Purāṇa; Tamil tradition
nodes.characterTrait: youthful, fierce-warrior, six-faced, Tamil-celebrated as Murugan
nodes.characterTrait_source: Kumārasambhava; Skanda Purāṇa; Tamil Murugan tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Six-faced (ṣaḍ-ānana) and twelve-armed (supreme form); youthful (kumāra); golden-complexioned; rides the peacock Paravāṇi; bears the spear vēl. In Tamil iconography, often two-armed at the six aṟupaḍai-vīṭus (Six Abodes of Murugan — Palani, Tiruchendur, Pazhamudirsolai, etc.).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Kumārasambhava; Skanda Purāṇa; Tamil iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Born from Śiva's seed (nurtured by the six Kṛttikās of the Pleiades, hence Kārttikeya = 'son of the Kṛttikās') specifically to slay the demon Tāraka, who could be killed only by a son of Śiva. As a child becomes commander-in-chief of the divine army and slays Tāraka in cosmic battle. In Tamil tradition as Murugan, marries Vaḷḷi (hill-tribe girl) and Devasenā (Indra's daughter). Lost the cosmic-mango race to Gaṇeśa.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Kumārasambhava; Mahābhārata, Vana Parvan 224-230; Skanda Purāṇa
birthTypes: miraculous, from Śiva's seed nurtured by Kṛttikās
nodes.birthTypes_source: Kumārasambhava; Mahābhārata
nodes.birthCircumstances: Born from Śiva's seed (carried by Agni or Ganges); raised by the six Kṛttikās of the Pleiades.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Mahābhārata, Vana Parvan 224-230

nodes.name: Krishna
nodes.domain: supreme being (in Caitanya/Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism); eighth avatar of Viṣṇu; divine cowherd of Vṛndāvana; charioteer-teacher of the Bhagavad Gītā; slayer of Kaṃsa; lover of Rādhā and the gopīs; counselor of the Pāṇḍavas
nodes.domain_source: Bhagavad Gītā; Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10; Mahābhārata; Harivaṃśa; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5; Brahma Saṃhitā; Caitanya tradition
nodes.object: flute (vāṃśī, iconic); Sudarśana discus; Pāñcajanya conch; Kaumodakī mace; peacock-feather in crown; yellow garments (pītāmbara); cows of Vṛndāvana
nodes.object_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10; Gīta Govinda; Vaiṣṇava iconography
nodes.characterTrait: playful (līlā), beautiful, charming, mischievous as child, passionate as youth, wise as Gītā-teacher, strategic as Mahābhārata adviser, all-encompassing as supreme being
nodes.characterTrait_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10; Gīta Govinda; Bhagavad Gītā 11
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Dark-blue or cloud-colored (kṛṣṇa = 'dark'); youthful, beautiful; peacock-feather crown; yellow silken garments; standing in tribhaṅga (three-bend) pose with flute. As Pārtha-sārathi (charioteer), kingly attire; in the Viśvarūpa-theophany of Bhagavad Gītā 11, all of cosmos contained in his form.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10; Bhagavad Gītā 11; iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Born in prison to Devakī and Vasudeva while uncle Kaṃsa (told a son of Devakī would kill him) waited to slay him. Vasudeva escaped through opened doors with the infant, crossed the parting Yamunā, exchanged him for a girl-baby at Yaśodā and Nanda's home. Grew up among cowherds of Vṛndāvana: stealing butter; defeating serpent Kāliya; lifting Mount Govardhana on his finger for seven days against Indra's wrath; rāsa-līlā with the gopīs; slaying Kaṃsa. Later married Rukmiṇī and many others. In the Mahābhārata, charioteer of Arjuna at Kurukṣetra, where he reveals the Bhagavad Gītā. After the war, dies when struck in the heel by the hunter Jara's arrow.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10 (central); Harivaṃśa; Mahābhārata; Bhagavad Gītā
nodes.birthTypes_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.3
nodes.birthCircumstances: Born in prison to Devakī and Vasudeva while Kaṃsa awaited the prophesied child. Yogamāyā exchanged him for a girl-baby at Yaśodā's home.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.3
nodes.deathCircumstances: After the destruction of the Yādava clan, Kṛṣṇa retired to the forest, sat in meditation, was struck in the heel (his only vulnerable spot) by Jara's arrow.

nodes.name: Radha
nodes.domain: Kṛṣṇa's beloved; supreme devotee; personification of bhakti; chief of the gopīs of Vṛndāvana; in Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism, supreme to Lakṣmī as the eternal feminine principle paired with Kṛṣṇa
nodes.domain_source: Gīta Govinda (Jayadeva, 12th c. — Rādhā's first major elevation); Brahma-vaivarta Purāṇa, Kṛṣṇa-janma-khaṇḍa; Padma Purāṇa; Caitanya tradition; Vidagdha-Mādhava and Lalita-Mādhava (Rūpa Gosvāmin)
nodes.object: lotus; flute (sometimes shared with Kṛṣṇa); the swing on which she sits with Kṛṣṇa
nodes.object_source: Gīta Govinda; Caitanya iconography
nodes.characterTrait: loving, passionate, jealous (in viraha), supremely devoted, supremely beautiful, chief gopī; in Caitanya theology the hlādinī-śakti (bliss-power) of Kṛṣṇa
nodes.characterTrait_source: Gīta Govinda; Caitanya tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Fair-complexioned (golden, contrasting with Kṛṣṇa's dark blue); youthful gopī; cowherd-village attire (sometimes silken in temple-iconography); long hair; lotus-eyed.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Gīta Govinda; iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Chief gopī of Vṛndāvana, eternally beloved of Kṛṣṇa; their love is the subject of the Gīta Govinda, foundational poem of mature Rādhā-devotion. Celebrated for the depth of her longing (viraha) when separated from Kṛṣṇa — model for the bhakta's longing for God. In Caitanya theology, supreme expression of devotional love; Kṛṣṇa takes her bhāva and complexion to taste devotion to himself, the theological understanding of Caitanya's incarnation.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Gīta Govinda; Brahma-vaivarta Purāṇa; Caitanya-caritāmṛta
familyRoles: wife of the cowherd Āyana (in some parakīyā accounts)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Brahma-vaivarta Purāṇa
nodes.birthCircumstances: Born as gopī of Vṛndāvana; in cosmic-eternal terms, Kṛṣṇa's primordial hlādinī-śakti.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Brahma-vaivarta Purāṇa; Caitanya tradition

nodes.name: Rama
nodes.domain: seventh avatar of Viṣṇu; ideal king (maryāda-puruṣottama); exemplar of dharma; slayer of Rāvaṇa; husband of Sītā; hero of the Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.domain_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (c. 5th-2nd c. BCE); Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa; Tulsīdās's Rāmacaritamānasa (16th c.); Kamba Rāmāyaṇam (Tamil); Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.10-11
nodes.object: great bow Kodaṇḍa (or Śārṅga); arrows; ring he sends to Sītā via Hanumān
nodes.object_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.characterTrait: dharma-embodying, royal, just, devoted-husband, obedient-son (accepting exile to honor his father's word), restrained, sorrowful (over Sītā's losses)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; Rāmacaritamānasa
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Dark blue-green complexioned (śyāmala, like Viṣṇu and Kṛṣṇa); youthful, beautiful; tall; bearing the great bow; usually depicted with Sītā at his left, Lakṣmaṇa at his right, Hanumān bowing.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Born in Ayodhyā as eldest son of King Daśaratha by Kausalyā. Wins Sītā by stringing and breaking Śiva's bow at her svayaṃvara. On the eve of his coronation, stepmother Kaikeyī invokes an old boon demanding his exile and her son Bharata's coronation. Rāma accepts with perfect equanimity, going into 14-year forest exile with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa. The demon-king Rāvaṇa abducts Sītā. With Hanumān and Sugrīva's vānara army, Rāma builds a bridge to Laṅkā, slays Rāvaṇa, recovers Sītā. Returns to Ayodhyā as king (Rāma-rājya). Banishes the pregnant Sītā when gossip impugns her chastity; she gives birth to Lava and Kuśa; Rāma eventually meets his sons; Sītā returns to the earth.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (entire epic — seven kāṇḍas)
familyRoles: eldest son of Daśaratha and Kausalyā
nodes.birthTypes_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla-kāṇḍa 14-15
nodes.birthCircumstances: Born in Ayodhyā to Daśaratha and Kausalyā; conceived after the putreṣṭi yajña in which the sacrificial fire gave the king divine pāyasa for his three queens.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla-kāṇḍa 14-15
deathTypes: ascension to Vaikuṇṭha (entering the Sarayū river)
nodes.deathCircumstances: Returns to Vaikuṇṭha by walking into the Sarayū river with his subjects.

nodes.name: Sita
nodes.domain: Rāma's wife; the ideal woman (traditional Hindu conception); avatar of Lakṣmī; daughter of the earth (Bhū-devi); abducted by Rāvaṇa and rescued; queen of Ayodhyā
nodes.domain_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa; Rāmacaritamānasa; Sītā-Upaniṣad
nodes.object: lotus; fire (in the agni-parīkṣā ordeal); the plough-furrow (her name Sītā = 'furrow'); jewels she dropped from the air as Rāvaṇa carried her
nodes.object_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; Rāmacaritamānasa
nodes.characterTrait: devoted-wife (pativratā), patient, suffering (especially in abduction and forest-banishment), chaste, dignified, finally weary
nodes.characterTrait_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; bhakti tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Fair-complexioned (golden); supremely beautiful; royal; depicted to Rāma's left, usually demure.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Born from the furrow of the earth when King Janaka was ploughing a sacrificial field; raised as his daughter. Won by Rāma at her svayaṃvara when he strung Śiva's bow. Followed Rāma into 14-year exile. Abducted by Rāvaṇa from the forest hermitage; held captive in Laṅkā's Aśoka-vana. Rescued after Rāma's war with Rāvaṇa. Submitted to agni-parīkṣā to prove chastity. Banished by Rāma when gossip impugned her; gave birth to Lava and Kuśa in Vālmīki's hermitage. When recalled, called on her mother Earth instead of returning; the earth opened to take her back.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (entire epic)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla-kāṇḍa
nodes.birthCircumstances: Born from the furrow of the earth as King Janaka was ploughing.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla-kāṇḍa
nodes.deathCircumstances: When recalled by Rāma, called on her mother the Earth; the earth opened and she descended into it.

nodes.name: Lakshmana
nodes.domain: Rāma's devoted younger half-brother; servant-companion in 14-year exile; slayer of Indrajit; avatar of cosmic serpent Śeṣa
nodes.domain_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.10-11; Rāmacaritamānasa
nodes.object: bow and arrows; the rekhā (protective line he drew around Sītā during the abduction-scene)
nodes.object_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.characterTrait: devoted-servant-of-Rāma, fierce in battle, irascible, deeply protective, abstemious (slept little for 14 exile years)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Fair-complexioned (contrasting with dark Rāma); youthful warrior-handsome; bears bow and arrows.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Son of King Daśaratha by Sumitrā; twin of Śatrughna. Inseparable from Rāma. Followed him into exile, slept little for the 14 years. Slew the great rākṣasa Indrajit (Rāvaṇa's son) — the only being besides Rāma who could. Struck unconscious by Indrajit's brahmāstra; Hanumān saved him by fetching the sañjīvani herb. Eventually banished himself when Rāma was forced (by a previous boon to a sage) to put him to death.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9
nodes.birthTypes_source: Vaiṣṇava tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Born to Sumitrā after the putreṣṭi sacrifice; avatar of the cosmic serpent Śeṣa.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla-kāṇḍa
nodes.deathCircumstances: Cast himself into the Sarayū river after Rāma condemned him for breaking the seclusion with Time (Yama in disguise).

nodes.name: Hanuman
nodes.domain: supreme devotee of Rāma; vānara general; son of Vāyu; immortal (Cirañjīvī); leaper across the ocean to find Sītā; lifter of the Sañjīvani mountain; universally worshipped god of strength, devotion, courage, celibacy
nodes.domain_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Sundara-kāṇḍa; Hanumān Cālīsā (Tulsīdās); Rāmacaritamānasa; Mahābhārata; Skanda Purāṇa
nodes.object: mace (gadā); the Sañjīvani mountain (which he carried from Himalayas to Laṅkā); Rāma's ring (carried to Sītā); his own tail (which Rāvaṇa set fire to; with it Hanumān burned Laṅkā)
nodes.object_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Sundara and Yuddha kāṇḍas
nodes.animals_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa — Hanumān as vānara (monkey-being); this is his nature, not a symbolic mount
nodes.characterTrait: supremely-devoted-to-Rāma, immensely-strong, leaping-able (across oceans), celibate (brahmacārī), wise (Sanskrit grammarian), humble, immortal, ever-present where Rāma's name is sung
nodes.characterTrait_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; Hanumān Cālīsā
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Vānara (monkey-being); golden-complexioned, large, immensely strong; bears mace; broke his jaw as a child trying to grab the sun (hence Hanumān, hanu = 'jaw'); can grow to any size; can leap across the ocean.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Sundara-kāṇḍa
nodes.significantEvent: Son of Añjanā and Vāyu. As child, leapt up to grab the sun thinking it a fruit; Indra struck him down with the vajra, breaking his jaw. Granted many boons making him almost invincible. Joined Sugrīva's vānara army allied with Rāma. Leapt the ocean to Laṅkā to find Sītā (Sundara-kāṇḍa). Burned Laṅkā with his tail. Carried Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa in battle. Lifted the entire Sañjīvani mountain from the Himalayas (uncertain which herb was needed) to save Lakṣmaṇa. After the war, granted eternal life as Cirañjīvī. Present wherever Rāma's name is sung.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (Sundara and Yuddha kāṇḍas); Hanumān Cālīsā
nodes.birthTypes_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; Skanda Purāṇa
nodes.birthCircumstances: Born to Añjanā (an apsara cursed to vānara-form) and Vāyu; in some accounts, Śiva-aṃśa.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla-kāṇḍa
nodes.deathCircumstances: Immortal — one of the seven Cirañjīvīs; does not die.

nodes.name: Garuda
nodes.domain: Viṣṇu's eagle-mount; king of birds; slayer of serpents; freer of his mother Vinatā from enslavement; Vedic son of Kaśyapa
nodes.domain_source: Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan 16-34 (the central origin-narrative); Garuḍa Purāṇa (named after him); Bhāgavata Purāṇa; Viṣṇu Purāṇa
nodes.object: the amṛta-pot (stolen from Indra's heaven); his mother's bondage-debt
nodes.object_source: Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan 28-34
nodes.animals_source: Mahābhārata — Garuḍa IS the eagle-king; nature, not symbol
nodes.characterTrait_source: Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Vast eagle (often anthropomorphized as half-man/half-bird); golden-bodied with red wings, white face, eagle-beak; powerful enough to carry Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī. Born already gigantic from a long-incubated egg.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan
nodes.significantEvent: Son of Kaśyapa and Vinatā; nephew of Kadrū (mother of Nāgas). His mother Vinatā lost a wager to Kadrū about the color of Uccaiḥśravas's tail (Kadrū's serpent-sons clung to it making it appear black); Vinatā was enslaved. Garuḍa flew up to Indra's heaven, defeated the gods, seized the amṛta-pot, brought it down. The Nāgas demanded it to free Vinatā; Garuḍa placed it on kuśa-grass for them to ritually bathe; Indra recovered it; the Nāgas licked the grass, splitting their tongues (origin of serpent-tongues). Vinatā was freed. Garuḍa swore eternal serpent-enmity. Viṣṇu took him as his mount.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan 16-34
nodes.birthTypes_source: Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan 14
nodes.birthCircumstances: Born from a great egg laid by Vinatā (who waited five centuries for it to hatch).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan 14

nodes.name: Nandi
nodes.domain: Śiva's bull-mount and supreme devotee; chief of Śiva's gaṇas; gatekeeper of Kailāśa; the white humped-bull always before every Śiva-temple
nodes.domain_source: Śiva Purāṇa; Liṅga Purāṇa; Śaiva iconography; Periya Purāṇam (Tamil Śaiva)
nodes.object: bull-statue facing the liṅga in every Śiva-temple; bells around his neck
nodes.object_source: Śaiva temple iconography (from at least Gupta period)
nodes.animals_source: Nandi IS the bull — embodiment as Śiva's mount-and-devotee
nodes.characterTrait_source: Śaiva tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: White humped-bull (zebu); often anthropomorphized with bull-head and human body; bears Śiva and Pārvatī. In every Śiva-temple a Nandi-statue faces the central liṅga.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Śaiva iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Chief of Śiva's gaṇas; listened to all Śiva's teachings (the eight pramāṇa-yoga teachings were given by Śiva to Nandi first). Guards the door of Kailāśa. In some narratives originally a sage (the sage Śilāda's son) who gained Śiva's grace through tapas. The Tamil Periya Purāṇam tells of the devotee Sundarar's quarrel with Nandi at Tiruvārūr.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Śiva Purāṇa; Liṅga Purāṇa; Periya Purāṇam
familyRoles: mount and chief devotee of Śiva
birthTypes: son of the sage Śilāda (in some accounts); primordial mount-of-Śiva (in others)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Śiva Purāṇa
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of the sage Śilāda in some accounts; primordial mount of Śiva in others.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Śiva Purāṇa

nodes.name: Indra
nodes.domain: Vedic king of the gods; thunder-wielder; rain-bringer; slayer of dragon Vṛtra; lord of Svarga; defender of gods against asuras; soma-drinker; in later Purāṇic theology demoted but still king of devas
nodes.domain_source: Rig Veda (~25% of 1028 hymns to Indra — including 1.32); Atharva Veda; Mahābhārata, Vana Parvan; Purāṇic tradition
nodes.object: vajra (thunderbolt fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ from the bones of sage Dadhīci); bow; noose; great white elephant Airāvata (born from churning of the ocean); soma-cup
nodes.object_source: Rig Veda 1.32, 1.85; Mahābhārata, Anuśāsana Parvan
nodes.characterTrait: warlike, soma-drinking, boisterous, sometimes lustful (Ahalyā), often jealous (sending nymphs to disrupt sage-tapas), the Vedic divine warrior par excellence
nodes.characterTrait_source: Rig Veda; Mahābhārata; Rāmāyaṇa (Ahalyā)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Golden-complexioned, mighty-armed, bearing vajra; classical iconography four-armed; rides Airāvata. Called sahasrākṣa ('thousand-eyed') — originally cursed by Gautama with a thousand yonis on his body for the Ahalyā affair, later transformed into eyes.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Vedic-Purāṇic tradition
nodes.significantEvent: Vedic king of gods. Central deed: slaying the great dragon Vṛtra who had captured the cosmic waters (RV 1.32: 'with his hundred-jointed vajra he smote upon the back of Vṛtra'). Drinks soma for strength. In later mythology demoted: in the Govardhana narrative Kṛṣṇa lifts the mountain to defy his wrath. Periodic disgraces (Ahalyā curse, Kṛṣṇa-defiance, sage-tapas-fear) but remains king of devas through every cosmic cycle.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Rig Veda 1.32 (Vṛtra-slaying); Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla-kāṇḍa (Ahalyā); Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10 (Govardhana)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Vedic tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Aditi by Kaśyapa (in Vedic accounts, also of miraculous heaven-and-earth origin).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Rig Veda; Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan

nodes.name: Agni
nodes.domain: fire — sacrificial fire, household fire, digestive fire, cosmic fire; messenger between gods and humans (carrier of offerings via smoke); first word of the Rig Veda (RV 1.1.1 'agnim īḷe purohitam'); twin to Indra in Vedic ritual importance
nodes.domain_source: Rig Veda (~200 hymns to Agni, second only to Indra); Yajur Veda; Brāhmaṇa literature; Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan 220-224 (Khāṇḍava-dāha)
nodes.object: fire-altar (vedi); fire-brand (samidh); sacrificial ladle (sruvā/sruc); rams' fleece; spear in classical iconography
nodes.object_source: Vedic ritual tradition
nodes.characterTrait: all-consuming, purifying, messenger, twin-faced (seven-tongued in iconography), ravenous, priestly
nodes.characterTrait_source: Rig Veda; Mahābhārata
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Red-complexioned, two-faced (or seven-tongued); golden-bearded; rides a ram (meṣa); bears sacrificial implements; flames issuing from mouth or head.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Rig Veda; standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Mediator of every Vedic sacrifice — carries offerings from earth to gods via smoke. Rig Veda opens with him. In Mahābhārata, suffers from indigestion (from too many offerings); burns the Khāṇḍava forest with Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna's help; gives Arjuna the Gāṇḍīva-bow (from Varuṇa via Agni). Called Apām Napāt ('grandson of the waters') for his origin in lightning.
