nodes.significantEvent_source: Rig Veda 1.1; Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan 220-224
nodes.birthTypes_source: Vedic tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Cosmic-primordial; emerges from waters (Apām Napāt, the lightning-fire) or from friction of araṇi (fire-sticks).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Vedic tradition

nodes.name: Surya
nodes.domain: the sun; cosmic source of light and life; seven-horse-chariot-rider; eye of the cosmos; father of Yama and Yamunā (by dawn-goddess Saṃjñā); object of the Gāyatrī Mantra (RV 3.62.10)
nodes.domain_source: Rig Veda 1.50, 1.115 (Sūrya hymns); Gāyatrī mantra (RV 3.62.10); Mahābhārata, Vana Parvan 3, 290-294; Bhaviṣya Purāṇa; the Konārk Sun Temple (13th c.)
nodes.object: seven-horse chariot (driven by Aruṇa, his charioteer); discus; lotus in two hands; rays of light
nodes.object_source: Rig Veda 1.50; Bhaviṣya Purāṇa; Konārk imagery
nodes.characterTrait: radiant, all-seeing, life-giving, all-source, royal, generous
nodes.characterTrait_source: Vedic-Purāṇic tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Golden- or red-complexioned; two- or four-armed; mounted on chariot of seven horses (one per color of spectrum / day of week); driven by Aruṇa (his legless charioteer-brother); rays of light around him.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Rig Veda; Bhaviṣya Purāṇa; Konārk iconography
nodes.significantEvent: The cosmic sun in daily transit. Father of twins Yama (death) and Yamunā by his wife Saṃjñā. Saṃjñā fled his radiance, leaving her shadow-form Chāyā; Tvaṣṭṛ ground Sūrya's brilliance to one-eighth. Father of Karṇa, born to Kuntī before her marriage (Mahābhārata, Vana Parvan 290-294). Gave Yudhiṣṭhira the akṣaya-pātra (inexhaustible food-vessel) in forest exile.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Rig Veda; Mahābhārata, Vana Parvan 3, 290-294
familyRoles: father of Yama, Yamunā, Karṇa, the Aśvin-twins, Manu (Vaivasvata)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Vedic tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Aditi by Kaśyapa; one of the twelve Ādityas (sometimes the chief).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Rig Veda; Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan 65

nodes.name: Varuna
nodes.domain: Vedic period: supreme god of cosmic order (ṛta), all-seeing celestial sovereign, law-keeper, punisher of falsehood, paired with Mitra (Mitra-Varuṇa); later Hindu: demoted to lord of waters and western direction
nodes.domain_source: Rig Veda 1.25, 5.85, 7.86-89 (great Varuṇa-hymns); Atharva Veda; Brāhmaṇa literature; Purāṇic tradition (water-deity, lokapāla of west)
nodes.object: noose (pāśa, with which he binds the unrighteous); great makara (sea-monster/crocodile) mount; conch; umbrella
nodes.object_source: Vedic-Purāṇic iconography
nodes.characterTrait: all-seeing (spies sit by him observing truth/lies), wrath-bearing for falsehood, just, terrifying, finally water-bound
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Fair-complexioned, two- or four-armed; bears noose; rides makara (or swan or great fish in classical iconography); white garments. Originally sky-god of vast dignity; in classical Hindu iconography, water-deity.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Rig Veda; standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Vedic period: supreme celestial sovereign. RV 7.86 is one of the most extraordinary hymns of cosmic religious feeling in the corpus — the worshipper begs Varuṇa's forgiveness for unknown sins, recognizes his all-seeing presence. Over Vedic-to-Purāṇic transition, demoted: cosmic-law function passes partly to Yama, partly to Viṣṇu. In Mahābhārata, gives Arjuna divine weapons (Gāṇḍīva via Agni at Khāṇḍava). In Rāmāyaṇa, makes ocean cross-able when Rāma demands it for the Laṅkā-bridge.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Rig Veda 1.25, 5.85, 7.86-89; Mahābhārata; Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.birthTypes_source: Vedic-Purāṇic tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: One of the Ādityas — son of Aditi by Kaśyapa.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Vedic-Purāṇic tradition

nodes.name: Vayu
nodes.domain: wind, breath, vital force (prāṇa); father of Hanumān and Bhīma; swift-mover; messenger between worlds
nodes.domain_source: Rig Veda 1.2, 1.135, 7.90-92; Aitareya Upaniṣad; Mahābhārata; Vāyu Purāṇa
nodes.object_source: Vāyu-iconography
nodes.characterTrait_source: Vedic tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Two- or four-armed; rides chariot drawn by deer or antelopes (or horse); bears banner and goad; clothed in white.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Purāṇic iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Wind-god of Vedic and Purāṇic traditions. In Vedic religion, paired with Indra (Vāyu-Indra); receives the first soma-cup after Indra. Father of Hanumān (by Añjanā, Rāmāyaṇa) and Bhīma (by Kuntī, Mahābhārata) — both renowned for great strength. In Bṛhad-Āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3 wins the contest of the senses (Wind/Breath as most essential).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Rig Veda; Bṛhad-Āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3; Rāmāyaṇa; Mahābhārata
nodes.birthTypes_source: Vedic tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Cosmic-primordial wind-deity.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Vedic tradition

nodes.name: Soma
nodes.domain: moon; sacred plant whose juice was central Vedic ritual offering; moon-god (Candra); husband of the 27 nakṣatras (Dakṣa's daughters); ancestor of the Lunar dynasty (Soma-vaṃśa)
nodes.domain_source: Rig Veda 9 (entire Maṇḍala 9 — 114 hymns); Atharva Veda; Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan; Vāyu Purāṇa; Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9
nodes.object_source: Rig Veda 9; Purāṇic iconography
nodes.characterTrait: intoxicating, glowing, monthly-waxing-and-waning, fertile, favored-husband (Rohiṇī among 27 wives), cursed-then-blessed
nodes.characterTrait_source: Rig Veda 9; Mahābhārata; Bhāgavata Purāṇa
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Fair- or silver-complexioned; two- or four-armed; bears moon-crescent and lotus; sometimes on chariot drawn by ten white horses (or antelope).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Vedic stratum: central ritual-offering, the soma-juice pressed from a sacred plant, offered to Indra and the gods (entire RV Maṇḍala 9). The original soma-plant's botanical identity is debated. Purāṇic stratum: becomes Candra. Married the 27 daughters of Dakṣa; favored Rohiṇī; the other 26 complained; Dakṣa cursed Soma with wasting-disease. Soma fled to Śiva, who placed him on his head (hence Śiva is Candraśekhara, 'moon-crested') — but curse remained partly active, causing the moon to wax and wane.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Rig Veda 9; Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan; Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9
familyRoles: ancestor of Soma-vaṃśa (Lunar dynasty — Pāṇḍavas descend from it)
birthTypes: theogonic; from the eye of Atri in one account
nodes.birthTypes_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4
nodes.birthCircumstances: Born from the eye of sage Atri in one account; cosmic-primordial in others.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4

nodes.name: Ushas
nodes.domain: Vedic goddess of dawn — the daily-rejoicing-radiant dawn; daughter of heaven (Dyaus); sister of the Aśvin-twins; one of the most beautifully-celebrated Vedic goddesses
nodes.object: chariot drawn by red cows (or tawny horses); radiance of dawn
nodes.object_source: Rig Veda 1.113, 7.75
nodes.characterTrait: radiant, youthful (eternally), beautiful, fleeting, daily-renewing, awakening (rouses humans, beasts, birds), generous
nodes.characterTrait_source: Rig Veda 1.48, 1.92
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Beautiful young woman in brilliant red garment; rides chariot drawn by red cows or tawny horses; appears each morning in the eastern sky; her body is the dawning sky itself.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Rig Veda 1.92, 1.113
nodes.significantEvent: The daily-rejoicing-radiant dawn celebrated in some of the most beautiful hymns of the Rig Veda. RV 1.92.1-2: 'These dawns have raised their banners; in the eastern half of the sky they brighten with light; like warriors decked for battle.' The most personally-emotionally engaged Vedic goddess after Sarasvatī. In Purāṇic stratum largely supplanted by other goddesses and reduced to dawn-as-natural-phenomenon. The Aśvin-twins are her usual companions.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Rig Veda — the great Uṣas-hymns
nodes.birthTypes_source: Rig Veda
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Dyaus (sky-father). PIE-cognate with Greek Eos, Latin Aurora, Lithuanian Aušra, Slavic Zorya.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Rig Veda; comparative Indo-European tradition

nodes.name: Narasimha
nodes.domain: fourth avatar of Viṣṇu — the man-lion who slew Hiraṇyakaśipu; protector of devotee Prahlāda; the wrathful (ugra) form of Viṣṇu; the form between man and beast, day and night, inside and outside
nodes.domain_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.2-10 (central narrative); Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.16-20; Narasiṃha Purāṇa; Hari-vaṃśa
nodes.object: discus (Sudarśana), conch, mace, lotus; the entrails of Hiraṇyakaśipu (worn as garland)
nodes.object_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.8
nodes.animals_source: Narasiṃha IS the man-lion — embodiment via avatar-form
nodes.characterTrait_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.8
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Man-lion — human body with lion's head and claws; four-armed; immense and terrifying; eyes blazing with wrath; manifests by tearing out of a pillar with a great roar.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.8
nodes.significantEvent: Demon-king Hiraṇyakaśipu had performed such tapas that Brahmā granted him a boon: he could not be killed by man or beast, inside or outside, by day or night, on earth or in sky, by any weapon. He set himself up as god and tormented his Viṣṇu-devoted son Prahlāda. Prahlāda survived every murder-attempt. Hiraṇyakaśipu demanded he show Viṣṇu; Prahlāda said he was everywhere, including in this pillar. Hiraṇyakaśipu struck the pillar; Narasiṃha emerged with a roar. He took Hiraṇyakaśipu to the doorway (neither in nor out) at twilight (neither day nor night), placed him on his lap (neither earth nor sky), and tore out his entrails with his claws (not a weapon). Every condition was circumvented. Prahlāda finally pacified his wrath; in some narratives Śiva had to manifest as Śarabha to subdue him.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.2-10
nodes.birthTypes_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.8
nodes.birthCircumstances: Manifests from a pillar struck by Hiraṇyakaśipu's mace — fully formed as the man-lion.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.8

nodes.name: Varaha
nodes.domain: third avatar of Viṣṇu — the great boar who rescued earth (Bhū-devi) from the demon Hiraṇyākṣa, who had dragged her into the cosmic ocean
nodes.domain_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.13, 3.18-19; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.4; Varāha Purāṇa; Taittirīya Saṃhitā
nodes.object: the rescued earth on his tusks; conch, discus, mace, lotus (classical iconography)
nodes.object_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.13
nodes.animals_source: Varāha IS the great boar — embodiment via avatar-form
nodes.characterTrait_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.13
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Great boar with tusks (often depicted as human body with boar-head, four-armed, bearing Viṣṇu's emblems); immense — capable of carrying the earth on his tusks.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.13; iconography
nodes.significantEvent: When demon Hiraṇyākṣa (brother of Hiraṇyakaśipu) seized the earth and dragged her into the cosmic ocean, Viṣṇu manifested as Varāha. Plunged into the ocean, fought and slew Hiraṇyākṣa in thousand-year combat, lifted the earth back up on his tusks to her proper place in the cosmos.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.13, 3.18-19; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.4
birthTypes: avatar-emergence (from Brahmā's nostril in one account)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.13
nodes.birthCircumstances: In one account, manifests from Brahmā's nostril (size of a thumb-joint) and grows to immense size.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.13

nodes.name: Matsya
nodes.domain: first avatar of Viṣṇu — the great fish who saved Manu (the law-giver, first man of this kalpa) from the cosmic flood and preserved the Vedas
nodes.domain_source: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.8.1 (earliest); Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.24; Matsya Purāṇa; Mahābhārata, Vana Parvan 187
nodes.object: the Vedas (preserved during the flood); his fishing-horn; the boat (in which Manu sailed)
nodes.object_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.24; Matsya Purāṇa
nodes.animals_source: Matsya IS the great fish — embodiment via avatar-form
nodes.characterTrait: flood-saving, Veda-preserving, growing-rapidly (from minnow to cosmic-fish), guiding
nodes.characterTrait_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.24
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Great fish (sometimes with a horn on the head to which Manu tied his boat); classical iconography often half-fish/half-human.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Iconography
nodes.significantEvent: When Manu was performing morning ablutions, a tiny fish leapt into his hands asking for protection. Manu placed it in a jar; it grew until it filled the jar. He placed it in a pond; it filled the pond. He placed it in a river; it filled the river. He placed it in the ocean; it filled the ocean. Then it revealed itself as Viṣṇu and warned of imminent cosmic flood. Told Manu to build a great boat and gather the seven sages, the seeds of all life, and the Vedas. When the flood came, Manu tied his boat to the fish's horn; the fish-Viṣṇu towed him through the floodwaters to safety. After the flood, life and the Vedas were re-established. Also slew the demon Hayagrīva who had stolen the Vedas at the start of the cycle.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.24; Matsya Purāṇa; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.8.1
nodes.birthTypes_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.24
nodes.birthCircumstances: Appears as a tiny fish in Manu's hands during morning ablutions.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.24

nodes.name: Kurma
nodes.domain: second avatar of Viṣṇu — the great turtle who supported Mount Mandara on his back during the churning of the cosmic ocean
nodes.domain_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.7-8 (central narrative); Kūrma Purāṇa; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.9; Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan 18
nodes.object: Mount Mandara (which he supported); the cosmic ocean's churning-vessel
nodes.object_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.7
nodes.animals_source: Kūrma IS the great turtle — embodiment via avatar-form
nodes.characterTrait_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.7
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Vast turtle/tortoise (sometimes depicted with human upper body and tortoise lower body); back broad enough to support Mount Mandara.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.7; iconography
nodes.significantEvent: When the gods and demons together churned the cosmic ocean to obtain amṛta (using the Vāsuki serpent as churning-rope around Mount Mandara), the mountain began to sink into the ocean. Viṣṇu took the form of Kūrma — a vast turtle — and dove beneath the mountain to support it on his back. From the churning emerged the fourteen ratnas (cosmic treasures): the goddess Lakṣmī, the goddess of wine Vāruṇī, the divine elephant Airāvata, the cosmic horse Uccaiḥśravas, the kalpa-tree, Kāmadhenu (wish-cow), the moon, the apsaras Rambhā, the halāhala poison (drunk by Śiva), Dhanvantari (god of medicine) bearing the amṛta-pot, the conch Pāñcajanya, the bow Śārṅga, and finally the amṛta itself.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.7-8; Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan 18
nodes.birthTypes_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.7
nodes.birthCircumstances: Manifests as a vast turtle beneath the cosmic ocean to support Mount Mandara.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.7

nodes.name: Ravana
nodes.domain: ten-headed king of Laṅkā; chief rākṣasa adversary of Rāma; supreme devotee of Śiva (paradoxically); abductor of Sītā; in some traditions a learned brahmin (his father Viśravas), in others the supreme demon
nodes.domain_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (entire epic, but especially Yuddha-kāṇḍa); Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.10; Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa; Rāmacaritamānasa; Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa; Śiva Purāṇa (the Rāvaṇa as Śiva-devotee narratives)
nodes.object: his ten heads (each representing one of the ten qualities of intellect — though some readings make them his ten Vedas-knowledge); the bow he tried to lift but could not (the same Śiva-bow Rāma broke at Sītā's svayaṃvara); the Puṣpaka vimāna (flying chariot stolen from Kubera)
nodes.object_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.characterTrait: ten-headed, learned (a brahmin by paternal lineage, scholar of Vedas), boon-blessed (almost invincible), lust-driven (the Sītā abduction), proud, ultimately devoted to Śiva, fearsome king
nodes.characterTrait_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; Śiva Purāṇa
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Ten-headed; twenty-armed; rākṣasa-king of great stature and learning; dark-complexioned; wearing royal ornaments; armed with many weapons.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Son of the brahmin Viśravas and the rākṣasī Kaikasī; grandson of the sage Pulastya. Performed such great tapas that Brahmā granted him the boon of invincibility against gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas — but he disdained to include humans and animals (his eventual downfall, since Rāma is incarnated and Hanumān is vānara). Seized Laṅkā from his half-brother Kubera, stealing also the Puṣpaka vimāna. Abducted Sītā from the forest hermitage (taking advantage of Lakṣmaṇa-rekhā's break). Refused to return her despite warnings. Was slain by Rāma in vast cosmic battle at Laṅkā. In a separate famous narrative, Rāvaṇa is also the supreme devotee of Śiva — performed terrifying tapas including offering his own ten heads one by one; composed the Śiva Tāṇḍava Stotra; tried to carry Mount Kailāśa to Laṅkā, was pinned beneath it by Śiva's toe.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, especially Bāla, Araṇya, and Yuddha kāṇḍas; Śiva Purāṇa, Rāvaṇa-saṃhitā
nodes.birthTypes_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; Uttara-kāṇḍa
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of brahmin sage Viśravas and the rākṣasī Kaikasī (who deliberately sought a great rākṣasa son).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Uttara-kāṇḍa
deathTypes: slain by Rāma in cosmic battle
nodes.deathCircumstances: Slain by Rāma after his abduction of Sītā provoked the cosmic war at Laṅkā. Rāma used the brahmāstra (Brahmā's weapon) given by Agastya to pierce his heart, since his boon protected him from gods but not humans.

nodes.name: Hiranyakashipu
nodes.domain: demon-king; father of the Viṣṇu-devotee Prahlāda; slain by Narasiṃha; the recipient of Brahmā's circumvented boon
nodes.domain_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.2-10 (the central narrative); Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.16-20; Hari-vaṃśa; Narasiṃha Purāṇa
nodes.object: his mace (with which he struck the pillar from which Narasiṃha emerged); the throne he usurped
nodes.object_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.8
nodes.characterTrait: proud, boon-blessed, anti-Viṣṇu, tyrannical, son-persecuting (against the devoted Prahlāda), self-deifying
nodes.characterTrait_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Mighty demon-king; immense, royal-attired; bearing weapons; tyrannical countenance.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7
nodes.significantEvent: After his brother Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by Viṣṇu's Varāha avatar, Hiraṇyakaśipu vowed to be invincible and performed such great tapas that Brahmā granted him a boon: he could not be killed by man or beast, inside or outside, day or night, on earth or in sky, by any weapon. Set himself up as god; persecuted devotees of Viṣṇu. His own son Prahlāda became a great Viṣṇu-devotee, surviving every attempted murder by his father. Finally, demanding Prahlāda show him Viṣṇu, Hiraṇyakaśipu struck a pillar in his palace with his mace; Narasiṃha (Viṣṇu's man-lion avatar) emerged. Narasiṃha took him to the doorway (neither in nor out) at twilight (neither day nor night), placed him on his lap (neither earth nor sky), and tore out his entrails with his claws (not a weapon). Every condition of the boon was circumvented.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.2-10
nodes.birthTypes_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Diti and Kaśyapa; one of the daityas (descendants of Diti).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7
nodes.deathCircumstances: Slain by Narasiṃha by circumventing every condition of his boon: at the threshold (neither inside nor outside), at twilight (neither day nor night), on Narasiṃha's lap (neither earth nor sky), with claws (not a weapon).

nodes.name: Mahishasura
nodes.domain: the buffalo-demon — chief asura defeated all male gods, against whom Durgā was created and by whom slain in the central narrative of the Devī Māhātmya
nodes.domain_source: Devī Māhātmya (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 81-93), chapters 2-3 (the central narrative); Devī-Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.2-20; Skanda Purāṇa
nodes.object: his many weapons (he wields each in his various forms during the battle with Durgā); his buffalo-form itself
nodes.object_source: Devī Māhātmya 2-3
nodes.animals_source: Mahiṣa IS the buffalo (in his original form) — embodiment via shapeshifting between buffalo, lion, elephant, man-buffalo, and full demon-form
nodes.characterTrait: shapeshifter (buffalo-lion-elephant-warrior-buffalo), boon-blessed (could not be killed by any male being), tyrannical, defeats-of-gods
nodes.characterTrait_source: Devī Māhātmya 2-3
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: In his demon-king form, mighty asura warrior; in his buffalo form, vast water-buffalo (mahiṣa = buffalo); can shapeshift between forms in battle.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Devī Māhātmya 2-3
nodes.significantEvent: Performed such great tapas that Brahmā granted him the boon of invincibility against any male being. Set himself up against the gods, defeated Indra and all the devas, drove them from heaven. The gods, helpless, fled to the Trimūrti. Their combined wrath-tejas (radiance) emerged as the supreme goddess Durgā, who alone could kill him since she was female. In the ensuing battle (Devī Māhātmya 2-3), Mahiṣa shapeshifted into many forms — buffalo, lion, elephant, warrior — while Durgā defeated him in each form. Finally, in his buffalo form, she pierced him with her trident and beheaded him. The Durgā-pūjā festival of Bengal centers on this victory.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Devī Māhātmya 2-3; Devī-Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.2-20
birthTypes: son of the asura Rambha and a buffalo-cow
nodes.birthTypes_source: Skanda Purāṇa; Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of the asura Rambha and a buffalo-cow (according to one tradition, his mother was an apsara cursed to buffalo-form); hence his ability to shapeshift between buffalo and man-form.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Skanda Purāṇa; Devī-Bhāgavata Purāṇa
nodes.deathCircumstances: Slain by Durgā after his shapeshifting battle: she pierced him with her trident in his buffalo form and beheaded him.

nodes.name: Yama (Hindu)
nodes.domain: god of death; lord of the dead; first man to die (path-finder for all who follow); judge of the dead; lord of southern direction; son of Sūrya; twin of Yamī (the Yamunā river)
nodes.domain_source: Rig Veda 10.10 (Yama-Yamī dialogue); RV 10.14 (funeral hymn); Atharva Veda; Kaṭha Upaniṣad (Yama as death-teacher of Naciketas); Mahābhārata, Vana Parvan; Garuḍa Purāṇa; Yama-Smṛti
nodes.object: noose (pāśa, to draw out the soul); mace (daṇḍa); great water-buffalo Mahiṣa as vāhana; Citragupta-ledger (his scribe records every deed)
nodes.object_source: Vedic-Purāṇic iconography
nodes.characterTrait: just, terrible, impartial, inescapable, great teacher of mortality, kind-to-the-righteous, fearsome-to-the-wicked
nodes.characterTrait_source: Kaṭha Upaniṣad; Mahābhārata
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Dark-complexioned, two- or four-armed; bears noose and mace; rides great water-buffalo (Mahiṣa); often with Citragupta beside him.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Garuḍa Purāṇa; iconography
nodes.significantEvent: First of mortals to die — found the path to the world of ancestors (Pitṛloka) and became its lord (RV 10.14: 'who explored the way for many — King Yama'). In RV 10.10, his twin Yamī tries to seduce him; he refuses on dharma-grounds. In Kaṭha Upaniṣad, teaches the central death-immortality teaching to young Naciketas. In Mahābhārata, tests Yudhiṣṭhira as a yakṣa at the lake (Yakṣa-praśna). Judges every soul; righteous go to Svarga, wicked to the narakas. His scribe Citragupta keeps the ledger.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Rig Veda 10.10, 10.14; Kaṭha Upaniṣad; Mahābhārata, Vana Parvan 313-315
nodes.birthTypes_source: Rig Veda; Mahābhārata
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Sūrya (Vivasvant) and Saṃjñā; twin of Yamī; first mortal to die and become lord of dead.
nodes.deathCircumstances: As lord of death, does not die in cosmic-functional sense; was first to die in primordial time and thereby became immortal-as-death-lord.

nodes.name: Nephthys
nodes.domain: mourning, the dead, protection of the deceased; the dark counterpart of Isis; sister-wife of Set; one of the four canopic-jar protectresses (with Isis, Neith, Selket)
nodes.domain_source: Pyramid Texts; Coffin Texts; Book of the Dead; the Lamentations of Isis and Nephthys; Plutarch, Isis and Osiris 14, 38
nodes.object: the throne-and-basket hieroglyph (her name nbt-ḥwt = 'lady of the temple'); ankh; sometimes a vessel for ritual mourning
nodes.object_source: Standard Nephthys iconography
nodes.characterTrait: mourning, protective-of-the-dead, ambivalent (married to Set but loyal to Osiris and Isis), childless-with-Set (in most traditions), assisting-Isis
nodes.characterTrait_source: Plutarch 14, 38; Lamentations of Isis and Nephthys
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Anthropomorphic woman wearing the hieroglyph of her name (throne and basket) on her head; often depicted as the mirror-image of Isis; sometimes winged.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography; the canopic-jar protectress depictions
nodes.significantEvent: Daughter of Geb and Nut, one of the five children born on the epagomenal days. Sister-wife of Set; mother of Anubis (in most traditions — Plutarch 14 explicitly says she conceived Anubis by Osiris, mistaking him for Set; in other versions, by Set alone). Aided Isis in mourning Osiris and collecting his dismembered body; the two together became the model for ritual mourners in Egyptian funerals. One of the four canopic-jar protectresses (Nephthys guards Hapi, the lung-jar). Her plaintive role appears throughout funerary literature.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Plutarch 14, 38; Lamentations of Isis and Nephthys; Pyramid Texts
familyRoles: mother of Anubis (by Osiris in Plutarch; by Set in other versions)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Plutarch 12
nodes.birthCircumstances: One of the five children of Geb and Nut, born on the epagomenal days.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Plutarch 12

nodes.name: Anubis
nodes.domain: embalming, mummification, the dead, the necropolis, the weighing of the heart, the opening of the mouth ceremony, the underworld jackals — 'lord of the sacred land', 'foremost of the westerners' (khentamentyu); psychopomp
nodes.domain_source: Pyramid Texts (the earliest Anubis-references — he is the original lord of the dead before Osiris's rise); Coffin Texts; Book of the Dead (especially ch. 125, the weighing of the heart); the Embalming Ritual (Papyrus Boulaq 3); Plutarch, Isis and Osiris 14, 44
nodes.object: embalming-table; the flail; the was-scepter; the heart-balance; mummification tools
nodes.object_source: Standard Anubis iconography; the Embalming Ritual
nodes.animals_source: Anubis is depicted as a jackal-headed man, but per the schema the head-form is iconographic; he doesn't symbolically embody-as-jackal in the way Apep IS the serpent. His sacred animal (jackal) is canonical but as a head-attribute not a fully embodied form
nodes.characterTrait: psychopomp-grave, just (weigher of hearts), protective of the dead, embalming-knowledgeable, guide-of-souls
nodes.characterTrait_source: Pyramid Texts; Book of the Dead; Embalming Ritual
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Jackal-headed man, often wearing the nemes-headdress and bearing was-scepter and flail; sometimes fully jackal (a black jackal — black for the color of mummification's bitumen and Nile-silt of regeneration); guarding necropolis-entrances.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard Anubis iconography from Old Kingdom onward
nodes.significantEvent: The original lord of the dead in pre-Osirian Egyptian religion (the title khentamentyu, 'foremost of the westerners', is originally Anubis's, later transferred to Osiris). Embalmed Osiris's body — establishing the prototype mummification. In the Book of the Dead 125 (the Judgment-Hall of Osiris), Anubis leads the deceased into the hall, weighs the heart against Ma'at's feather, with Thoth recording the result. If the heart balances, the deceased proceeds to Osiris's throne; if heavier, Ammit devours it. Anubis also conducts the Opening of the Mouth ceremony on the mummified corpse.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Pyramid Texts; Book of the Dead 125; Embalming Ritual; the Anubis-shrines at Tomb of Tutankhamun
nodes.eventTypes_source: Pyramid Texts; Book of the Dead 125; Embalming Ritual
familyRoles: son of Nephthys (by Osiris in Plutarch 14, by Set in other versions)
adopted by Isis (who raised him as her own)
birthTypes: child of Nephthys (by Osiris or Set)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Plutarch 14
nodes.birthCircumstances: Born to Nephthys after she conceived by Osiris (whom she had tricked Set-like, in Plutarch's version) — or by Set in other versions. Raised by Isis.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Plutarch 14

nodes.name: Apep
nodes.domain: the cosmic serpent of chaos; eternal adversary of Ra; the embodiment of isfet (chaos and wrongdoing) opposing Ma'at (order); attacked the solar barque every night and was repulsed; never destroyed, eternally renewing
nodes.domain_source: Coffin Texts spell 160 (the early Apep-references); Book of the Dead chapters 7, 39, 108; Book of Gates; Book of Caverns; Amduat; the Book of Apep (the Bremner-Rhind Papyrus — the central ritual text against Apep)
nodes.object: his immense serpent-body; the knives, fire-spears, and ropes used against him by Ra's defenders
nodes.object_source: Bremner-Rhind Papyrus (the Apep-destruction ritual texts); Book of Gates; Amduat
nodes.animals_source: Apep IS the serpent — embodiment as the cosmic-chaos-serpent
nodes.characterTrait: chaos-embodying, swallowing-the-sun, eternally-defeated-and-renewing, voiceless (his roar shakes the cosmos), hungry
nodes.characterTrait_source: Bremner-Rhind Papyrus; Book of Gates
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Immense serpent (the Egyptian texts describe him as approximately 16 meters long); in tomb-depictions, often shown being speared, cut into pieces, set on fire; never fully destroyed.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Book of Gates illustrations; Bremner-Rhind Papyrus
nodes.significantEvent: Attacks Ra's solar barque every night during its passage through the Duat (especially at the seventh hour). Set, the cat-form of Ra (or a cat-aspect of Ra called the Great Cat of Heliopolis), Mehen, and other defenders battle Apep on Ra's behalf — spearing, cutting, burning. Apep is repulsed every night but reforms by the next night, embodying the principle that chaos can be defeated but never permanently destroyed; only daily-renewed vigilance keeps the cosmos turning. The Bremner-Rhind Papyrus preserves an extensive apotropaic ritual: drawing Apep on papyrus, spitting on it, stabbing it, and burning it to magically reinforce his nightly defeat.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Bremner-Rhind Papyrus; Book of Gates; Amduat hour 7
nodes.birthTypes_source: Coffin Texts; Bremner-Rhind
nodes.birthCircumstances: Primordial chaos-serpent; uncreated, predating the cosmos in some accounts; in others, emerged from Nun's waters before Ra.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Bremner-Rhind Papyrus
nodes.deathCircumstances: Defeated every night by Ra and his defenders but never permanently destroyed — reforms by the next night. The defeat-renewal pattern itself is the cosmic mechanism by which order is maintained.

nodes.name: Ammit
nodes.domain: the soul-devourer; annihilator of the unjustified dead; standing at the scales in the Judgment-Hall of Osiris to eat the hearts that weigh heavier than Ma'at's feather; the second death (final annihilation, not afterlife)
nodes.domain_source: Book of the Dead ch. 125 (the central source — the judgment-hall scene); Hunefer Papyrus (Dynasty 19 — the famous illustrated weighing-of-the-heart scene); standard funerary tradition
nodes.object: her own monstrous body (the hybrid of three man-eating creatures); position at the scales beside Anubis and Thoth
nodes.object_source: Hunefer Papyrus; Book of the Dead 125 illustrations
nodes.animals_source: Ammit is a composite-creature — fundamentally an embodied monster combining lion, hippo, crocodile parts; her composite-form IS her nature, an extreme case where the schema's animals-field is appropriately empty since she has no separable 'sacred animal' — she is the assembled monstrous form
nodes.characterTrait: devouring, hungry, monstrous-composite, eternal-annihilator, hall-stationary (does not move from the scales)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Book of the Dead 125
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Composite monster: head of a crocodile, fore-quarters of a lion, hind-quarters of a hippopotamus (the three most-feared man-eaters of Egypt). Stations herself at the scales in the Judgment-Hall of Osiris.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Hunefer Papyrus; Book of the Dead 125 illustrations from the New Kingdom onward
nodes.significantEvent: Sole role in extant tradition: positioned at the scales in the Judgment-Hall of Osiris during the weighing-of-the-heart. Anubis leads the deceased in; the heart is placed on one pan, Ma'at's feather on the other; Thoth records the result. If the heart balances (or is lighter than the feather), the deceased is justified and ushered to the throne of Osiris for eternal afterlife. If the heart is heavier — proving the deceased committed wrongdoing — Ammit devours it. The annihilation is total — the 'second death' from which there is no return. Hers is the threat behind the 42 Negative Confessions; the deceased declares innocence against every offense to avoid Ammit's hunger.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Book of the Dead 125; Hunefer Papyrus
nodes.birthTypes_source: Funerary tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Functional being of the judgment-hall; no birth-narrative.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Funerary tradition

nodes.name: Naunet
nodes.domain: primordial waters (female-pair-aspect); consort of Nun in the Hermopolitan Ogdoad; the watery chaos before creation
nodes.domain_source: Hermopolitan cosmogony texts (preserved in the Karnak inscriptions and Ptolemaic Esna and Edfu temple texts)
nodes.object_source: Hermopolitan cosmogony
nodes.animals_source: Ogdoad females are depicted as serpent-headed women (the male pair-members are frog-headed); but the serpent-head is iconographic, not embodiment
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hermopolitan cosmogony
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Serpent-headed woman (Ogdoad females are serpent-headed, the males frog-headed — the convention from Karnak inscriptions onward).
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Karnak and Esna iconography
nodes.significantEvent: One of the eight primordial beings of the Hermopolitan Ogdoad — paired with Nun as the female-aspect of the primordial waters. Before creation, the Ogdoad-eight together constituted the undifferentiated chaos from which the cosmic egg or lotus eventually emerged.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hermopolitan cosmogony; Karnak inscriptions
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hermopolitan cosmogony
nodes.birthCircumstances: Pre-cosmic; uncreated.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hermopolitan cosmogony

nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Karnak and Esna iconography

nodes.name: Takemikazuchi
nodes.domain: thunder, swords, martial valor, the subjugation of the land; one of the central warrior-kami; kami of Kashima Jingū; emerged from the blood of Kagutsuchi on Izanagi's sword
nodes.domain_source: Kojiki, scrolls I-II (the central source — birth from Kagutsuchi's blood, the subjugation of Ōkuninushi); Nihon Shoki; Kashima Jingū traditions
nodes.object_source: Kojiki; Kashima Jingū traditions
nodes.characterTrait: fierce-warrior, sword-wielding, martial, subjugating, the divine general of the kuni-yuzuri
nodes.characterTrait_source: Kojiki — the central subjugation-of-Ōkuninushi narrative
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Warrior-kami; depicted with sword; in late tradition sometimes depicted seated cross-legged on the tip of his own sword embedded in the earth (the famous Kashima posture)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Kashima Jingū iconographic tradition
nodes.significantEvent: Emerged from the blood that flowed from Izanagi's sword Ame-no-Ohabari when Izanagi beheaded Kagutsuchi. Together with Futsunushi (or in some versions Ame-no-Torifune), sent by Amaterasu and Takamimusubi to subjugate the earthly land for Ninigi's descent. Confronted Ōkuninushi at Inasa-no-Hama (Inasa beach in Izumo); seated himself on his sword's tip embedded in the waves; demanded the land. Ōkuninushi referred them to his son Kotoshironushi, who agreed; Takeminakata resisted but was defeated in a wrestling-match. The kuni-yuzuri ('transfer of the land') was thus completed.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Kojiki — kuni-yuzuri narrative; Kashima Jingū traditions
nodes.birthTypes_source: Kojiki
nodes.birthCircumstances: Emerged from the blood of Kagutsuchi on Izanagi's sword Ame-no-Ohabari after Kagutsuchi's beheading.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Kojiki

nodes.name: Kotoshironushi
nodes.domain: the 'thing-knowing master'; son of Ōkuninushi who agreed to the kuni-yuzuri; oracular kami; fishing; one of the central earthly-kami of the Izumo cycle
nodes.domain_source: Kojiki, scrolls I-II (the kuni-yuzuri narrative); Nihon Shoki; Izumo Taisha traditions; later identified with Ebisu in some traditions
nodes.object: fishing rod and tai (sea-bream, his catch when the messengers arrived)
nodes.object_source: Kojiki — found fishing at Mihonosaki when the heavenly messengers came
nodes.characterTrait: agreeable, oracular, fishing-loving, son who deferred to his father's wisdom
nodes.characterTrait_source: Kojiki
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Earthly kami; iconography minimal in early sources; later identified with Ebisu (the fishing god of the Shichifukujin) due to his fishing-at-Miho activity at the moment of the kuni-yuzuri
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Kojiki; later syncretic Ebisu-iconography
nodes.significantEvent: When Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi arrived demanding the transfer of the land, Ōkuninushi said he would consent only if his sons agreed. Kotoshironushi was found fishing at Mihonosaki; messengers reported the demand to him; he agreed immediately, struck his hands together to make an 'eight-fold reverse-clap' (yaegaki) seal that turned his boat into a green leafy fence, and concealed himself within it. His agreement (and his brother Takeminakata's defeat) completed the kuni-yuzuri.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Kojiki — kuni-yuzuri
nodes.birthTypes_source: Kojiki
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Ōkuninushi.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Kojiki

nodes.name: Jimmu
nodes.domain: legendary first emperor of Japan; great-grandson of Ninigi; descendant of Amaterasu; conqueror of Yamato; conventional founding date 660 BCE
nodes.domain_source: Kojiki, scroll II-III (the central Jimmu narrative — Eastern Expedition); Nihon Shoki, scroll III; the imperial chronology traces from him
nodes.object: the imperial regalia inherited from Ninigi (mirror, jewel, sword); his bow on which the kite-spirit (kite of light) perched at Tomi
nodes.object_source: Kojiki — Eastern Expedition; the Three Sacred Treasures continuity
nodes.characterTrait_source: Kojiki — Eastern Expedition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Legendary first emperor; conventionally lived 660-585 BCE; iconography of imperial founder
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard imperial tradition
nodes.significantEvent: Great-grandson of Ninigi (son of Ugayafukiaezu and Tamayori-hime). Departed from Hyūga in Kyūshū to subdue the central lands; led the Eastern Expedition through the Inland Sea; encountered resistance at Naniwa and Tomi; the eight-handed golden kite of light perched on his bow and blinded his enemies; eventually reached Yamato and was enthroned at Kashihara, founding the imperial line. The conventional date of his enthronement (11 February 660 BCE) is celebrated as the National Foundation Day of Japan.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Kojiki — Eastern Expedition; Nihon Shoki
familyRoles: founder of the Yamato imperial dynasty
nodes.birthTypes_source: Kojiki
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Ugayafukiaezu (himself son of Hoori and Toyotama-hime) and Tamayori-hime.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Kojiki

nodes.name: Daikokuten
nodes.domain: wealth, harvest, the kitchen; one of the Seven Lucky Gods (Shichifukujin); syncretic — combines the Hindu-Buddhist Mahākāla with the Shintō Ōkuninushi (their names share the same characters 大国 'great country')
nodes.domain_source: Shichifukujin tradition (consolidated 15th-17th c.); Daikoku-kō folk worship; the Mahākāla-Daikoku syncretism
nodes.object: great sack of treasures slung over shoulder; magic mallet (uchide-no-kozuchi); seated or standing on rice bales
nodes.object_source: Shichifukujin iconography
nodes.characterTrait_source: Shichifukujin tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Smiling plump man with mallet and sack; black hood; standing on rice bales (a pun on his name); often paired with Ebisu in domestic shrines
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Shichifukujin iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Originally the Hindu-Buddhist Mahākāla (a fierce form of Śiva) absorbed via Tantric Buddhism into Japan. The character-pun 大国 (Daikoku = 'great country') matched Ōkuninushi's name (Ōkuninushi means 'great-country-master', written 大国主), leading to medieval syncretic identification. By the Edo period, Daikokuten became the central wealth-and-kitchen kami of the Shichifukujin. Often paired with Ebisu in domestic worship (both are wealth-givers).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Shichifukujin tradition; Mahākāla-Daikoku syncretism
familyRoles: one of the Seven Lucky Gods
syncretic combination of Mahākāla, Daikoku, Ōkuninushi
nodes.birthTypes_source: Shichifukujin tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Origin in Hindu-Buddhist Mahākāla; absorbed via Tantric Buddhism into Japan; medieval syncretic identification with Ōkuninushi via name-pun.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Shichifukujin tradition

nodes.name: Ebisu
nodes.domain: fishing, merchants, prosperity, sea-borne luck; one of the Seven Lucky Gods (Shichifukujin); often identified with Kotoshironushi (son of Ōkuninushi) or with the unwanted firstborn Hiruko (the 'leech-child' of Izanagi and Izanami)
nodes.domain_source: Shichifukujin tradition; Nishinomiya Jinja traditions (the head Ebisu shrine); Kojiki (the Hiruko narrative)
nodes.object: fishing rod; a large red sea-bream (tai) under his arm
nodes.object_source: Shichifukujin iconography
nodes.characterTrait: smiling, laughing, fishing-loving, plump, deaf in one ear (in the Hiruko-identification tradition), patron of commerce
nodes.characterTrait_source: Shichifukujin tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Smiling plump man wearing a tall pointed hat; holding fishing rod and a large red sea-bream; often depicted laughing
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Shichifukujin iconography
nodes.significantEvent: The only kami of the Seven Lucky Gods who is purely Japanese in origin. Identified variously: (a) with Hiruko ('leech-child'), the first child of Izanagi and Izanami who was deformed and abandoned in a boat at sea, returning later as the lucky Ebisu; or (b) with Kotoshironushi (son of Ōkuninushi) who was found fishing during the kuni-yuzuri. By the Edo period he became the central merchant-and-fishing kami, his cult especially strong in Osaka and the trade-cities.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Shichifukujin tradition; Kojiki (Hiruko narrative); Nishinomiya Jinja traditions
familyRoles: one of the Seven Lucky Gods
nodes.birthTypes_source: Shichifukujin tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Origin variously traced to Hiruko (the abandoned firstborn of Izanagi and Izanami) or to Kotoshironushi (son of Ōkuninushi).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Shichifukujin tradition

nodes.name: Bishamonten
nodes.domain: war, warriors, dignity, the protection of Buddhist law; one of the Seven Lucky Gods; one of the Four Heavenly Kings (Shi Tennō) of Buddhism; the Japanese form of the Buddhist Vaiśravaṇa / Kubera
nodes.domain_source: Shichifukujin tradition; Buddhist Vaiśravaṇa-Kubera continuum; Shitennōji Temple (the central Four Heavenly Kings shrine, founded 593 CE)
nodes.object: spear; pagoda (the stūpa of Buddhist Law); armor; sometimes a treasure-tower
nodes.object_source: Shichifukujin iconography; Buddhist Vaiśravaṇa iconography
nodes.characterTrait_source: Shichifukujin tradition; Buddhist tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Armored warrior holding spear and treasure-pagoda; often standing on a demon (representing trampled evil); fierce visage
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Buddhist iconographic tradition
nodes.significantEvent: The Japanese form of the Buddhist Vaiśravaṇa / Hindu Kubera (lokapāla of the north, god of wealth and warriors). As one of the Four Heavenly Kings, guardian of the north. As one of the Seven Lucky Gods, patron of warriors and bestower of dignity and martial luck. Especially worshipped by the samurai class during the medieval period.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Shichifukujin tradition; Buddhist tradition
familyRoles: one of the Seven Lucky Gods
one of the Four Heavenly Kings of Buddhism
nodes.birthTypes_source: Buddhist tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Buddhist deity Vaiśravaṇa (a form of Kubera) imported into Japanese tradition.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Buddhist tradition

nodes.name: Hotei
nodes.domain: happiness, contentment, abundance; one of the Seven Lucky Gods; based on the historical Chinese Chan Buddhist monk Budai (10th century); identified as the future Buddha Maitreya
nodes.domain_source: Shichifukujin tradition; Chinese Chan tradition of the monk Budai (布袋, lit. 'cloth-sack'); the Maitreya-incarnation tradition
nodes.object: large cloth sack containing his possessions and gifts for children; sometimes a fan
nodes.object_source: Shichifukujin iconography
nodes.characterTrait: fat-bellied, smiling, generous, children-loving, content-with-little, wandering
nodes.characterTrait_source: Chinese Chan tradition; Shichifukujin tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Vastly fat-bellied monk in simple robes with bare chest; carrying a large cloth sack; smiling broadly; sometimes surrounded by children
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard Hotei iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Based on the historical Chinese Chan Buddhist monk Budai (布袋, d. 916 CE), an eccentric mendicant who wandered Zhejiang Province with a cloth sack of possessions, smiling and laughing, giving gifts to children. After his death, recognized as an incarnation of the future Buddha Maitreya. Imported to Japan during the Muromachi period (1336-1573) and incorporated into the Shichifukujin as the kami of contentment, generosity, and abundance.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Chinese Chan tradition; Shichifukujin tradition
familyRoles: one of the Seven Lucky Gods
historically the Chinese Chan monk Budai
nodes.birthTypes_source: Chinese Chan tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Based on the historical Chinese Chan Buddhist monk Budai (d. 916 CE); imported to Japan during the Muromachi period.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Chinese Chan tradition

nodes.name: Jurojin
nodes.domain: longevity, wisdom; one of the Seven Lucky Gods; identified with the Chinese Daoist immortal Shou-lao (Star God of Longevity); often paired with or merged with Fukurokuju
nodes.domain_source: Shichifukujin tradition; Chinese Daoist tradition of Shou-lao (the southern-polar Star God of Longevity)
nodes.object: staff to which a scroll containing the lifespans of all beings is tied; sometimes a fan; sometimes accompanied by a black deer (symbol of longevity)
nodes.object_source: Shichifukujin iconography
nodes.characterTrait_source: Shichifukujin tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Tall thin elderly man with extremely long head (tall-domed) and a long white beard; bears a staff with scroll; often accompanied by a deer, crane, or tortoise (all longevity symbols)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard Jurojin iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Japanese form of the Chinese Daoist immortal Shou-lao (壽老 'Old Longevity'), the deified southern-polar star (Canopus). One of the Three Stars of Fortune (Fu Lu Shou). Imported into Japan and incorporated into the Shichifukujin. Often confused or merged with Fukurokuju.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Chinese Daoist tradition; Shichifukujin tradition
familyRoles: one of the Seven Lucky Gods
nodes.birthTypes_source: Chinese Daoist tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Japanese form of the Chinese Daoist immortal Shou-lao, the deified Canopus star.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Chinese Daoist tradition

nodes.name: Fukurokuju
nodes.domain: happiness (fuku), wealth (roku), longevity (ju); one of the Seven Lucky Gods; Daoist origin — combining Three Stars of Fortune (Fu Lu Shou) into a single deity
nodes.domain_source: Shichifukujin tradition; Chinese Daoist tradition of the Three Stars of Fortune (Fu Lu Shou)
nodes.object: staff; sometimes a scroll; often accompanied by a crane (longevity symbol)
nodes.object_source: Shichifukujin iconography
nodes.characterTrait_source: Shichifukujin tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Elderly man with extremely elongated head (the top of his head forms a high dome — the most distinctive iconographic feature, signifying his exceptional wisdom and long life); long white beard; carrying staff; accompanied by crane or tortoise
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard Fukurokuju iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Japanese deity combining Chinese Daoist Three Stars of Fortune (Fu 福 happiness, Lu 禄 wealth/rank, Shou 寿 longevity) into a single figure. Imported into Japan during the late medieval period. Often paired or even confused with Jurojin (both based on the Daoist longevity-tradition).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Chinese Daoist tradition; Shichifukujin tradition
familyRoles: one of the Seven Lucky Gods
Daoist Three Stars of Fortune combined
nodes.birthTypes_source: Chinese Daoist tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Combined Japanese form of the Chinese Daoist Three Stars of Fortune.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Chinese Daoist tradition

nodes.name: Poseidon
nodes.domain: sea, earthquakes, horses; one of the three sons of Cronus who divided the cosmos (Zeus-sky, Poseidon-sea, Hades-underworld); 'Earth-shaker' (Ἐνοσίγαιος); creator of horses
nodes.domain_source: Homer, Iliad (Iliad 13, his interventions on behalf of the Achaeans) and Odyssey (Odysseus's persecutor); Hesiod, Theogony 453-457; Homeric Hymn 22; Apollodorus 1.4.5; Pausanias 7.21.7; the Isthmia and Onchestos cult-centers
nodes.object: trident (his primary emblem); the chariot drawn by horses or hippocamps over the waves; the salt-spring he produced on the Acropolis (defeated by Athena's olive in the contest for Athens)
nodes.object_source: Standard Poseidonian iconography
nodes.animals_source: Poseidon's sacred animals: horse (he created it, and in some traditions raped Demeter while both were in horse-form, producing the horse Areion); bull (his sacrificial animal); dolphin
nodes.characterTrait: wrathful, persecuting (Odysseus, Minos's queen Pasiphae for his pleasure), competitive (lost Athens to Athena, lost Argos to Hera), proud, prolific-of-monsters
nodes.characterTrait_source: Homer, Odyssey (the Odysseus-persecution); Apollodorus 3.14.1 (Athens contest); 3.1.4 (Minoan bull)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Standard Poseidon iconography — mature bearded king resembling Zeus, distinguished by trident; sometimes riding hippocamps; the great chryselephantine statue at Isthmia
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Brother of Zeus and Hades; received the sea in the threefold division of the cosmos. Lost the contest for Athens to Athena (his salt-spring vs. her olive). Sent the Minotaur-engendering bull to Minos; Pasiphae lusted after it and bore the Minotaur. Created the horse Areion by raping Demeter when both were in horse-form. Persecuted Odysseus through the Odyssey after Odysseus blinded his son Polyphemus. Fathered many monsters and heroes: the Cyclops Polyphemus, the giants Otus and Ephialtes, Pegasus (from Medusa whom he raped), Theseus (some traditions).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Homer, Odyssey; Apollodorus 3.1.4, 3.14.1, 3.15.6; Hesiod, Theogony 453-457
familyRoles: brother of Zeus, Hades, Hera, Demeter, Hestia
father of Triton (by Amphitrite), Polyphemus, Theseus, Pegasus, and many others
birthTypes: child of Cronus and Rhea; swallowed and regurgitated
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 453-457
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 453-457 — swallowed by Cronus, regurgitated when Zeus tricked him.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony

nodes.name: Hades
nodes.domain: the underworld realm and its god; lord of the dead; the chthonic counterpart of Olympian Zeus; in late tradition also Plouton, lord of mineral wealth beneath the earth; 'the unseen one' (ἀ-ἰδης)
nodes.domain_source: Homer, Iliad and Odyssey (especially Od. 11 — the Nekyia); Hesiod, Theogony 311, 455, 768-774; Homeric Hymn to Demeter (his abduction of Persephone); Apollodorus 1.5; Pausanias 1.28.6 (the Athenian Ploutonion)
nodes.object: the helmet of invisibility (κυνέη Ἄϊδος — given to him by the Cyclopes during the Titanomachy; Perseus borrowed it for the Medusa beheading); bident or sceptre; key (in late iconography); the rivers of the underworld (Styx, Acheron, Cocytus, Phlegethon, Lethe)
nodes.object_source: Standard Hadean tradition; Apollodorus 1.2.1 (Cyclopes' gift)
nodes.animals_source: Hades's associated animals: Cerberus (his three-headed dog); black ram (his sacrifice); cypress (his tree)
nodes.characterTrait: stern, grim, unmoved by prayer (no temples), abduction-loving (Persephone), wealth-bringing (Plouton-aspect), inescapable
nodes.characterTrait_source: Homer; Homeric Hymn to Demeter; Greek prayer-and-cult tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Standard Hades iconography — mature bearded king resembling Zeus, but darker, often enthroned with Persephone beside him; sometimes turned away (referencing his name 'unseen'); the κυνέη of invisibility as attribute
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Brother of Zeus and Poseidon; received the underworld in the threefold division. Almost no narrative-mythology — Greeks generally avoided naming him directly. Central narrative: the abduction of Persephone (Homeric Hymn to Demeter), whom he made his queen. Refused to release Persephone but agreed she could spend part of each year with Demeter after she ate the pomegranate seeds. Hosted the visiting heroes (Heracles for Cerberus, Orpheus for Eurydice, Theseus and Pirithous for Persephone, Odysseus in the Nekyia).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Homeric Hymn to Demeter; Homer, Odyssey 11; Apollodorus 1.5, 2.5.12 (Heracles)
familyRoles: brother of Zeus, Poseidon, Hera, Demeter, Hestia
birthTypes: child of Cronus and Rhea; swallowed and regurgitated
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 453-457
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 453-457 — swallowed by Cronus, regurgitated when Zeus tricked him.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony

nodes.name: Ares
nodes.domain: war (especially the violent, bloody aspect — contrast with Athena's strategic-just war), violence, frenzy of battle, courage
nodes.domain_source: Homer, Iliad 5 (where he is wounded by Diomedes) and Iliad 21; Homeric Hymn 8 (to Ares); Hesiod, Theogony 921-923; Apollodorus 1.3.1; Pausanias 1.28.5
nodes.object: spear; sword; helmet; shield; chariot drawn by four fire-breathing immortal horses (Aithon, Konabos, Phlogeus, Phobos)
nodes.object_source: Homer; standard Areian iconography
nodes.animals_source: Ares's sacred animals: dog (sacrificial); vulture (battlefield carrion-bird); woodpecker; the four immortal fire-breathing horses
nodes.characterTrait: bloodthirsty, frenzied, cowardly (in Iliad 5, fled in pain after Diomedes wounded him; called 'most hateful' by Zeus); contrast with Athena's strategic war
nodes.characterTrait_source: Homer (especially Iliad 5.890 — Zeus calls him 'most hateful'); Hesiod
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Standard Ares iconography — armored warrior; helmeted; bearing spear; often paired in scenes with Aphrodite (his lover) or Eros and Phobos (his sons)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Son of Zeus and Hera; the disreputable war-god whom the Greeks themselves considered unloved (much more honored among Thracians). The Ares-Aphrodite adulterous affair (Odyssey 8.266-366) — caught by Hephaestus in the golden net. Wounded by Diomedes (with Athena's help) in Iliad 5. Father (by Aphrodite) of Eros, Anteros, Phobos, Deimos, Harmonia. Father of many heroes including Diomedes of Thrace (whose man-eating mares Heracles tamed).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Homer, Iliad 5, Odyssey 8; Hesiod, Theogony 921-923
familyRoles: father of Eros, Phobos, Deimos, Harmonia (by Aphrodite)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 921-923
nodes.birthCircumstances: Son of Zeus and Hera.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony

nodes.name: Hestia
nodes.domain: hearth, home, the sacred fire of the household and the polis; one of the three virgin goddesses (with Athena and Artemis); first child of Cronus and Rhea (and thus first swallowed, last regurgitated)
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 453-454; Homeric Hymn 5 (to Aphrodite, mentioning Hestia's virginity-vow); Homeric Hymn 24, 29 (to Hestia); Plutarch; Pausanias 5.14.4 (Olympia's altar-of-the-twelve-gods)
nodes.object: the hearth-fire itself (her primary 'object' — the household altar); ladle; staff
nodes.object_source: Standard Hestian cult tradition
nodes.characterTrait: modest, virginal, stationary (never leaves Olympus), gentle, peace-loving, accepting-of-replacement (gave her seat among the Twelve Olympians to Dionysus in some traditions)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Homeric Hymn 5 and 29; the Hestian cult tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Hestia iconography — veiled matronly goddess, modestly draped, often standing rather than enthroned (since her place is the central hearth); minimally depicted in surviving Greek art
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: First-born of Cronus and Rhea (and thus first swallowed by Cronus, last regurgitated). Refused marriage offers from Poseidon and Apollo, vowing eternal virginity on Zeus's head. Received the central hearth of every Greek home and every city as her sacred place. In the Roman tradition Vesta — central to civic religion. Sometimes counted as the twelfth Olympian, sometimes replaced by Dionysus in canonical lists.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 453-454; Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite 21-32 (the virginity-vow)
familyRoles: eldest daughter of Cronus and Rhea
sister of Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Hades, Demeter
one of the three virgin goddesses (with Athena and Artemis)
sometimes the twelfth Olympian (sometimes replaced by Dionysus)
birthTypes: child of Cronus and Rhea; swallowed and regurgitated
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony — swallowed by Cronus first (as eldest), regurgitated last when Zeus tricked him.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony

nodes.name: Thanatos
nodes.domain: death (specifically peaceful or natural death — contrast with Ker, violent death); twin of Hypnos (Sleep); son of Nyx
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 211-212, 758-766 (the dwellings of Sleep and Death); Homer, Iliad 14.231, 16.682 (Sleep carrying Sarpedon's body with Death); Apollodorus 1.9.15 (Sisyphus and Thanatos)
nodes.object: inverted torch (in late iconography); sword (in some depictions)
nodes.object_source: Late-classical and Hellenistic iconography
nodes.characterTrait: inescapable, dark, twin of Hypnos, occasionally outsmarted (Sisyphus bound him; Heracles wrestled him for Alcestis)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Apollodorus 1.9.15; Euripides, Alcestis (Heracles wrestles Thanatos)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Thanatos iconography — variable: sometimes winged youth with inverted torch (the late-classical 'sleep-of-death' figure); sometimes bearded and dark; on the Euphronios krater (c. 515 BCE) Hypnos and Thanatos carry Sarpedon's body
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Late-classical iconography; Euphronios krater
nodes.significantEvent: Twin of Hypnos (Sleep), son of Nyx (Night). Sisyphus bound him with chains so that no one could die until Ares freed him (Apollodorus 1.9.15). Heracles wrestled Thanatos to save Alcestis (Euripides, Alcestis). In the Iliad, with Hypnos he carried the body of Sarpedon from the battlefield to Lycia for burial.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 758-766; Apollodorus 1.9.15; Euripides, Alcestis; Homer, Iliad 16
familyRoles: sibling of Moirai, Keres, Nemesis, Eris, and many other dark-children of Night
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 211-225
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 211-225 — born parthenogenetically of Nyx along with his many dark-siblings.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 211-225

nodes.name: Chaos
nodes.domain: the primordial Yawning-Void from which everything else came; the first of all things; not 'disorder' in the modern sense but 'gap' or 'chasm' (χάος, root *ǵheh₂- 'to gape')
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 116-122 (the central source — 'in truth, first of all came Chaos to be, but next broad-bosomed Earth'); Aristophanes, Birds 693-702 (the comic-Orphic cosmogony); Plato, Timaeus; Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.5-7
nodes.characterTrait: primordial, void, gaping, undifferentiated, the pre-cosmic abyss
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hesiod, Theogony
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Not anthropomorphic in Hesiod; in late tradition sometimes personified
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Hesiod
nodes.significantEvent: Hesiod, Theogony 116-122: 'In truth, first of all came Chaos to be, but next broad-bosomed Earth (Gaia), the ever-secure foundation of all the immortals who hold the peaks of snowy Olympus, and misty Tartarus in a recess of the broad-pathed earth, and Eros, who is the most beautiful among the immortal gods.' From Chaos came Erebus and Nyx (Night).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 116-125
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 116
nodes.birthCircumstances: Uncreated; the first of all things in Hesiod's cosmogony.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 116

nodes.name: Ouranos
nodes.domain: the primordial sky, the starry heaven; first cosmic ruler before being castrated by Cronus; mate of Gaia and father (by her) of Titans, Cyclopes, Hekatonkheires
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 126-138, 154-210 (the central source); Apollodorus 1.1.1-4; Orphic theogony fragments; Plato, Timaeus and Cratylus
nodes.object_source: Standard cosmic-personification
nodes.characterTrait: primordial, son-imprisoning (kept the Cyclopes and Hekatonkheires within Gaia), castrated, blood-engendering (the Erinyes, Gigantes, and Meliai sprang from his spilt blood; Aphrodite from his severed genitals)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hesiod, Theogony 154-210
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Anthropomorphized as a great male figure who covers Gaia; the starry-sky mantle; in archaic and classical art rare; in Roman period sometimes shown as a star-cloak-bearing mature male
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Hesiod; later iconographic tradition
nodes.significantEvent: Hesiod, Theogony 126-138 — born from Gaia parthenogenetically as her equal, to cover her on every side; mated with her to produce the Titans (Oceanus, Coeus, Crius, Hyperion, Iapetus, Theia, Rhea, Themis, Mnemosyne, Phoebe, Tethys, Cronus), the three Cyclopes (Brontes, Steropes, Arges), the three Hekatonkheires (Cottus, Briareus, Gyges). Hated his offspring and imprisoned them in Gaia's womb-depths. Gaia, in pain, urged her children to revolt; only Cronus dared. Cronus castrated Ouranos with a sickle of adamant while Ouranos was mating with Gaia; cast the genitals into the sea (Aphrodite arose from the foam); the blood that fell on Gaia produced the Erinyes (Furies), the Giants, and the Meliai (ash-tree nymphs).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 126-210
familyRoles: father of the Titans, Cyclopes, Hekatonkheires; from his castration the Erinyes, Giants, and Aphrodite emerged
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 126-127
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 126-127 — Gaia produced him from herself, parthenogenetically.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 126-127
nodes.deathCircumstances: Castrated by his son Cronus with a sickle of adamant while mating with Gaia; cast off his cosmic-rule role.

nodes.name: Tartarus
nodes.domain: the deepest abyss of the cosmos, beneath Hades; the prison of the Titans after the Titanomachy; both a place and a primordial being
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 119, 718-735, 820-868 (the central source); Homer, Iliad 8.13-16 (Zeus's threat: 'as far below Hades as heaven is above earth'); Apollodorus 1.1.2
nodes.object: the great bronze-walled prison enclosing the defeated Titans
nodes.object_source: Hesiod, Theogony 726-733
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hesiod
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Both a primordial being and a place: 'as far below the earth as earth is below the heavens' (Hesiod, Theogony 720-721). Bronze-walled with bronze gates; surrounded by triple-darkness; where day and night meet but pass each other.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Hesiod, Theogony 720-735
nodes.significantEvent: One of the four primordial beings (with Chaos, Gaia, Eros). After the Titanomachy, Zeus imprisoned the defeated Titans in Tartarus. Mated with Gaia to produce the monstrous Typhon. The greatest punishments are inflicted in Tartarus — Tantalus, Sisyphus, Ixion, the Danaids, Tityus all suffer there.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 119, 820-868; Homer, Odyssey 11.576-600
birthTypes: uncreated; one of the first primordials
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 119
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 119 — emerged with Chaos, Gaia, and Eros as one of the first primordial beings.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 119

nodes.name: Erebus
nodes.domain: primordial darkness; the dark space between earth and Hades through which the dead pass; son of Chaos, mate of Nyx
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 123-125; Apollodorus 1.1.1; Cicero, De Natura Deorum 3.17
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hesiod, Theogony
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Not anthropomorphized in Hesiod; in late tradition sometimes personified as a dark-cloaked figure
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Hesiod; later tradition
nodes.significantEvent: Hesiod, Theogony 123-125: 'And from Chaos there came forth Erebus and dark Night; but from Night were Aether and Day born.' Mated with Nyx to produce Aether (the bright upper-sky) and Hemera (Day) — paradoxically, light emerges from primal darkness. In some traditions also father of Charon, Geras, Hypnos, Thanatos.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 123-125
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 123-124
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 123-124 — emerged from Chaos with Nyx.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 123-124

nodes.name: Pontus
nodes.domain: primordial sea; pre-Olympian sea-deity (predating Poseidon's Olympian sea-rule); son of Gaia parthenogenetically
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 131-132, 233-239; Apollodorus 1.1.4
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hesiod, Theogony
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Primordial sea-personification; rarely depicted
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Hesiod; later tradition
nodes.significantEvent: Hesiod, Theogony 131-132 — born parthenogenetically of Gaia. Mated with Gaia to produce Nereus (the Old Man of the Sea), Thaumas, Phorcys, Ceto, and Eurybia — the older generation of sea-deities, displaced by Poseidon's Olympian rule.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 131-132, 233-239
familyRoles: father (with Gaia) of Nereus, Thaumas, Phorcys, Ceto, Eurybia
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 131-132
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 131-132 — Gaia produced him from herself.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 131-132

nodes.name: Oceanus
nodes.domain: the world-encircling river (Ὠκεανός); the great freshwater stream surrounding the disk of the earth; eldest of the Titans; father of all rivers and Oceanids
nodes.domain_source: Homer, Iliad 14.201, 14.246 ('Oceanus, origin of the gods'); Hesiod, Theogony 133, 337-370 (the catalogue of his children); Pherecydes; Plato, Timaeus 40e
nodes.object: the river-stream itself encircling the earth-disk
nodes.object_source: Standard Greek cosmography
nodes.animals_source: Oceanus's emblematic animal: the snake-tailed depiction (river-god convention)
nodes.characterTrait: primordial, encircling, peaceful (refused to join the Titanomachy), prolific (3,000 sons + 3,000 daughters)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hesiod, Theogony 337-370
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Oceanus iconography — bearded mature god with bull-horns or crab-claws (river-god convention); snake-tail; sometimes depicted as a great encircling river-figure
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography (e.g., the Pergamon Altar friezes)
nodes.significantEvent: Eldest of the Titans, born of Ouranos and Gaia. Married his sister Tethys; together they produced 3,000 river-gods (the Potamoi) and 3,000 Oceanids (sea-nymphs). Did not join the Titanomachy; remained aloof; therefore was not imprisoned in Tartarus.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 337-370
familyRoles: father of all rivers and Oceanids
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 133
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 133 — eldest son of Ouranos and Gaia, born first of the Titans.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 133

nodes.name: Tethys
nodes.domain: Titaness of the sea (the freshwater-source aspect — mother of all freshwater rivers); sister-wife of Oceanus; mother of the Oceanids and Potamoi (river-gods)
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 136, 337-370, 362; Pherecydes (the Hera-fostered-by-Tethys tradition)
nodes.characterTrait: maternal (3,000 daughters and 3,000 sons), nurturing (raised Hera during the Titanomachy according to Iliad 14.201), aloof-from-Titanomachy
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hesiod; Homer, Iliad 14.201
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Tethys iconography — matronly Titaness with the conventional sea-attributes
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Titaness born of Ouranos and Gaia; sister-wife of Oceanus. Mother of 3,000 Oceanids and 3,000 Potamoi. Fostered Hera during the Titanomachy according to Iliad 14.201-204. Did not join the Titanomachy.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 337-370; Homer, Iliad 14.201-204
familyRoles: mother of all rivers and Oceanids
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 136
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 136 — daughter of Ouranos and Gaia.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 136

nodes.name: Amphitrite
nodes.domain: the sea (its surface); queen of the sea as Poseidon's wife; one of the fifty Nereids (daughters of Nereus)
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 243; Homer, Odyssey 3.91, 12.60; Apollodorus 1.4.6; Pausanias 1.17.3
nodes.object: trident (paired with Poseidon's); the chariot of hippocamps; the crab-claw crown in some depictions
nodes.object_source: Standard iconography
nodes.animals_source: Amphitrite's emblematic creatures: dolphin (who persuaded her to accept Poseidon's suit), hippocamps
nodes.characterTrait_source: Apollodorus 1.4.6 (Eratosthenes traces — the dolphin-suitor narrative)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Amphitrite iconography — Nereid-queen, often with crab-claw or shell crown; enthroned beside Poseidon; sometimes with dolphins or hippocamps
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Daughter of Nereus and Doris; one of the fifty Nereids. Poseidon sought her hand; she fled to Atlas. A dolphin (later placed in the heavens as Delphinus) located her and persuaded her to accept. Mother of Triton, Rhode, Benthesicyme, and others by Poseidon.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 243; Apollodorus 1.4.6
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 243
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 243 — daughter of Nereus and Doris.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 243

nodes.name: Triton
nodes.domain: merman messenger of the sea; son of Poseidon and Amphitrite; trumpets the sea-storm with his conch
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 930-933; Pausanias 9.20.4-21.6 (the Tritons-as-class tradition); Apollonius, Argonautica 4.1551-1622
nodes.object: great conch-trumpet (the κῆρυξ — the curving sea-shell horn used to whip up or calm the waves)
nodes.object_source: Hesiod; iconographic tradition
nodes.animals_source: Triton himself is half-fish (merman-form); his emblematic creature is the conch
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hesiod, Theogony 930-933
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Triton iconography — merman with bearded man-torso and fish-tail; sometimes two-tailed; blowing his great spiral conch-shell trumpet
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Son of Poseidon and Amphitrite; the herald of the sea. Aided the Argonauts when they were stranded in Lake Tritonis (Apollonius, Argonautica 4.1551-1622), guiding them back to the Mediterranean.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 930-933; Apollonius, Argonautica 4
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 930-933
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 930-933 — son of Poseidon and Amphitrite.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 930-933

nodes.name: Nereus
nodes.domain: Old Man of the Sea (γέρων ἁλίος); the pre-Olympian wise sea-god; shapeshifter; father of the fifty Nereids
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 233-239 (and 240-264, the Nereid catalogue); Homer, Iliad 18; Apollodorus 2.5.11 (Heracles wrestling Nereus for directions to the Hesperides)
nodes.animals_source: Nereus is conventionally fish-tailed
nodes.characterTrait: truth-telling (no falsehood in his mouth — Hesiod), shapeshifting (to evade questioners), wise, prophetic
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hesiod, Theogony 233-236
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Nereus iconography — bearded old man with fish-tail; sometimes shown shapeshifting (during Heracles's wrestling)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Eldest son of Pontus and Gaia; the pre-Olympian sea-god of truthful prophecy. Married Doris (an Oceanid); fathered the fifty Nereids (including Amphitrite, Thetis, Galatea, Psamathe). Heracles wrestled him in shapeshifting form for directions to the Hesperides (Apollodorus 2.5.11).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 233-264; Apollodorus 2.5.11
familyRoles: father of the fifty Nereids (including Amphitrite, Thetis, Galatea)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 233
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 233 — son of Pontus and Gaia.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 233

nodes.name: Eros
nodes.domain: love, desire; the Olympian Eros (son of Aphrodite) — distinct from the primordial Eros (Hesiod, Theogony 120)
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 120 (primordial), 201 (son of Aphrodite); Apollonius, Argonautica 3 (his arrows hit Medea); Apuleius, Metamorphoses 4-6 (Cupid and Psyche); the Anacreontea; the Hellenistic playful-child-Eros tradition
nodes.object: bow and arrows (golden for love, leaden for aversion); torch; sometimes wings
nodes.object_source: Standard Eros iconography
nodes.characterTrait: playful, mischievous, irresistible-arrow-archer, sometimes-blindfolded (in late tradition)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Apollonius; Anacreontea
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Eros iconography — varies wildly: archaic and classical depict him as youth (e.g., the Eros of Centocelle); the Hellenistic and Roman period collapses him into the chubby winged infant (the προtothype of the Roman Cupid and modern Cupid)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Two distinct figures collapsed under the same name: (1) the primordial Eros of Hesiod's Theogony 120, born from Chaos as one of the original cosmic principles; (2) the Olympian Eros, son of Aphrodite (in most traditions, by Ares), the arrow-shooter who makes gods and mortals fall in love. The Cupid-and-Psyche narrative (Apuleius, Met. 4-6) is the most extended Eros-narrative; in Apollonius's Argonautica 3, his arrows hit Medea making her fall for Jason.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 120, 201; Apollonius, Argonautica 3; Apuleius, Metamorphoses 4-6
familyRoles: (primordial) one of the first cosmic beings emerging from Chaos
(Olympian) son of Aphrodite, often by Ares
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 120, 201
nodes.birthCircumstances: Two birth-traditions: primordial (one of the first beings emerging from Chaos) and Olympian (son of Aphrodite, often by Ares).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 120, 201

nodes.name: Tyche
nodes.domain: fortune, luck, chance — both good and bad; the personification of how things 'fall out'; daughter of Oceanus (or other variant parentage)
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 360 (as Oceanid); Pindar, Olympian 12; Plutarch, On the Fortune of the Romans; the Hellenistic Tyche-cult (her popularity exploded after Alexander as people sought-pattern-in-chance); the famous Tyche of Antioch (Eutychides, c. 300 BCE)
nodes.object: cornucopia; rudder (governing the unstable course of fortune); ball (fortune's instability); wings (in some traditions)
nodes.object_source: Hellenistic Tyche-iconography
nodes.characterTrait_source: Plutarch; Hellenistic tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Tyche iconography — woman with cornucopia and rudder, sometimes wings; her city-Tyche depictions wear a mural crown (the city-walls atop her head); the Tyche of Antioch enthroned with the river-god Orontes at her feet
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Hellenistic iconography (especially the Tyche of Antioch by Eutychides)
nodes.significantEvent: Originally a minor figure (in Hesiod, just one of the 3,000 Oceanids), Tyche became enormously important in the Hellenistic period when sudden political upheavals made fortune-as-cosmic-force feel pressingly real. Every city had its own Tyche personified with a mural-crown. The Roman Fortuna inherits this tradition.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 360; Plutarch; Hellenistic tradition
familyRoles: daughter of Oceanus (Hesiod) or of Zeus (Pindar)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 360
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 360 — daughter of Oceanus and Tethys (one of the Oceanids).
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 360

nodes.name: Moirai
