nodes.domain: the three Fates — Clotho (the Spinner), Lachesis (the Allotter), Atropos (the Inflexible); deities of human destiny who spin, measure, and cut the thread of each life
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 217-222, 904-906; Homer, Iliad 20 and 24; Plato, Republic 10.617c-d (the famous Vision of Er); Apollodorus 1.3.1
nodes.object: thread, distaff, scroll/book, scissors or shears, scales
nodes.object_source: Standard iconography (Clotho with distaff, Lachesis with measuring-rod or scroll, Atropos with shears)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Homer (the gods cannot save their favorites past their fated death); Hesiod
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Moirai iconography — three women (variously aged in late tradition: maiden, mother, crone — though this triple-aged-goddess assimilation is largely modern); spinning, measuring, cutting
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: In Hesiod's two genealogies, the Moirai are either: (a) daughters of Nyx parthenogenetically (Theogony 217-222), in which case they sit alongside the dark powers (Death, Sleep, Discord); or (b) daughters of Zeus and Themis (Theogony 904-906), in which case they share their mother's righteous-divine-order function. Clotho spins the thread of each life; Lachesis measures it; Atropos cuts it. Even the gods cannot override them — in Iliad 16 Zeus considers saving Sarpedon but is told he cannot defy Moira.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 217-222, 904-906; Homer, Iliad 16.431-461
familyRoles: the three Fates: Clotho, Lachesis, Atropos
either daughters of Nyx (parthenogenetically) or of Zeus and Themis
birthTypes: two traditions: parthenogenetic from Nyx; or daughters of Zeus and Themis
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 217-222 and 904-906
nodes.birthCircumstances: Two traditions: Hesiod, Theogony 217-222 makes them parthenogenetic daughters of Nyx; Theogony 904-906 makes them daughters of Zeus and Themis.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 217-222, 904-906

nodes.name: Typhon
nodes.domain: monstrous storm-serpent; the last child of Gaia and Tartarus; the gravest threat ever faced by Zeus; father of many other monsters by Echidna
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 820-880 (the central source — the Typhonomachy); Homeric Hymn to Apollo 305-355; Apollodorus 1.6.3; Pindar, Pythian 1 and 8; Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound 351-372
nodes.object: his hundred serpent-heads, fire-belching mouths, the volcanoes (Etna especially, where he was imprisoned)
nodes.object_source: Hesiod, Theogony; Pindar, Pythian 1 (Etna)
nodes.animals_source: Typhon IS the cosmic-serpent monster — embodiment; specifically described as having a hundred serpent-heads and snake-coils for legs (in Hesiod)
nodes.characterTrait: monstrous, primordial-chaos-serpent, Zeus's-near-defeater, volcanic, fire-belching, hundred-headed
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hesiod, Theogony 820-880
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Hesiod, Theogony 820-835: hundred serpent-heads with black tongues, fire blazing from their eyes, voices of every kind (bulls, lions, dogs); snake-tails for legs; reaching up to the stars when he stood erect.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Hesiod, Theogony 820-835
nodes.significantEvent: Born of Gaia and Tartarus to oppose Zeus after the Titanomachy. In the cosmic battle (the Typhonomachy), nearly defeated Zeus — in one version, removed Zeus's sinews and hid them in a bear-skin, leaving him helpless until Hermes and Aigipan recovered them. Zeus eventually defeated him with thunderbolts and imprisoned him beneath Mount Etna, whose volcanic eruptions are his flaming breath. Father (by Echidna) of Cerberus, the Hydra, the Chimera, the Sphinx, the Nemean lion, and other monsters.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 820-880; Apollodorus 1.6.3; Pindar, Pythian 1
familyRoles: father (with Echidna) of Cerberus, Hydra, Chimera, Sphinx, Nemean lion
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 820-823
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 820-823 — Gaia bore Typhon to Tartarus to oppose Zeus after the Titanomachy.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 820-823
deathTypes: defeated by Zeus; imprisoned beneath Mount Etna
nodes.deathCircumstances: Defeated by Zeus with thunderbolts and imprisoned beneath Mount Etna, where his fiery breath fuels the eruptions.

nodes.name: Echidna
nodes.domain: monster-mother (the 'mother of all monsters'); half-woman, half-snake; mate of Typhon; bore most of the famous Greek monsters
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 295-336 (the central source — Echidna's appearance and her catalogue of children); Apollodorus 2.1.2; Hyginus, Fabulae 151
nodes.animals_source: Echidna IS the half-woman half-snake monster — embodiment
nodes.characterTrait_source: Hesiod, Theogony 295-305
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Hesiod, Theogony 295-305: half-nymph (a fair-cheeked woman from the waist up), half-serpent (huge, terrible, dappled, eating raw flesh in the depths of holy earth); dwells in a cave in the land of the Arimoi.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Hesiod, Theogony 295-305
nodes.significantEvent: Daughter of Phorcys and Ceto (or in alternative tradition Tartarus and Gaia). Mother (with Typhon) of: Orthus (Geryon's two-headed dog), Cerberus (three-headed dog of Hades), the Lernaean Hydra, the Chimera, the Sphinx, the Nemean lion, the Caucasian eagle (that ate Prometheus's liver), Ladon (Hesperides' serpent). Through her offspring she is the source of nearly every famous Greek monster.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Hesiod, Theogony 306-336
familyRoles: daughter of Phorcys and Ceto (Hesiod) or Tartarus and Gaia (alternative)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 295
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 295 — daughter of Phorcys and Ceto.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 295
nodes.deathCircumstances: Immortal in Hesiod; in Apollodorus 2.1.2, killed by Argus Panoptes (the hundred-eyed) while she slept.

nodes.name: Hydra
nodes.domain: the Lernaean Hydra — many-headed water-serpent of the swamp of Lerna; slain by Heracles as his second labor; head-regenerating
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 313-318; Apollodorus 2.5.2 (the central source for the labor); Diodorus Siculus 4.11.5-6; Hyginus, Fabulae 30
nodes.object: the swamp of Lerna; her own multiple heads; her venom
nodes.object_source: Apollodorus 2.5.2
nodes.animals_source: Hydra IS the water-serpent — embodiment
nodes.characterTrait: head-regenerating (cut one head, two grow back), venomous, swamp-dwelling, immortal-head-bearing
nodes.characterTrait_source: Apollodorus 2.5.2
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Water-serpent with multiple heads (variously 7, 9, or many — Hesiod doesn't specify); one head immortal; venomous breath; dwells in the swamp of Lerna in the Argolid.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Apollodorus 2.5.2
nodes.significantEvent: Daughter of Typhon and Echidna; raised by Hera specifically to be Heracles's challenge. Heracles's second labor: he attacked her in the swamp of Lerna, but each head he cut off grew back as two; his nephew Iolaus cauterized the necks with fire as Heracles severed each head, preventing regeneration; the one immortal head he buried under a great rock. Used the Hydra's venomous blood to poison his arrows — these eventually caused his own death (via the Nessus-shirt).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Apollodorus 2.5.2; Hesiod, Theogony 313-318
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 313-315
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 313-315 — daughter of Typhon and Echidna.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 313-315
deathTypes: slain by Heracles and Iolaus (heads severed and cauterized)
nodes.deathCircumstances: Slain by Heracles (with Iolaus's help) in his Second Labor.

nodes.name: Cerberus
nodes.domain: the three-headed dog of Hades; guards the gates of the underworld so that the dead cannot leave and the living cannot enter without divine permission
nodes.domain_source: Hesiod, Theogony 311-312, 769-774; Homer, Iliad 8.366-369 (the labor-of-Cerberus reference); Apollodorus 2.5.12 (Heracles's labor); Virgil, Aeneid 6.417-425; Plato, Republic 588c
nodes.object: his three heads; the chain by which Heracles led him out of Hades
nodes.object_source: Apollodorus 2.5.12
nodes.animals_source: Cerberus IS the underworld-dog — embodiment
nodes.characterTrait_source: Apollodorus 2.5.12; Virgil, Aeneid 6
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Hesiod, Theogony 311-312: fifty-headed in Hesiod (a maximalist version); standard tradition three-headed; with a mane of snakes and a serpent's tail; bronze-voiced.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Hesiod, Theogony 311-312; Apollodorus 2.5.12 (the canonical three-headed form)
nodes.significantEvent: Born of Typhon and Echidna. Guards the gates of Hades. Heracles's twelfth and final labor was to capture Cerberus and bring him to Eurystheus alive; Heracles wrestled him into submission and brought him to the surface, then returned him. Orpheus enchanted him with the lyre to enter for Eurydice; Psyche fed him honey-cakes (Apuleius); the Sibyl threw him drugged cakes for Aeneas to pass (Virgil).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Apollodorus 2.5.12; Virgil, Aeneid 6; Apuleius, Metamorphoses 6
familyRoles: sibling of Hydra, Chimera, Orthus, Nemean lion
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 311
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 311 — son of Typhon and Echidna.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 311
nodes.deathCircumstances: Immortal; not killed by Heracles, only borrowed and returned.

nodes.name: Chimera
nodes.domain: fire-breathing composite monster: lion-fore, goat-middle, serpent-tail; slain by Bellerophon riding Pegasus
nodes.domain_source: Homer, Iliad 6.179-183 (the central archaic source); Hesiod, Theogony 319-325; Apollodorus 2.3.1; Pindar, Olympian 13.84-92
nodes.object_source: Homer, Iliad 6.182
nodes.animals_source: Chimera IS the composite monster — embodiment
nodes.characterTrait_source: Homer; Hesiod; Apollodorus
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Hesiod, Theogony 319-324: three heads — a lion in front, a fire-breathing she-goat in the middle (from her back), a serpent for tail; Homer, Iliad 6.181: 'lion in front, snake behind, goat in the middle, breathing dreadful fire'
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Homer, Iliad 6.181; Hesiod, Theogony 319-324
nodes.significantEvent: Daughter of Typhon and Echidna; raised by Amisodarus in Lycia (or born there). Ravaged Lycia. Bellerophon, riding Pegasus, killed her by attaching lead to the tip of his spear which the Chimera's fire-breath melted, suffocating her with molten lead (one variant; in others, he simply impaled her from above).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Homer, Iliad 6.179-183; Apollodorus 2.3.1
familyRoles: sibling of Hydra, Cerberus, Orthus, Nemean lion
nodes.birthTypes_source: Hesiod, Theogony 319
nodes.birthCircumstances: Hesiod, Theogony 319 — daughter of Typhon and Echidna.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Hesiod, Theogony 319
nodes.deathCircumstances: Slain by Bellerophon (mounted on Pegasus) over Lycia.

nodes.name: Minotaur
nodes.domain: the Minotaur of Crete — half-bull, half-man, monstrous offspring of Queen Pasiphae and the Cretan bull; confined in the Labyrinth built by Daedalus; slain by Theseus
nodes.domain_source: Apollodorus 3.1.4 and 3.15.8 (the central source); Plutarch, Theseus 15-19; Diodorus Siculus 4.61; Catullus 64 (Ariadne's lament)
nodes.object: the Labyrinth (built by Daedalus to confine him); his bull-horns
nodes.object_source: Apollodorus 3.1.4
nodes.animals_source: Minotaur IS the bull-headed man — embodiment
nodes.characterTrait: bull-headed, man-bodied, devouring (the Athenian youth-tribute), confined-in-Labyrinth, defeated-by-thread
nodes.characterTrait_source: Apollodorus; Plutarch
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Half-bull, half-man — usually a man's body with a bull's head; lived in the Labyrinth; named Asterion or Asterius in some traditions.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Queen Pasiphae of Crete was made to lust after the magnificent bull (which Poseidon had sent for Minos to sacrifice but which Minos had instead kept); Daedalus built her a wooden cow inside which she copulated with the bull, conceiving the Minotaur. Minos imprisoned the Minotaur in the Labyrinth; Athens was required to send seven youths and seven maidens every nine years (in some versions every year) as tribute to feed him. Theseus volunteered; with the help of Ariadne's thread he traversed the Labyrinth, killed the Minotaur, and escaped.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Apollodorus 3.1.4, 3.15.8; Plutarch, Theseus 15-19
familyRoles: son of Pasiphae (queen of Crete) and the Cretan Bull
nodes.birthTypes_source: Apollodorus 3.1.4
nodes.birthCircumstances: Conceived by Queen Pasiphae copulating with the Cretan bull inside a wooden cow constructed by Daedalus.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Apollodorus 3.1.4
deathTypes: slain by Theseus in the Labyrinth
nodes.deathCircumstances: Slain by Theseus in the Labyrinth; Theseus escaped by following Ariadne's thread.

nodes.name: Jupiter
nodes.domain: supreme god of the Roman state; sky, thunder, the oaths of state; chief of the Capitoline Triad; 'Iuppiter Optimus Maximus' (the great-and-best Jupiter, the central state-cult title); descendant of PIE *Dyḗws ph₂tḗr
nodes.domain_source: Virgil, Aeneid (especially Book 1's prophecy); Ovid, Metamorphoses and Fasti; Livy 1.10-12 (the Capitoline foundation); the Capitoline temple inscriptions; the Salian hymns; Macrobius, Saturnalia
nodes.object: thunderbolt (fulmen); eagle (his sacred bird and messenger); sceptre; the spolia opima (great spoils dedicated by victorious generals — only three were ever offered, the last by M. Claudius Marcellus in 222 BCE)
nodes.object_source: Standard Jupiter iconography; Livy 1.10
nodes.animals_source: Jupiter's sacred animals: eagle (his messenger, in Roman augury the eagle's flight is his sign); ox (the central state-sacrifice, the bos eximius); the bull (the form of his abduction of Europa, inherited from Zeus)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Virgil; Ovid; Roman state cult
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Standard Jupiter iconography — mature bearded enthroned king with thunderbolt and sceptre; the great chryselephantine statue in the Capitoline Temple (modeled on Pheidias's Zeus at Olympia)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Identified with Greek Zeus (the interpretatio Romana). Chief of the Capitoline Triad (Jupiter-Juno-Minerva), housed in the great Temple on the Capitoline Hill dedicated in 509 BCE under the last Tarquin / first year of the Republic. The dies Iovis (Thursday) is his day. As Iuppiter Feretrius received the spolia opima. As Iuppiter Stator stayed Roman flight at the Battle of the Sabines. As Iuppiter Capitolinus the supreme state-god whose temple's burning was treated as cosmic-emergency (the burnings of 83 BCE under Sulla, 69 CE in the year of four emperors, and 80 CE under Titus).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Livy 1.10-12; Virgil, Aeneid 1.254-296; Tacitus, Histories 3 (the 69 CE burning)
familyRoles: father of Mars, Vulcan, Mercury, Minerva, Apollo, Diana, Bacchus, Hercules, Castor, Pollux, and many more (importing the Zeus-genealogy)
birthTypes: child of Saturn and Ops; swallowed and regurgitated (importing the Hesiodic narrative)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Roman interpretation of Hesiodic tradition
nodes.birthCircumstances: Importing the Greek narrative: hidden on Crete (or sometimes on Mount Ida in Phrygia in Roman variants) by Ops against Saturn who swallowed his other children.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Ovid, Fasti 4.197-214 (importing Hesiodic narrative)

nodes.name: Mars
nodes.domain: war (especially in its just-aggressive aspect, contrast Bellona's wild battle-frenzy); agriculture (his pre-Greek Italic origin); father of Romulus and Remus; second-rank god of the state after Jupiter
nodes.domain_source: Ovid, Fasti 3 (the central source for the March festivals); Livy 1.4 (Romulus and Remus); Virgil, Aeneid; Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.12; the Salian hymns (the carmen Saliare, archaic Latin); the Suovetaurilia ritual (Cato, De Agri Cultura 141)
nodes.object: spear (the hasta Martis, kept in the regia and shaken when war was declared); shield (the ancile, fallen from heaven, with 11 copies made to disguise it); the wolf, the woodpecker (picus Martius), the bull
nodes.object_source: Ovid; Livy 1.20 (the ancilia); Roman state cult
nodes.animals_source: Mars's sacred animals: wolf (who suckled Romulus and Remus); woodpecker (picus Martius — who fed them); bull (sacrificial); the Suovetaurilia combination (pig-sheep-bull)
nodes.characterTrait: warlike, agricultural-protector (in Italic origin), father-of-Romans, sometimes-adulterous (with Venus per Greek tradition)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Ovid; Livy
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Standard Mars iconography — armored mature warrior; helmet with crest; spear and shield; sometimes nude (the Mars Borghese type); the Mars Ultor (Avenger) cult-statue established by Augustus in his Forum
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Originally an indigenous Italic agricultural/boundary deity (the lustration of the fields with the Suovetaurilia is in his honor — Cato Agr. 141); identified with Greek Ares in the late-Republican literary tradition but always maintained higher dignity than Greek Ares ever had. Father of Romulus and Remus by the Vestal Rhea Silvia (Livy 1.4). Patron of the Roman state (the Campus Martius, his sacred field). March (Martius) is his month. The Mars Ultor cult was central to Augustan religious reform.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Livy 1.4; Ovid, Fasti 3; Roman state cult
familyRoles: son of Juno (parthenogenetically in some Roman traditions, e.g. Ovid Fasti 5.229-258 — Juno conceives him touching a flower without Jupiter)
father of Romulus and Remus by Rhea Silvia
birthTypes: son of Juno (sometimes parthenogenetically); identified with Ares (son of Zeus and Hera)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Ovid, Fasti 5.229-258 (parthenogenetic Juno); standard Greek interpretatio
nodes.birthCircumstances: Ovid Fasti 5.229-258: Juno, in jealousy at Jupiter's having birthed Minerva from his head, was given a magical flower by Flora that made her conceive Mars without male intervention. (This is uniquely Roman — the standard Greek interpretatio makes him son of Zeus and Hera.)
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Ovid, Fasti 5.229-258

nodes.name: Mercury
nodes.domain: commerce, trade, messengers, travel, eloquence, thieves; psychopomp; identified with Hermes; god of merchants (his name from merx, merchandise)
nodes.domain_source: Ovid, Fasti 5.663-692 (the central Roman Mercury narrative); Livy 2.21 (the founding of his temple in 495 BCE); Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.19; Tacitus, Germania 9 (Mercury as supreme German god in interpretatio Romana)
nodes.object: caduceus (winged staff with serpents); winged petasos and sandals; purse (his commercial-deity aspect); rooster (his sacred bird)
nodes.object_source: Standard Mercury iconography
nodes.animals_source: Mercury's sacred animals: rooster (his herald-bird); tortoise (the lyre-shell origin); ram
nodes.characterTrait_source: Ovid; Tacitus; Roman cult tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Standard Mercury iconography — youthful athletic male with winged sandals, winged petasos, and caduceus (all inherited from Hermes); often carrying a purse signifying commerce
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Identified with Greek Hermes. His Roman cult was founded relatively late (495 BCE on the Circus Maximus side of the Aventine) and emphasized his commercial-patron aspect (his temple was the headquarters of the guild of merchants, mercatores). The Mercuralia festival on May 15. Tacitus, Germania 9 records that the Germans worshipped 'Mercury' (presumably Wotan/Odin) above all others — an interpretatio Romana that has been crucial to Germanic religious history.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Livy 2.21; Tacitus, Germania 9; Macrobius
birthTypes: identified with Hermes (son of Zeus and Maia)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Standard interpretatio

nodes.name: Vulcan
nodes.domain: fire (especially destructive volcanic fire), forge, metalworking; identified with Hephaestus; god of the Comitium and the original Roman state-fire
nodes.domain_source: Ovid, Fasti 6.628-636 (Vulcanalia); Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.12.18; Livy 1.20 (the early establishment of Volcanal); Vitruvius 1.7 (the Volcanal placement)
nodes.object: hammer; tongs; anvil; the forge under Mount Etna or beneath the Forum
nodes.object_source: Standard Vulcan iconography
nodes.animals_source: Vulcan's sacred animals: red calf or boar (his sacrificial animals at the Vulcanalia of Aug 23 — burned alive in propitiation against the harvest-fire-danger)
nodes.characterTrait: lame, smith-skilled, destructive-fire-personifying, indigenous-Italic (Volcanus is an old Italic name)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Macrobius; Roman cult tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Standard Vulcan iconography — bearded lame smith identical to Hephaestus; wearing pilos-cap; bearing hammer and tongs
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Originally an indigenous Italic fire-deity especially associated with destructive volcanic fire and the harvest-time fire-danger; identified with Greek Hephaestus. The Volcanal (his oldest sanctuary, in the Roman Forum near the Comitium) was probably 7th century BCE or earlier. The Vulcanalia (August 23) propitiated him against summer-fire-danger by burning live fish or small animals (substitutes for the human harvest). After the Great Fire of Rome in 64 CE, Nero added a major shrine to Vulcan.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Macrobius; Tacitus, Annales 15.43; Roman cult tradition
familyRoles: son of Jupiter and Juno (or of Juno alone parthenogenetically, importing the Greek narrative)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Standard interpretatio

nodes.name: Neptune
nodes.domain: the sea, water, horses, earthquakes; identified with Poseidon; originally an Italic freshwater-and-spring deity before the Greek identification
nodes.domain_source: Ovid, Fasti and Metamorphoses; Virgil, Aeneid; Servius on Virgil; the Neptunalia festival (July 23); Livy 5.13
nodes.object_source: Standard Neptune iconography (all inherited from Poseidon)
nodes.animals_source: Neptune's sacred animals: horse (he was originally an equestrian deity in Italic religion before the Poseidon-identification)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Servius; Roman cult tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Standard Neptune iconography — mature bearded king with trident; identical to Poseidon visually
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Originally an indigenous Italic freshwater deity (the Neptunalia took place in midsummer to propitiate against drought, suggesting freshwater origin); also early associated with horses (Neptunus Equestris). Identified with Greek Poseidon by the late Republic. Built temples include the one in the Campus Martius (modern Pantheon area). Under Agrippa heavily promoted as a Augustan-Republican-victory deity (after the naval victories of Mylae and Actium).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Servius; Roman cult tradition
familyRoles: brother of Jupiter, Pluto, Juno, Ceres, Vesta
birthTypes: identified with Poseidon (child of Saturn and Ops)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Standard interpretatio

nodes.name: Pluto
nodes.domain: the underworld; lord of the dead; identified with Hades (specifically the Plouton aspect — lord of mineral wealth beneath the earth)
nodes.domain_source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 5; Virgil, Aeneid 6 (the underworld katabasis); Statius, Thebaid 8; Claudian, De Raptu Proserpinae
nodes.object: bident (his two-pronged spear, distinguishing him from Neptune's trident); helmet of invisibility (from Greek tradition); key (in late iconography); cornucopia (his Plouton-as-wealth aspect)
nodes.object_source: Standard iconography
nodes.animals_source: Pluto's sacred animals: Cerberus; the black ram
nodes.characterTrait_source: Standard tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Standard iconography — mature bearded king resembling Jupiter, darker, enthroned with Proserpina; the Pluto-aspect emphasizes his mineral-wealth function (compared with the more austere Greek Hades)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Identified with Greek Hades; the Roman tradition emphasized the Plouton-as-wealth aspect (cf. Cicero, De Natura Deorum 2.66: 'whose name in Greek is Plouton, signifying wealth, because everything comes back to him in the end'). The Roman Pluto absorbed indigenous Italic elements as Dis Pater (the chthonic-wealth Father Dis, attested in Plautus and Cicero).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Cicero, De Natura Deorum 2.66; Virgil, Aeneid 6; Roman cult tradition
familyRoles: syncretized with Dis Pater (the Italic underworld-wealth deity)
brother of Jupiter, Neptune, Juno, Ceres, Vesta
nodes.birthTypes_source: Standard interpretatio

nodes.name: Saturn
nodes.domain: agriculture, time (in late tradition via etymological association with Greek Kronos-Chronos), sowing; ruler of the Golden Age; the central god of the December Saturnalia festival
nodes.domain_source: Ovid, Fasti 1.193-254 and Metamorphoses 1.89-112 (Golden Age); Macrobius, Saturnalia (the entire literary work named after his festival); Virgil, Aeneid 8.319-327; Cicero, De Natura Deorum 2.64
nodes.object: sickle or pruning-hook (falx — his agricultural implement; Roman tradition emphasized his agricultural role over Greek-Cronus's castration-instrument); cornucopia
nodes.object_source: Standard Saturn iconography; Macrobius
nodes.characterTrait_source: Virgil, Aeneid 8.319-327; Macrobius
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Standard Saturn iconography — mature bearded elder with sickle; veiled in some traditions (Saturn was depicted in his temple veiled — the velatio Saturni)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Identified with Greek Cronus, but Roman tradition emphasizes his role as ruler of the Italic Golden Age — fled to Latium after being deposed from Olympus, ruled Latium during the aurea aetas when humans lived without labor or war (Virgil, Aen. 8.319-327). The December 17-23 Saturnalia was Rome's most beloved festival — masters served slaves, gambling was permitted, gifts exchanged, a Saturnalicius princeps elected to preside over revelries. His temple was the central state-treasury (the aerarium Saturni).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Virgil, Aeneid 8.319-327; Macrobius; Roman state cult
familyRoles: father of Jupiter, Juno, Neptune, Pluto, Ceres, Vesta
Italic ruler of Latium during the Golden Age (uniquely Roman tradition)
birthTypes: identified with Cronus (son of Caelus/Ouranos and Tellus/Gaia)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Standard interpretatio
nodes.deathCircumstances: Roman tradition: not slain, but fled to Latium after the Titanomachy; ruled the Italic Golden Age

nodes.name: Bacchus
nodes.domain: wine, ecstatic religion, the Bacchic mysteries; identified with Dionysus and Liber; banned by the Senate in 186 BCE (Senatusconsultum de Bacchanalibus) before being re-incorporated under Augustus
nodes.domain_source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3-4 (Pentheus, Bacchus-pirate, Bacchus-Ariadne); Livy 39.8-19 (the central source — the suppression of 186 BCE); the Senatusconsultum de Bacchanalibus inscription (CIL I² 581, Tiriolo, 186 BCE); the Villa of the Mysteries fresco-cycle (Pompeii, 1st c. BCE)
nodes.object: thyrsus; wine-cup (kantharos); ivy and grape-vine wreath; the panther-pelt (nebris)
nodes.object_source: Standard iconography (inherited from Dionysus)
nodes.animals_source: Bacchus's sacred animals: bull; goat; leopard/panther (chariot); snake
nodes.characterTrait: ecstatic, wine-bringing, dual-natured, savage-and-civilized, mystery-initiating, dangerous-to-the-state (per Livy 39)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Livy 39; Ovid; Villa of the Mysteries
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Bacchus iconography — variable: youthful effeminate (late-classical Greek-derived) or mature-bearded (earlier); ivy-crowned; carrying thyrsus; sometimes riding panther
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Identified with Greek Dionysus and the older Italic Liber (the patrician Bacchus and the plebeian Liber sometimes distinguished). The Bacchanalia (the mystery-cult festivals) became sufficiently widespread by the early 2nd c. BCE that the Senate in 186 BCE suppressed them with the Senatusconsultum de Bacchanalibus — a famous early-Republican religious-police action documented in Livy 39.8-19. The cult was later re-incorporated under Augustus and especially Antony (who personally identified with Bacchus). The Villa of the Mysteries at Pompeii preserves the most famous fresco-cycle of the mysteries.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Livy 39.8-19; the Senatusconsultum inscription; Villa of the Mysteries
nodes.birthTypes_source: Standard interpretatio

nodes.name: Liber
nodes.domain: wine, vines, fertility (especially male fertility); the plebeian counterpart of patrician Bacchus; one of the Aventine Triad (Ceres-Liber-Libera); his festival the Liberalia (March 17)
nodes.domain_source: Ovid, Fasti 3.713-790 (Liberalia); Cicero, De Natura Deorum 2.62; Augustine, De Civitate Dei 7.21 (preserving Varro)
nodes.object: wine-cup; phallus (especially central to Liberalia processions, per Augustine quoting Varro)
nodes.object_source: Ovid; Augustine quoting Varro
nodes.animals_source: Liber's sacred animals: goat
nodes.characterTrait_source: Roman cult tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Liber iconography — usually identified visually with Bacchus by the late Republic
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Indigenous Italic fertility deity, partly identified with Bacchus. Forms one of the Aventine Triad (Ceres-Liber-Libera) — the plebeian counterpart to the patrician Capitoline Triad. The Liberalia (March 17) marked the day Roman youths assumed the toga virilis (adult-toga). The phallic processions at the Liberalia (described by Augustine, Civ. Dei 7.21, quoting Varro) were prominent.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Ovid, Fasti 3.713-790; Augustine, Civ. Dei 7.21
familyRoles: one of the Aventine Triad with Ceres and Libera
nodes.birthTypes_source: Roman cult tradition

nodes.name: Quirinus
nodes.domain: indigenous Sabine deity of war; identified with the deified Romulus; one of the Archaic Triad with Jupiter and Mars
nodes.domain_source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 14.805-851 (Romulus deification as Quirinus); Livy 1.16 (Romulus's apotheosis at the Caprae Palus); Plutarch, Romulus 27-29; Servius on Aeneid 1.292
nodes.object_source: Standard iconography
nodes.characterTrait: Sabine-origin, warrior, deified-Romulus, civic-rather-than-aggressive (his war-aspect was 'in peace' compared with Mars's 'in war')
nodes.characterTrait_source: Servius; Roman cult tradition
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Quirinus iconography — bearded warrior with spear; sometimes identified iconographically with Romulus
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Originally a Sabine war-deity worshipped on the Quirinal Hill (named for him) — predating the Roman-Sabine union. By Republic times identified with the deified Romulus (Romulus's apotheosis: Livy 1.16 describes Romulus disappearing in a sudden storm at the Caprae Palus and then appearing to Julius Proculus declaring he was now the god Quirinus). One of the Archaic Triad (Jupiter-Mars-Quirinus), the older state-cult before the Capitoline Triad (Jupiter-Juno-Minerva) replaced it.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Livy 1.16; Plutarch, Romulus 27-29; Ovid, Met. 14
birthTypes: indigenous Sabine origin; later identified with Romulus
nodes.birthTypes_source: Roman cult tradition; Livy 1.16

nodes.name: Sol
nodes.domain: the sun; identified with Helios; reintroduced as Sol Invictus by Aurelian in 274 CE as a state-cult; partly displaced by Sol's solar-monotheistic late-Empire role
nodes.domain_source: Tacitus, Annales 15.74; Vitruvius 1.7.1; CIL VI (the Sol Invictus inscriptions); Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.17-23 (the great solar-theological compendium); the Codex-Calendar of 354
nodes.object: chariot of four horses (quadriga); the solar disk; the radiate crown (the corona radiata, especially on imperial coinage)
nodes.object_source: Standard iconography
nodes.animals_source: Sol's sacred animals: the four chariot-horses
nodes.characterTrait: radiant, daily-transiting, supreme (in the Sol Invictus tradition), unconquered
nodes.characterTrait_source: Sol Invictus cult tradition; Macrobius
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Sol iconography — youthful male with radiate-crown (the corona radiata, prominently on imperial coinage from Caracalla through Constantine); driving the four-horse chariot
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Imperial coinage; Sol Invictus statuary
nodes.significantEvent: An old Roman solar-cult of indigenous origin (Sol Indiges, perhaps Sabine), but rose to massive prominence in the late Empire when Aurelian re-established the cult as Sol Invictus ('Unconquered Sun') in 274 CE following his Eastern campaign — bringing in elements of Syrian Elagabal-worship and Mithraic solar-theology. Constantine's December 25 'Day of Sol' was the same date later assigned to Christmas (the Sol Invictus-to-Christ-Sol transition). Macrobius (early 5th c.) presents the Saturnalia as essentially a treatise on solar-theology, with all gods identified as aspects of Sol.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Tacitus; Macrobius; Sol Invictus cult inscriptions; Codex-Calendar of 354
nodes.birthTypes_source: Standard interpretatio

nodes.name: Faunus
nodes.domain: wild-places, forests, herds; rustic god of the agricultural population; identified later with Greek Pan; central to the Lupercalia
nodes.domain_source: Ovid, Fasti 2.267-452 (Lupercalia); Livy 1.5; Horace, Carmina 3.18; Servius on Virgil, Aeneid 7.81; the Lupercal cave (the Romulus-Remus suckling site, sacred to Faunus)
nodes.object: shepherd's crook; the Lupercal cave; the wool-strips (februa) used in the Lupercalia
nodes.object_source: Roman cult tradition
nodes.animals_source: Faunus's sacred animals: goat (sacrificed at the Lupercalia, the goat-skin februa used to strike women for fertility)
nodes.characterTrait: rustic, wild, prophetic (the oracle of Faunus at Albunea), woodland-dwelling
nodes.characterTrait_source: Virgil, Aen. 7.81-101 (the oracle of Faunus consulted by Latinus); Horace
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Faunus iconography — bearded male, sometimes with horns or goat-legs (in the later Pan-identification); rustic dress; carrying shepherd's crook
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography (variable due to Pan-syncretism)
nodes.significantEvent: Indigenous Italic god of wild-places and herding; later identified with Greek Pan. Central to the Lupercalia (Feb 15) — the great winter-purification festival in which the Luperci (priests) ran around the Palatine boundary nearly-naked, striking women with wool-strips (februa) to ensure fertility (this gave February its name and is the origin of the Feast of St. Valentine which superseded it in the 5th c. CE). Faunus's oracle at Albunea consulted by Latinus in Aeneid 7.81-101.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Ovid, Fasti 2.267-452; Virgil, Aen. 7.81-101; Plutarch, Romulus 21
familyRoles: sometimes called son of Picus (the woodpecker-deity)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Roman cult tradition

nodes.name: Silvanus
nodes.domain: forests, fields, woodland boundaries; rural protective deity; never officially in the state-cult but extremely popular in epigraphic record
nodes.domain_source: Cato, De Agri Cultura 83; Virgil, Aeneid 8.597-602; Ovid, Metamorphoses 14.638; massive epigraphic attestation (CIL volumes — Silvanus has hundreds of dedicatory inscriptions, mostly modest)
nodes.object: pruning-hook; pine-branch wreath; sometimes the silvula (small branch)
nodes.object_source: Standard iconography
nodes.animals_source: Silvanus's sacred animals: dog (his common companion in dedicatory reliefs)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Cato; Virgil; epigraphic record
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Silvanus iconography — bearded mature male in rustic dress; pruning-hook and pine-branch; sometimes accompanied by a dog; modest depictions on small votive reliefs
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography (small-relief tradition)
nodes.significantEvent: Indigenous Italic god of forests and woodland-boundaries. Never officially included in the Roman state-cult but exceptionally popular in the epigraphic record — there are more Silvanus inscriptions than for many state gods, mostly modest dedications from soldiers, freedmen, and rural workers. Cato Agr. 83 prescribes an agricultural ritual to Silvanus. Often invoked together with Mars Silvanus (the boundary-Mars).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Cato; epigraphic record (CIL)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Roman cult tradition

nodes.name: Vertumnus
nodes.domain: seasonal changes, harvest, garden-fruit-ripening; metamorphosis; Etruscan god (Voltumna) imported to Rome; husband of Pomona
nodes.domain_source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 14.622-771 (the central Vertumnus-Pomona narrative); Propertius 4.2 (the Vertumnus elegy with archaeological detail); Varro, De Lingua Latina 5.46
nodes.object: pruning-knife; cornucopia of fruit (especially apples and pears); his shape-changing forms
nodes.object_source: Ovid; Propertius
nodes.characterTrait_source: Ovid; Propertius
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Vertumnus iconography — typically a mature gardener; able to take any human form (Ovid Met. 14 narrates his many disguises courting Pomona); the famous statue of Vertumnus stood on the Vicus Tuscus
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Originally the Etruscan god Voltumna (head of the Etruscan League's cult at Volsinii); imported to Rome after Volsinii's destruction in 264 BCE. His statue stood at the Vicus Tuscus (the Etruscan Quarter). Ovid Met. 14.622-771 narrates his courtship of Pomona — he disguised himself as a series of figures (reaper, plowman, fisherman, soldier, old woman) before revealing his true form and winning her. Propertius 4.2 is a long elegy in his voice.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Ovid, Met. 14.622-771; Propertius 4.2; Varro
nodes.birthTypes_source: Varro; Roman cult tradition

nodes.name: Cupid
nodes.domain: love, desire; identified with Greek Eros; son of Venus; the central male figure of Apuleius's Cupid and Psyche; in late-classical and Roman iconography increasingly the chubby winged infant
nodes.domain_source: Ovid, Metamorphoses (passim); Apuleius, Metamorphoses 4-6 (Cupid and Psyche — the central Latin Eros narrative); Virgil, Aeneid 1.657-722 (Cupid in disguise as Ascanius)
nodes.object: bow and golden arrows (love) or leaden arrows (aversion); torch; quiver; sometimes wings
nodes.object_source: Standard iconography
nodes.characterTrait_source: Apuleius; Ovid
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Cupid iconography — increasingly in Roman period the chubby winged child (putto-prototype); the Apuleian Cupid-and-Psyche tradition retains him as a beautiful youth on Olympus
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Identified with Greek Eros; son of Venus and (in most accounts) Mars. The Cupid-and-Psyche narrative in Apuleius's Metamorphoses 4-6 is the central Latin narrative — Psyche the mortal princess's love affair with Cupid, her trials (sorted-grains, golden-fleece-gathering, water-from-Styx, jar-from-Proserpina), and final immortalization. Virgil Aen. 1.657-722: Venus sends Cupid disguised as Ascanius to make Dido fall in love with Aeneas.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Apuleius, Metamorphoses 4-6; Virgil, Aeneid 1; Ovid
nodes.birthTypes_source: Standard interpretatio

nodes.name: Hercules
nodes.domain: great hero of strength; identified with Greek Heracles; the cult of Hercules Invictus at the Ara Maxima Herculis Invicti in the Forum Boarium (Rome's oldest cult of a deified hero)
nodes.domain_source: Virgil, Aeneid 8.184-279 (Hercules and Cacus — the Aventine narrative); Livy 1.7 (the Hercules-Cacus narrative); Ovid, Fasti 1.543-585; Macrobius, Saturnalia 3.6; the Ara Maxima cult tradition
nodes.object_source: Standard iconography
nodes.animals_source: Hercules's sacred animal: bull (sacrificial — the great bulls offered at the Ara Maxima); lion (his skin)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Virgil; Livy; Macrobius
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Standard iconography — muscular bearded hero in lion-skin with club; identical to Heracles
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Identified with Greek Heracles, but the Italic cult had distinct origins — the Ara Maxima Herculis Invicti at the Forum Boarium was reputedly founded by Evander (the Arcadian who preceded Aeneas in Rome) when Hercules killed Cacus, the cattle-stealing fire-breathing monster of the Aventine (Virgil Aen. 8.184-279; Livy 1.7). The Ara Maxima was Rome's oldest hero-cult, with distinctive practices (tithing, sworn-oath dedications, dietary restrictions — no dogs allowed). Hercules served as patron of generals taking the tithe of war-spoils.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Virgil, Aen. 8.184-279; Livy 1.7; Macrobius, Sat. 3.6
familyRoles: indigenous Italic Ara Maxima cult predates the interpretatio
nodes.birthTypes_source: Standard interpretatio

nodes.name: Aesculapius
nodes.domain: medicine, healing; identified with Greek Asclepius; brought to Rome in 293 BCE from Epidaurus in serpent-form to stop a plague
nodes.domain_source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.622-744 (the central narrative of the snake's arrival on Tiber Island); Livy, Periochae 11; Valerius Maximus 1.8.2
nodes.object: serpent-entwined staff (the Asklepian rod); the temple-snakes (sacred to him on Tiber Island)
nodes.object_source: Standard iconography
nodes.animals_source: Aesculapius's sacred animal: serpent (he himself was brought to Rome in serpent-form; sacred snakes were kept in his temple on Tiber Island and used in healing rituals)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Ovid; Livy
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Aesculapius iconography — bearded mature healer with serpent-staff; identical to Asclepius; sometimes accompanied by his daughter Hygieia
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Identified with Greek Asclepius. In 293 BCE, during a great plague, Rome consulted the Sibylline Books, which directed them to bring Aesculapius from Epidaurus. An embassy went; a great snake (the god in his snake-form) boarded their ship and traveled to Rome; on arrival the snake slithered to Tiber Island where his temple was built. The plague ended. Tiber Island, shaped like a ship, remains a hospital site to this day.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Ovid, Met. 15.622-744; Livy, Periochae 11; Valerius Maximus 1.8.2
nodes.birthTypes_source: Standard interpretatio

nodes.name: Romulus
nodes.domain: founder of Rome (traditional date 753 BCE); first king (r. 753-716 BCE); deified as Quirinus after his disappearance/apotheosis; son of Mars and Rhea Silvia
nodes.domain_source: Livy 1.4-16 (the central source); Plutarch, Romulus (the most detailed surviving biography); Ovid, Fasti 2.381-422 (the foundation), 5.453-484 (the Lemuria etiology); Cicero, De Re Publica 2; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 1-2
nodes.object: spear (later the spear of Romulus on the Palatine — said to have miraculously sprouted into a cornel-tree); the augural lituus (the curved staff used in his auspices)
nodes.object_source: Plutarch, Romulus; Roman tradition
nodes.animals_source: Romulus's associated animals: she-wolf (the lupa that suckled the twins); woodpecker (which also fed them, the picus Martius); vulture (twelve appeared in his auspice contest with Remus)
nodes.characterTrait: founder, warrior, fratricidal (killed Remus), king, apotheosized
nodes.characterTrait_source: Livy; Plutarch
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Romulus iconography — armored warrior-king; sometimes shown with augural staff; the famous Capitoline-Wolf bronze (5th c. BCE Etruscan with Renaissance twins added) shows him and Remus as infants suckling the wolf
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Capitoline Wolf; Roman tradition
nodes.significantEvent: Twin of Remus; sons of Mars and the Vestal Rhea Silvia. Their grand-uncle Amulius (who had usurped his brother Numitor's throne at Alba Longa) had them exposed in a basket on the Tiber; the river carried them to the Lupercal cave where the she-wolf suckled them and the woodpecker fed them; the shepherd Faustulus and his wife Acca Larentia raised them. Killed Amulius and restored Numitor; founded Rome on the Palatine (753 BCE); killed Remus in a quarrel over the auspices/the walls. Ruled 38 years; promoted population by the Rape of the Sabine Women; disappeared in a sudden storm at the Caprae Palus (Livy 1.16) and was deified as Quirinus.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Livy 1.4-16; Plutarch, Romulus; Ovid, Fasti
familyRoles: son of Mars and Rhea Silvia (Vestal)
birthTypes: miraculous (son of Mars by a Vestal)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Livy 1.4; Plutarch
nodes.birthCircumstances: Mars impregnated the Vestal Rhea Silvia (sometimes described as a violation); she gave birth to the twins; Amulius exposed them.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Livy 1.4
nodes.deathCircumstances: Disappeared in a sudden storm at the Caprae Palus while reviewing the army; appeared to Julius Proculus declaring he was now Quirinus.

nodes.name: Remus
nodes.domain: twin of Romulus; co-founder candidate of Rome; killed by Romulus in the famous walls/auspices quarrel
nodes.domain_source: Livy 1.4-7; Plutarch, Romulus; Ovid, Fasti 4.809-862; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 1.85-88
nodes.object: his spear; the unfinished or trampled wall
nodes.object_source: Roman tradition
nodes.characterTrait_source: Livy; Plutarch
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Roman tradition — identical twin of Romulus
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Roman tradition
nodes.significantEvent: Twin of Romulus. Disputed the founding-site with him; in the auspice-contest Romulus saw twelve vultures, Remus six (or Remus first six, then Romulus twelve — the order being disputed). Killed by Romulus in their quarrel — versions vary: he leapt over Romulus's wall in mockery and was killed by Romulus or his lieutenant Celer; or fell in general fighting between their followers (Livy 1.7 acknowledges variant traditions). His death haunted the Roman religious imagination — the fratricidal foundation.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Livy 1.7; Plutarch, Romulus 9-10; Ovid, Fasti 4
familyRoles: son of Mars and Rhea Silvia (Vestal)
killed by Romulus or his men

nodes.deathCircumstances: Killed by Romulus or his lieutenant Celer in the quarrel over the walls — versions vary.

nodes.name: Lares
nodes.domain: household deities — guardian spirits of the family and the home (Lares Familiares); also of crossroads (Lares Compitales), the city (Lares Praestites), the state (Lares Augusti)
nodes.domain_source: Cato, De Agri Cultura; Plautus (the Lar-prologue of Aulularia); Ovid, Fasti 2.583-616 (the etiology of the Lares Compitales); Tibullus 1.10; the household-shrine (lararium) tradition (Pompeii preserves the best examples)
nodes.object: the lararium (household shrine); cornucopia and drinking-horn (the standard Lar iconography); their statuettes
nodes.object_source: Standard iconography (Pompeii lararia)
nodes.animals_source: The Lares are not typically associated with animals; the lararium reliefs sometimes depict a serpent (representing the household-genius)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Cato; Plautus; Ovid
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Lares iconography — youthful dancing figures, paired, in short tunics, with raised drinking-horns and bowls; the famous Lares-statuettes from Pompeii lararia (1st c. CE); their hair-flowing and posture suggest divine dance
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography (Pompeii)
nodes.significantEvent: The Lares were among the most pervasive of Roman household and civic deities. Each home had a lararium where daily offerings were made to the Lares Familiares (the household-guardians). The Lares Compitales were worshipped at crossroads-shrines (the Compitalia festival). Augustus institutionalized the Lares Augusti and Genius Augusti in every district-shrine, creating an empire-wide network linking emperor-worship to local household-religion.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Cato; Plautus; Ovid; Augustan religious reforms
familyRoles: linked to Mania (the Lares-mother in some traditions)
nodes.birthTypes_source: Roman cult tradition

nodes.name: Penates
nodes.domain: guardian deities of the household pantry/storeroom (penus); the di Penates extend to the state-cult (the Penates publici); Aeneas brought the Trojan Penates to Italy
nodes.domain_source: Virgil, Aeneid (especially 2.293-295 and 3.148-152 — the Penates speaking to Aeneas); Cicero, De Natura Deorum 2.67; the Lavinium cult of the Penates publici
nodes.object: the penus (storeroom) of the house; small statuettes in the lararium alongside the Lares
nodes.object_source: Standard iconography
nodes.characterTrait_source: Cicero; Virgil
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Penates iconography — small statuettes alongside Lares in lararia; sometimes paired-deity reliefs
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: The Penates guarded the household's food-store (the penus from which they take their name). They extended to the state-level: Aeneas brought the Trojan Penates to Italy with him (Virgil, Aen. 2.293-295) — they spoke to him at Crete telling him to seek Italy (Aen. 3.148-152); they were eventually housed at Lavinium (the Latin cult-center). The Penates publici were among the central state-cults of Rome, with their own pontifex.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Virgil, Aeneid 2-3; Cicero; Lavinium tradition
nodes.birthTypes_source: Roman cult tradition

nodes.name: Ometeotl
nodes.domain: 'Two God' / 'God of Duality' — the supreme creator-deity as the unified aspect of the male-female duality Ometecuhtli + Omecihuatl; dwells in the thirteenth heaven Omeyocan; the primordial principle from which all other gods emanate
nodes.domain_source: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, *Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España*, 1545-1590); Codex Borgia, Borbonicus, Magliabechiano, Telleriano-Remensis; Codex Chimalpopoca (*Leyenda de los Soles*); Diego Durán, *Historia de las Indias de Nueva España*; Crónica Mexicáyotl (Tezozomoc) — the supreme cosmic principle; Florentine Codex 6.7; the Cantares Mexicanos and Romances de los Señores de Nueva España (which preserve the Nahua-philosophical poetry of Nezahualcoyotl, the 'philosopher-king' of Texcoco, contemplating Ometeotl)
nodes.object: the thirteenth heaven Omeyocan (his/her abode); the cosmic axis
nodes.object_source: Florentine Codex 6.7
nodes.characterTrait_source: Cantares Mexicanos; Florentine Codex
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Rarely depicted directly; often shown as the bisexual creator-pair (Tonacatecuhtli and Tonacacihuatl, or Ometecuhtli and Omecihuatl) in the central panel of the Tonalamatl; in Nezahualcoyotl's philosophical poetry, treated as an abstract cosmic principle transcending image.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Codex Borgia (creator-pair); Nezahualcoyotl's poetry
nodes.significantEvent: The supreme creator-deity in unified-duality aspect. From Ometeotl emanated the four directional creator-deities (the Tezcatlipocas — Black north, Red east, Blue south, White west) who in turn created the cosmos and humanity. Nezahualcoyotl (1402-1472), the 'philosopher-king' of Texcoco, composed extensive Nahua-philosophical poetry contemplating Ometeotl as the abstract supreme being beyond all anthropomorphic representation — a striking parallel to monotheistic-philosophical theology elsewhere.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Cantares Mexicanos; Romances de los Señores; Florentine Codex 6.7
familyRoles: parent of the four directional Tezcatlipocas
nodes.birthTypes_source: Florentine Codex 6.7
nodes.birthCircumstances: Uncreated; the primordial dual-aspect deity from which all others emanated.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Florentine Codex 6.7

nodes.name: Tlaloc
nodes.domain: rain, thunder, lightning, fertility of the earth; second in cult-importance only to Huitzilopochtli; ruler of the fourth heaven Tlalocan (paradise of the drowned and lightning-struck); one of the two co-equal deities of the Templo Mayor at Tenochtitlan
nodes.domain_source: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, *Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España*, 1545-1590); Codex Borgia, Borbonicus, Magliabechiano, Telleriano-Remensis; Codex Chimalpopoca (*Leyenda de los Soles*); Diego Durán, *Historia de las Indias de Nueva España*; Crónica Mexicáyotl (Tezozomoc) — Sahagún Books 1.4, 7.2; Tlalocan-paradise descriptions (Codex Vaticanus A); the Templo Mayor (the Great Pyramid of Tenochtitlan had twin shrines at the top — Tlaloc's on the north side, Huitzilopochtli's on the south)
nodes.object: lightning-axe (the 'lightning-serpent'); jade-water-jars; the four cosmic water-jars (one for each direction, containing different qualities of rain); his characteristic goggle-eye mask
nodes.object_source: Codex Borgia and Magliabechiano; standard Tlaloc iconography
nodes.animals_source: Tlaloc's sacred animals: heron (his attendant); jaguar (in some forms); his Tlaloque (assistants) appear as small water-deities
nodes.characterTrait: rain-giving, life-sustaining, capricious (could send floods or drought), fertility-presiding
nodes.characterTrait_source: Florentine Codex 1.4
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Codex Borgia and Templo Mayor sculpture — distinctive goggle-eyes (large circular eye-rings) and serpent-fang mouth; blue or green body-paint; lightning-serpent in hand; the most-easily-identifiable Mesoamerican deity-icon (goes back to Teotihuacan, c. 200-700 CE — Tlaloc is Aztec-period inheritor of a much older Mesoamerican deity-complex)
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Codex Borgia; Templo Mayor sculpture; Teotihuacan murals
nodes.significantEvent: Co-equal with Huitzilopochtli at the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan (the great pyramid had twin shrines). Husband of Chalchiuhtlicue (his sister-wife). In the Five Suns narrative, was the third sun (ended by fire-rain). Ruler of Tlalocan, the paradise of the drowned, the lightning-struck, and those who died of water-related diseases — the only Aztec paradise other than the warrior-paradise. Children were sacrificed to him on the mountain-tops (the most disturbing aspect of Aztec child-sacrifice was Tlaloc-cult, in which the children's tears were thought to bring rain).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Florentine Codex 1.4, 7.2; Crónica Mexicáyotl
nodes.birthTypes_source: Teotihuacan archaeological record
nodes.birthCircumstances: Pre-Aztec; the Aztec Tlaloc is an inheritor of the much older Mesoamerican rain-god complex (back to Teotihuacan, c. 200 CE), parallel to Maya Chaac.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Mesoamerican archaeological record

nodes.name: Chalchiuhtlicue
nodes.domain: 'She of the Jade Skirt' — goddess of lakes, rivers, springs, fresh water; sister-wife of Tlaloc; patroness of childbirth (the water at birth) and the baptismal ritual
nodes.domain_source: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, *Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España*, 1545-1590); Codex Borgia, Borbonicus, Magliabechiano, Telleriano-Remensis; Codex Chimalpopoca (*Leyenda de los Soles*); Diego Durán, *Historia de las Indias de Nueva España*; Crónica Mexicáyotl (Tezozomoc) — Sahagún Book 1.4; Codex Borgia 16, 65
nodes.object: jade-skirt (her name and emblem); jade-jar of water; spindle (in some depictions)
nodes.object_source: Codex Borgia; standard iconography
nodes.animals_source: Chalchiuhtlicue's sacred animals: serpent (her water-form)
nodes.characterTrait_source: Florentine Codex 1.4
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Codex Borgia — beautiful young woman in jade-decorated skirt of blue-green; sometimes shown with stream of water flowing from her
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Standard iconography
nodes.significantEvent: Sister-wife of Tlaloc. In the Five Suns narrative, she was the fourth sun, whose age ended in a great flood; she warned the righteous couple Tata and Nene who survived by becoming fish. Presided over the Aztec child-water-naming ritual (the closest analog to baptism) — newborns were washed in her name with a ritual prayer commending the child's life to her.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Florentine Codex 6.32, 7.4; Leyenda de los Soles
nodes.eventTypes_source: Florentine Codex; Leyenda de los Soles
familyRoles: fourth sun in the Five Suns
nodes.birthTypes_source: Mesoamerican archaeological record
nodes.birthCircumstances: Pre-Aztec Mesoamerican water-goddess.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Mesoamerican tradition

nodes.name: Coyolxauhqui
nodes.domain: 'She of the Golden Bells' — moon-goddess; sister of Huitzilopochtli and the 400 Centzon Huitznahua; the dismembered moon whose monolith was placed at the foot of the Templo Mayor
nodes.domain_source: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, *Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España*, 1545-1590); Codex Borgia, Borbonicus, Magliabechiano, Telleriano-Remensis; Codex Chimalpopoca (*Leyenda de los Soles*); Diego Durán, *Historia de las Indias de Nueva España*; Crónica Mexicáyotl (Tezozomoc) — Sahagún Book 3.1; the great Coyolxauhqui monolith (Templo Mayor, c. 1473, the most famous excavated Aztec stone)
nodes.object: her cheek-bells (giving her name); her warrior-armor and weapons
nodes.object_source: Coyolxauhqui monolith
nodes.characterTrait_source: Florentine Codex 3.1
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: The Coyolxauhqui monolith — circular stone (3.25m diameter, 8 tons) depicting her decapitated and dismembered body with head, arms, and legs separated, golden bells on her cheeks; placed at the foot of the Templo Mayor pyramid where she fell when Huitzilopochtli threw her down. The monolith was discovered in 1978 during electrical excavation, triggering the modern excavation of the Templo Mayor sacred precinct.
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Coyolxauhqui monolith (Museo del Templo Mayor)
nodes.significantEvent: When Coatlicue miraculously conceived Huitzilopochtli on Coatepec, Coyolxauhqui — ashamed of her mother's apparent dishonor — led her 400 brothers the Centzon Huitznahua to kill Coatlicue. Huitzilopochtli emerged fully-armed from his mother's womb at the last moment and slew Coyolxauhqui, dismembering her and throwing her body down the mountain — the etiology of the moon's lunation (the body's reassembly and dismemberment monthly) and of the moon's distance from earth. Every prisoner sacrificed at the top of the Templo Mayor and rolled down the stairs replayed this primordial event — landing at the foot of the pyramid where the Coyolxauhqui monolith lay.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Florentine Codex 3.1; Templo Mayor archaeological record
nodes.birthTypes_source: Florentine Codex 3.1
nodes.birthCircumstances: Daughter of Coatlicue.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Florentine Codex 3.1
nodes.deathCircumstances: Slain and dismembered by Huitzilopochtli on Mount Coatepec; her body thrown down the mountain.

nodes.name: Mictlantecuhtli
nodes.domain: 'Lord of Mictlan' — lord of the underworld; one of the principal Aztec deities; ruler of the ninth and lowest underworld; co-ruler with Mictlancihuatl
nodes.domain_source: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, *Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España*, 1545-1590); Codex Borgia, Borbonicus, Magliabechiano, Telleriano-Remensis; Codex Chimalpopoca (*Leyenda de los Soles*); Diego Durán, *Historia de las Indias de Nueva España*; Crónica Mexicáyotl (Tezozomoc) — Sahagún Books 1.5, 3.1-2 (the death-realm geography); Codex Borgia 13, 18; the Templo Mayor 'House of the Eagles' Mictlantecuhtli statues

nodes.characterTrait_source: Florentine Codex; Codex Borgia
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Codex Borgia — skeletal anthropomorphic figure, often with eyeballs in his joints, liver hanging from his ribcage, papal-fan headdress of cone-shaped paper, owl-feathers; the famous life-size ceramic Mictlantecuhtli statues from the House of the Eagles at the Templo Mayor have his liver hanging out
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Codex Borgia; House of the Eagles statues
nodes.significantEvent: Lord of Mictlan, the ninth and final underworld. Souls of most dead (those who died normal deaths — not warriors, women in childbirth, or those killed by water) journeyed through nine increasingly-difficult underworld-layers for four years before reaching Mictlantecuhtli's court and being annihilated. Quetzalcoatl famously descended to Mictlan to retrieve the bones of past humanity to create the present (fifth) age; Mictlantecuhtli reluctantly gave them but had Quetzalcoatl pursued by quail who startled him into dropping and breaking the bones (etiology for human-stature differences).
nodes.significantEvent_source: Florentine Codex 3.1-2; Leyenda de los Soles
nodes.eventTypes_source: Florentine Codex 3.1-2; Leyenda de los Soles

nodes.domain: 'Lady of Mictlan' — queen of the underworld; co-ruler with Mictlantecuhtli
nodes.domain_source: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, *Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España*, 1545-1590); Codex Borgia, Borbonicus, Magliabechiano, Telleriano-Remensis; Codex Chimalpopoca (*Leyenda de los Soles*); Diego Durán, *Historia de las Indias de Nueva España*; Crónica Mexicáyotl (Tezozomoc) — Sahagún Book 3.1; Codex Borgia

nodes.name: Tonatiuh
nodes.domain: 'He Goes Forth Shining' — the sun, specifically the fifth sun of the present age; the principal solar-deity; the warrior-paradise (Tonatiuh Ichan, the eastern paradise of dead warriors); the sun who demands blood-sacrifice to continue his daily journey
nodes.domain_source: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, *Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España*, 1545-1590); Codex Borgia, Borbonicus, Magliabechiano, Telleriano-Remensis; Codex Chimalpopoca (*Leyenda de los Soles*); Diego Durán, *Historia de las Indias de Nueva España*; Crónica Mexicáyotl (Tezozomoc) — Sahagún Books 6, 7; the famous Stone of the Sun (also called Aztec Calendar Stone, dedicated 1479 under Axayácatl, now in Museo Nacional de Antropología)

nodes.object_source: Stone of the Sun
nodes.animals_source: Tonatiuh's sacred animals: eagle (the eagle-warriors were his); the rattlesnake of the Stone of the Sun
nodes.characterTrait_source: Stone of the Sun; Florentine Codex 6
nodes.physicalCharacteristics: Stone of the Sun central face — sun-disk with a face emerging, tongue extending as an obsidian sacrificial knife; surrounded by the four previous suns and the cosmic-direction symbols
nodes.physicalCharacteristics_source: Stone of the Sun (1479)
nodes.significantEvent: The current (fifth) sun. According to the Leyenda de los Soles, after the destruction of the fourth sun, the gods gathered at Teotihuacan to choose a new sun. The proud and wealthy Tecuciztecatl volunteered first; the diseased and humble Nanahuatzin also volunteered. They were to throw themselves into the great cosmic fire. Tecuciztecatl approached four times but recoiled from the heat each time; Nanahuatzin threw himself in immediately and became Tonatiuh (the sun). Tecuciztecatl, shamed, then threw himself in and became Metztli (the moon) — but the gods threw a rabbit at his face to dim him, which is why the moon has a rabbit on it.
nodes.significantEvent_source: Leyenda de los Soles; Florentine Codex 7
familyRoles: identified with Nanahuatzin (the diseased god who became him)
presides over the warrior-paradise Tonatiuh Ichan
nodes.birthTypes_source: Leyenda de los Soles
nodes.birthCircumstances: Created when Nanahuatzin threw himself into the cosmic fire at Teotihuacan.
nodes.birthCircumstances_source: Leyenda de los Soles

nodes.name: Metztli
nodes.domain: 'The Moon' — moon-deity; identified with Tecuciztecatl (the moon-god who hesitated at Teotihuacan and became the moon)
nodes.domain_source: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, *Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España*, 1545-1590); Codex Borgia, Borbonicus, Magliabechiano, Telleriano-Remensis; Codex Chimalpopoca (*Leyenda de los Soles*); Diego Durán, *Historia de las Indias de Nueva España*; Crónica Mexicáyotl (Tezozomoc) — Florentine Codex 7.2; Leyenda de los Soles

nodes.significantEvent: At Teotihuacan, when the gods gathered to choose a new sun after the destruction of the fourth age, Nanahuatzin and Tecuciztecatl volunteered. Tecuciztecatl, rich and proud, volunteered first; Nanahuatzin, diseased and humble, also offered himself. When the cosmic fire was lit, Tecuciztecatl approached four times and recoiled. Nanahuatzin threw himself in immediately and emerged as Tonatiuh, the fifth sun. The narrative is the central Aztec moral exemplum of humility-as-glory.

The gods threw a rabbit at his face to dim him; he became Metztli the moon, with the rabbit visible.

nodes.domain: 'Our Revered Mother' — collective title-aspect of the mother-goddess complex (Coatlicue, Cihuacoatl, Tlazolteotl, Teteoinnan); famously the pre-Conquest goddess of Tepeyac, on whose shrine the Basilica of Guadalupe was built (1531)

nodes.significantEvent: Tonantzin was the title under which the great mother-goddess was worshipped at Tepeyac (the hill outside Tenochtitlan). In December 1531 — ten years after the Conquest — an indigenous man named Juan Diego reported a Marian apparition at Tepeyac; the Basilica of Guadalupe was built on the site of the Tonantzin shrine. The continuity between pre-Conquest Tonantzin and post-Conquest Guadalupe is one of the most famous and controversial cases of religious syncretism in the Americas; Sahagún himself remarked on it in Florentine Codex 11 with concern.

news.title: Presenting SHADOWS at the 5th Annual Conference of Computational Literary Studies, Potsdam
news.content:
On May 28th, 2026, the SHADOWS team will present a poster at the 5th Annual Conference of Computational Literary Studies (CCLS) in Potsdam, Germany. The poster, titled "Shadows: A Computational Knowledge Graph of Mythological and Literary Characters for Cross-Cultural Narrative Analysis," introduces the project's framework, methodology, and current corpus to the international computational literary studies community.

  This marks the first public presentation of SHADOWS, only three months after the team began working on the project in earnest. The poster outlines the rationale for modeling mythological and literary figures as nodes in a unified knowledge graph — enriched with attributes such as domain, associated objects and animals, character traits, physical characteristics, narrative events, birth and death types, gender, and family roles — and demonstrates how graph-based methods can reveal structural correspondences across traditions that are difficult to surface through close reading alone.

  We will also discuss the project's mixed-method data acquisition strategy, which combines AI-assisted extraction, structured manual encoding, and collaborative scholarly validation, as well as the multi-phase roadmap that will extend the corpus from mythological figures to canonical fairy tales and global literary fiction.

  CCLS brings together researchers working at the intersection of computational methods and literary scholarship, and we are excited to share SHADOWS with this community, gather feedback on its conceptual and technical foundations, and explore opportunities for collaboration. If you will be in Potsdam, please come find us at the poster session — we would love to discuss the project with you.

news.title: Shadows Alpha Version Released Following February 2026 Hackathon
news.content:
We are pleased to announce that the alpha version of the Shadows platform is now online.

This first functional iteration of the project was completed during a four-day development hackathon held from 24 to 27 February 2026, bringing together members of the core research and technical team. The hackathon focused on implementing the initial graph architecture, integrating the first mythology datasets, and deploying a working prototype of the web interface.

The current alpha release allows users to explore the first network visualizations of mythological entities and archetypal correspondences across traditions. While still under active development, this version establishes the structural and technical foundations of the project and will serve as the basis for future expansions, including database growth, analytical tools, and collaborative research features.

publications.title: Testing the Structure of the Great Mother: A Graph-Theoretical Evaluation of Erich Neumann's Archetypal Model Using Large-Scale Comparative Mythology Data
publications.authors: Laura Duparc, Camille Bertrand, Ami Nagai
publications.abstract: This article evaluates Erich Neumann's structural model of the Great Mother archetype using large-scale graph analysis derived from the Shadows comparative mythology database. Neumann's schema proposes recurrent symbolic proximities among feminine figures across cultures, grouping entities such as Kali and Hecate within destructive or "terrible" maternal domains and Mary or Sophia within nurturing and spiritual domains. We test whether these hypothesized relationships emerge empirically within a relational mythology graph constructed from cross-cultural textual corpora. Using network proximity measures and clustering analysis, the study examines whether figures associated in Neumann's model occupy similar structural neighborhoods in the graph and whether broader archetypal polarities appear as detectable network patterns. The results contribute to ongoing discussions on whether archetypal structures reflect interpretative frameworks or measurable regularities within large-scale mythological data.
